c: Most people expect their own future to go better than the average person's.

In 1980 the psychologist Neil Weinstein asked college students to rate their chances of a list of life events against those of their classmates. They put good things, like a long life or a satisfying job, above average for themselves, and bad things, like a divorce or an illness, below. That can't be right for everyone, since half of any group is at or below the middle. Mild optimism can help you keep going. The risk comes when it makes us skip the insurance, the savings or the doctor's visit.
We are surer of our answers than our accuracy deserves.

Researchers have run a simple test for decades. They ask people questions like "how long is the Nile?" and ask them to give a range they're 90% sure contains the true answer. If people were well calibrated, about nine in ten ranges would hit. In the classic studies, only about half to two-thirds did. People weren't ignorant, they just drew the lines too narrow. The cheap fix is to widen your ranges until they feel uncomfortably wide, then check how often you're right.
Owning something makes you value it more than you did a minute before.

In 1990 Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler tried a neat experiment with coffee mugs. Half the students in a classroom were given a mug and the rest got nothing. Then they traded. The owners wouldn't sell for less than about $7, but the others wouldn't pay more than a little under $3. If it were only about the mug, there'd be plenty of deals. The mug hadn't changed, only who held it, and giving something up hurts more than not having it ever did.
Given a choice, we tend to stay with what we have, even when a change would be better.

When William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser looked at how people chose among options in the late 1980s, they saw a strong pull toward whatever they already had or whatever was marked as the default. At Harvard, long-time employees mostly stayed in their old health plans, while newly hired ones chose the newer plans far more often. Doing nothing feels safe because the current state is the baseline against which everything else looks like a risk. The cost is the better option you never looked at because you didn't have to.
The option that is pre-selected wins far more often than it should.

In some countries you become an organ donor only if you tick a box to opt in. In others you're a donor unless you tick a box to opt out. Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared the two systems in 2003. In Germany, where you opt in, about 12% were registered, and in Austria, where you opt out, it was almost everyone, 99.98%. People didn't suddenly differ in generosity. Most simply went with whatever the form did if they did nothing.
One good trait makes us assume other good traits.

Psychologist Edward Thorndike noticed in 1920 that army officers who rated soldiers on separate traits gave suspiciously similar scores across all of them. A good impression in one area seemed to glow onto everything else. In a later experiment, Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson had students watch a lecturer who was either warm or cold to them. Those who saw the cold version found his accent and mannerisms more irritating. Both groups saw the same man; he just acted differently. They also insisted that liking him hadn't affected their ratings.
We credit ourselves for successes and blame circumstances for failures.

When something goes well, we tend to say it's because of our ability and effort. When it goes badly, we point to bad luck, a hard test or other people. It reverses for others, where we're quicker to blame their character for their failures. Researchers have found this pattern across many kinds of tasks. Some of it may be honest guesswork, since you know your own effort better than anyone's. But part of it clearly protects how we feel about ourselves.
We want to believe people get what they deserve, so we blame victims.

Melvin Lerner got curious about why people blame victims. In a 1966 study with Carolyn Simmons, volunteers watched what looked like a woman being given painful shocks as part of a memory experiment. When they couldn't help, and she seemed to keep suffering, they began to rate her as less likable and less worthy. We like to think the world is fair, so if something bad happened to someone, it can feel safer to believe they somehow earned it.
The more often we see something, the more we tend to like it.

In the 1960s Robert Zajonc showed people a series of made-up words and Chinese-looking characters, some once and some many times. Later he asked which seemed to mean something good. The ones people had seen more often got better ratings, even though no one knew what any of them meant. The effect works without our noticing. It helps explain why familiar songs, brands and faces start to feel likable, and why advertisers repeat themselves so much.
In a list, we remember the first items and the last ones best.

If you read someone a list of twenty words and ask them to write down all they can remember, the result tends to look like a U. People recall the first few words well, probably because they had time to rehearse them into long-term memory. They also recall the last few, which are still sitting in short-term memory. The words in the middle fade. It's why the beginning and end of a talk stick, and why it's wise to put what matters most in one of those spots.
Vague descriptions feel personal when we are told they are about us.

In 1948 Bertram Forer gave his students a personality sketch and said it had been written just for them from a test. Every student actually got the same text, assembled from lines of a newsstand horoscope. Lines like "you have a need for others to like you" and "at times you doubt yourself." They rated how well it described them from 0 to 5, and the average was 4.26. Vague statements that apply to nearly everyone feel personal when we think they're about us.
Holding two clashing beliefs, or acting against a belief, is uncomfortable, so we change one.

Leon Festinger's idea was that holding two conflicting thoughts is uncomfortable, and we work to ease it. In his classic 1959 experiment, people did a very dull task, then were paid either $1 or $20 to tell the next person it was fun. Those paid $1 later rated the task as more enjoyable than those paid $20. The $20 group had a good reason to say something untrue. The $1 group had only the thought "I said it was fun," so some of them quietly decided it must have been.
Rewarding something people already enjoy can make them enjoy it less.

Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett studied preschoolers who liked to draw. Some were promised a "good player" certificate for drawing, some got one as an unexpected surprise, and some got nothing. A week or two later, the children who'd expected a reward spent less time drawing on their own than the others. A reward given for something already enjoyed can turn it into work. We may start to think we're doing it for the prize.
We see links between things that are not really linked.

Loren and Jean Chapman wanted to understand why clinicians kept trusting the Draw-a-Person test. They showed students drawings paired with symptoms, but the pairings were random. The students still reported the same links that the clinicians believed in, such as big eyes going with suspiciousness. It showed that those links were in people's heads, not in the data. When we expect two things to go together, we notice the cases that fit and forget the many that don't.
We avoid information that might be bad news.

Researchers looked at how often investors in Sweden logged in to check their accounts, and found a pattern. After the stock market had gone down, people looked less often than after it had gone up. Avoiding the news felt like avoiding the loss. It's a very human response, but it can be costly. If a bill, a test result or a bank statement is waiting, not looking won't change what it says, and it takes away your chance to respond early.
We prefer to wipe out one risk completely rather than cut a larger total risk by more.

Suppose you can make one hazard vanish entirely or cut a bigger hazard by more than that. Many people prefer the first, because getting to zero feels like a clean win. In surveys on cleaning up hazardous waste sites, Jonathan Baron and colleagues found people did lean toward plans that removed a small risk completely, even if another plan would reduce the total risk by more. The comfort of "none" can steer resources away from where they'd do the most good.
Does a basketball player who has hit several shots in a row become more likely to hit the next?

Basketball fans believe a player who has made several shots in a row is more likely to make the next. In 1985 Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky looked at the data and said no, it was an illusion, and the paper became a famous example of a bias. In 2018 Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo found a subtle statistical error in how the streaks had been counted. When they corrected it, a small real hot-hand effect appeared. A good reminder that even famous findings get revised.
Once you know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it.

In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, then a Stanford student, asked people to tap out the rhythm of a well-known song like "Happy Birthday" on a table, while a listener tried to guess it. The tappers predicted listeners would get half of them. Listeners guessed correctly only about 2.5% of the time. The tappers could hear the tune in their heads and couldn't imagine not hearing it. This is why experts can be poor teachers, and why a first draft often makes sense only to its author.
We treat money differently depending on its label, though a dollar is a dollar.

Richard Thaler suggested that people don't treat money as one big pot, but keep mental accounts with different rules. Kahneman and Tversky made it vivid with two stories. Someone loses a $10 ticket to a play and has to decide whether to buy another, and 46% said they would. Someone else loses $10 in cash on the way in, and 88% still bought a ticket. In both cases they were out $10, but the ticket seemed to belong to the "entertainment" account.
A reward now looks much bigger than the same reward a little later.

Most of us value now more than later, but the odd part is how the discount changes with distance. Someone might take $50 today rather than $100 in a year. Yet that same person, asked to choose between $50 in five years and $100 in six, will usually wait for the larger sum. The gap is the same, but when the first reward is close, it's irresistible. That's why we say we'll start saving or exercising "next month" and rarely do when next month comes.
Most of us think we are better than average at most things.

In 1981 the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson surveyed American drivers and asked how their skill compared with the others in the study. 93% said they were better than the median, which is mathematically impossible, since only half can be above it. The finding has been repeated for intelligence, humor and many other traits. Most of us rate ourselves above average, at least on things we care about, which may help us feel good but doesn't help us improve.
We see bias in other people but think we are fair.

Emily Pronin and her colleagues asked people how susceptible they were to a list of biases, then how susceptible the average American was. People rated themselves as less biased than others. In another part of the study, they were told about a bias, such as the tendency to take credit for good outcomes, and many still felt they were exempt. It's an uncomfortable finding, because knowing about the biases doesn't seem to protect us from them.
We think we see the world as it is, so people who disagree must be uninformed or biased.

Lee Ross and Andrew Ward described a common feeling that we see the world as it is, that reasonable people see it the same way, and that people who disagree must be misinformed, lazy or biased. Everyone feels this way, which means two people can each think the other is the one with the filter. It's a key idea in conflict research. It suggests that when we disagree, a good first question is what the other person has seen or experienced that we haven't.
Hearing a claim again and again makes it feel more true.

In 1977 Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino had people rate how true a series of statements were, over several weeks. The statements they'd seen before were rated as more likely true than new ones, whether they were true or not. A 2015 study by Lisa Fazio and colleagues found it holds even when people actually know better. Hearing something again and again makes it easy to process, and ease can feel a lot like truth.
We assume more people share our views and habits than really do.

In a 1977 study, Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House asked students whether they'd walk around campus for thirty minutes wearing a sandwich board that said "Eat at Joe's." Those who agreed thought most other students would agree too. Those who refused thought most would refuse. Each side saw its own choice as the common-sense one. We use our own views as a sample, and since we tend to know people who think like us, the sample is biased.
Everyone privately doubts a norm but thinks everyone else accepts it.

In the 1990s Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller asked Princeton students how comfortable they felt about the heavy drinking on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average student was. Individually, they were less comfortable than they imagined everyone else to be. Each person assumed they were the odd one out, so nobody said anything, and the norm everyone privately doubted stayed in place. It can happen in classrooms, meetings and families.
People often put in less effort when working as a group.

A French engineer, Max Ringelmann, noticed in the 1880s that people pulling on a rope pulled less hard per person as the group got bigger. In 1979 Bibb Latané and his colleagues tested it with shouting and clapping. They had people make as much noise as they could, either alone or in a group while blindfolded and wearing headphones. Each person was quieter in a group. When effort isn't visible, it's easy to let others carry it.
A false belief can cause the behavior that makes it come true.

The sociologist Robert Merton described in 1948 how a false belief can come true because of the way people respond to it. His example was a bank that was perfectly healthy until a rumor started that it was going to fail. Customers rushed to take out their money, and the bank did fail. The prediction caused the outcome. It works on a smaller scale too, when a teacher who expects less from a student gives them less chance to show what they can do.
Racing hearts get explained away by whatever is nearby.

Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron's 1974 experiment is famous. Men crossing either a high, swaying suspension bridge or a low solid one were met by a female interviewer, who gave them her phone number. The men on the scary bridge were more likely to call, which the researchers suggested was because they mistook the excitement from the heights for attraction. Later studies have had mixed results. Still, the idea that our bodies' signals can be misread is well supported.
A third, worse option can change which of the first two you choose.

Imagine choosing between two options, each better in some way. Add a third that is clearly worse than one of them but not the other. In studies starting with Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto in 1982, people tended to pick the one that made the third look bad. The decoy didn't have to be chosen to do its job. The effect shows up in many tests but not all, and some later studies found it vanishes when the numbers are easy to compare directly.
Too many options can freeze us or leave us less satisfied.

In 2000 Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting table of jam in a grocery store. One day there were 24 kinds, another day 6. More people stopped at the large display, but 30% of the people at the small display bought a jar, compared with 3% at the large one. It became a classic. When researchers pooled many such studies in 2010, the average effect was close to zero, so it seems to happen in some situations and not others.
Expect more from someone and they may deliver more.

In 1968 Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson told elementary school teachers that certain pupils had been identified by a test as likely to bloom intellectually that year. In fact, the pupils had been picked at random. At the end of the year, some of those children, mainly the youngest ones, had gained more on an IQ test. The study was criticized for its methods, but later research has found that teachers' expectations do have a small, real effect.
Fear of confirming a negative stereotype can hurt performance.

In 1995 Claude Steele and Joshua Aronson gave Black and white students difficult verbal questions. When the test was described as measuring intellectual ability, Black students did worse than when it was described as a problem-solving exercise. Steele suggested that worry about confirming a negative stereotype can use up mental effort. Later attempts to repeat it have found weaker and less consistent results, so the size and conditions of the effect are still debated.
Tight-knit groups can drift into agreeing too soon.

Irving Janis studied how smart, capable groups made terrible decisions, including the Kennedy administration's Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961. He argued that when a close group values agreement above all, it silences doubts, assumes it can't fail and ignores outside views. He named the pattern in 1972. Later research has found the model fits some famous failures but not all, and that careful, well-run groups can avoid it. Still, the habit of inviting dissent is wise.
Standing in a confident pose will change your hormones and your behavior.

In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that standing in an expansive "power pose" for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered cortisol and made people more willing to take risks. It spread widely, including in a popular TED talk. A larger replication in 2015 by Eva Ranehill and colleagues found no effect on hormones or on behavior. People did say they felt a bit more powerful. Carney later said she no longer believed the original effects were real.

The idea is that the muscles of your face can influence how you feel. In 1988 Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin and Sabine Stepper had people hold a pen in their teeth, which forces a smile, or with their lips, which blocks one, while rating cartoons. The smilers found them funnier. In 2016, seventeen labs tried to repeat the experiment and found no effect. Researchers still debate whether small effects exist under the right conditions.
Listening to Mozart will make you smarter.

In 1993 Frances Rauscher, Gordon Shaw and Katherine Ky reported that college students who listened to ten minutes of a Mozart sonata did slightly better on a spatial reasoning task. The press turned it into "Mozart makes you smarter," and one US state gave classical CDs to every newborn. The original effect was small and brief. A later review in 2010 concluded that any boost looks like a general effect of mood and alertness from music a person enjoys.
The brain finds faces and patterns in random shapes.

The human brain is tuned to spot faces, and it does so fast, even in clouds, electrical outlets and burned toast. In 1976 the Viking 1 orbiter photographed a mesa in the Cydonia region of Mars that looked like a human face, and it became a sensation. When NASA's later spacecraft took much sharper pictures in 1998 and 2001, the "face" was clearly an ordinary hill. Seeing faces everywhere is an easy mistake for a species that depends on faces.
People are hardly better than chance at spotting lies.

If you've ever thought you can tell when someone is lying, the research isn't encouraging. In 2006 Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo combined 206 studies and found that people correctly judged truth and lies about 54% of the time, only a little better than a coin flip. Police officers, judges and others who do this for a living did no better than students. The signals we think we see, like looking away, turn out not to be reliable.
We start by assuming people are telling the truth.

Tim Levine's research suggests that our tendency to believe others isn't a weakness so much as a reasonable way to live, since most people tell the truth most of the time. Checking everything would make social life exhausting. We normally switch from trust to doubt only when something strongly suggests we should. The downside is that a skilled liar can take advantage of our habit. Thoughtful skepticism means knowing which situations call for checking.
We know we changed a lot in the past, yet expect to stay about the same from now on.

In 2013 Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson surveyed about 19,000 people between 18 and 68. Some were asked how much they'd changed in the past ten years, and others how much they expected to change in the next ten. At every age, people said they'd changed a lot but expected to change little. Yet people ten years older reported more change than the younger ones predicted. We tend to treat who we are now as the finished version.
Attacking the person instead of the argument.

You hear it all the time: "You can't trust his budget plan, he went bankrupt once." Maybe his history is relevant, but whether the plan adds up is a separate question, and you can check the numbers without knowing a thing about the man. The Latin means "to the person." There's one exception worth keeping in mind. If someone has a real conflict of interest, pointing it out is fair, because it gives you a reason to look more closely at what they say.
Misrepresenting an argument so it is easier to knock down.

Someone says the schools in town need more funding, and the reply is, "So you want to bankrupt the country?" That's a straw man: a weaker, sillier version of the claim that's easy to knock over, set up in place of what was actually said. It works because the listener sees an argument being won and doesn't notice it was a different argument. If you catch yourself rebutting a position in its worst form, stop and restate theirs in its best.
Restating the other side's view in its strongest form before you answer it.

If a straw man is an easy version of someone's view, a steelman is the strongest one you can build. The philosopher Daniel Dennett, drawing on the game theorist Anatol Rapoport, suggests rules for criticism. First, restate their position so clearly that they say "I wish I'd put it that way." Second, list what you agree with. Only then say where you disagree. It takes effort, and it tends to make the argument that follows more honest and often shorter.
Treating two options as the only ones when more exist.

"You're either with us or against us" is a famous example of a trap in which a complicated situation is squeezed into two options. In real life there's usually a third: you might agree with some of it, want to wait, or object to the way the choice is framed. When someone offers you an either/or, the useful question is what's missing from the list. Sometimes the best answer is "neither," or "it depends on something you haven't mentioned yet."
Claiming one step will inevitably lead to a disaster without showing the steps between.

The claim goes: if we allow this small thing, the next step will happen, and then the next, until we reach a disaster. Sometimes that's true, and chains of events do happen. It becomes a fallacy when the links are just asserted rather than shown. A fair slope argument has to explain why each step would really lead to the next one, and why nothing could stop it along the way. Without that, it's a worry dressed up as a proof.
Accepting a claim because someone important said it, not because of the evidence.

We can't check everything ourselves, so relying on experts is normal and usually wise. The fallacy lies in leaning on someone's fame instead of their expertise. A celebrated physicist's opinion on nutrition doesn't count for much, and neither does a doctor's on geology. What does carry weight is the agreement of people who study the subject, since several independent experts agreeing is hard to dismiss. Even then, it's strong evidence, not proof, and experts do sometimes revise their views.
The conclusion is already hidden in the premise.

Here's a classic: "The book is true because it says so, and what it says is always true." The conclusion is hidden in the premise, so the argument goes in a circle and never gets anywhere new. It can be hard to spot when the circle is large, with a few steps in between. The older name is "begging the question," which in this use means assuming the thing you're supposed to prove. A good test is to ask whether someone who doubted the conclusion would accept your premises.
"After this, therefore because of this": assuming what came first caused what followed.

The Latin means "after this, therefore because of this." A rooster crows just before sunrise every morning, but nobody thinks the rooster raises the Sun. Yet we make the same mistake all the time. We start a new vitamin and the cold goes away, or we change a setting and the problem stops, so we credit the change. Something happening first is a clue about cause, but only a clue. It could be coincidence, or something else could be causing both.
Redefining a group after a counterexample so the generalization stays safe.

The philosopher Antony Flew gave an example in 1975. A man reads in the paper that a Scotsman did something terrible and says, "No Scotsman would do that." The next day he reads about a Scotsman who did, and answers, "Well, no true Scotsman would do that." The group has been redefined to keep the claim safe. Whenever a generalization faces a counterexample and someone changes the definition instead of the claim, you're probably seeing this move.
Dismissing a criticism because the critic does the same thing.

The Latin is "you too." A doctor who smokes tells a patient to quit, and the patient says, "You smoke, so why should I listen?" The doctor may be a hypocrite, and that may be worth saying. But smoking's dangers don't depend on who delivers the message. The charge of hypocrisy is about the speaker, not the claim. If you notice you're dismissing advice because the person giving it doesn't follow it, ask whether the advice is still correct.
Introducing an irrelevant topic to pull attention away from the point.

You ask a colleague why the report is late, and the answer is a long account of how hard the team has been working this month. All of it may be true, but it doesn't answer the question you asked. A red herring changes the subject to something nearby that feels related and is easier to talk about. You can often spot it by comparing the question with the reply. If the reply wouldn't change when the question did, you're being steered.
Using one word in two different senses within an argument.

A word can have more than one meaning, and an argument can quietly switch between them. "A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark." The first "light" means "not heavy" and the second means "not dark." The argument sounds valid until you notice the word has changed under your feet. It's common in debates over words like "theory," "natural" or "freedom." Asking "what do you mean by that word here?" can unravel it.
The one making the claim must support it; "prove me wrong" shifts the work to the wrong person.

Whoever makes a claim is responsible for supporting it. If a friend says there's a hidden ninth planet in our solar system, it's up to them to show the evidence. It's not up to everyone else to prove there isn't one. "Prove me wrong" quietly flips the burden, and it's a common tactic. It doesn't mean every claim needs a lab study. But the more surprising the claim, the more the person making it has to bring.
You cannot disprove a tiny teapot orbiting the Sun, and that is no reason to believe in it.

In 1952 the philosopher Bertrand Russell wrote that if he said a small china teapot orbits the Sun, between Earth and Mars, too small for any telescope to see, nobody could disprove it. But it would be absurd for him to expect people to believe it on that basis. His point was about the burden of proof. You can't disprove a claim that's built to be unfalsifiable, and that fact doesn't make the claim likely.
Firing at a barn wall, then painting the target around the bullet holes.

Imagine a man who fires shots at the side of a barn, then paints a bullseye around the tightest cluster and calls himself a marksman. That's the fallacy: looking at a lot of data, finding a pattern, and then presenting it as if you'd predicted it. With enough numbers, patterns appear by chance. A pattern is much more convincing if it was named before looking, or if it shows up again in fresh data that wasn't used to find it.
Assuming that natural means good or safe, and artificial means bad.

The idea that natural things are good for you and artificial things are bad sounds sensible, and it sells a lot of products. But arsenic, hemlock and tobacco are all perfectly natural. Vaccines, seat belts and most modern medicines were made by people. Where something comes from tells you little about whether it's safe. The question to ask is what evidence there is for this particular thing, at this dose, for this purpose.
Assuming something is right because it has always been done.

For roughly two thousand years, doctors treated many illnesses by draining blood from patients, and the practice only faded in the nineteenth century. It lasted because it was traditional and because people sometimes got better anyway. That a practice has been done for a long time shows that it's survived, not that it works. Tradition can carry real wisdom, but it needs testing the same way a new idea does.
Treating a claim as true because many people believe it.

For most of history, most people believed the Sun circled the Earth. They were wrong, and the number of believers had nothing to do with the truth. Popular opinion can be a useful clue, because sometimes many people really do know something. But that's the case only when they're independently informed, not just copying each other. How many people believe something can tell you about people. It doesn't tell you about the world.
Using feelings in place of reasons.

A charity commercial with a crying child can move you, and there's nothing wrong with that. But the commercial can't tell you whether the charity actually helps children, how much goes to overhead, or whether the money would do more good elsewhere. Feelings are a fine reason to care and to act. The mistake comes when a feeling stands in for evidence on a question that evidence could settle.
Judging an idea by where it came from instead of whether it is true.

This fallacy is about origins. It judges an idea by where it came from instead of by whether it holds up. A sound argument doesn't become unsound because someone disreputable made it, and a poor one isn't rescued by a prestigious source. The history of an idea can be interesting, and sometimes it points to a reason for caution. But when you want to know if it's true, you have to look at the idea itself.
Assuming what is true of the parts is true of the whole.

Just because every part has a property doesn't mean the whole does. A team of the best players in the league may still play badly together, because what matters is how they fit. Or think of a parade: you can see better by standing up, but if everyone stands, nobody sees any better. What's true for one person acting alone can fail when everyone does it. Check the leap from parts to whole.
Drawing a broad conclusion from a few cases.

You meet two rude people from a small town on one trip and decide the town is full of rude people. Two is too few to say much about a town of thousands. We all do this, because we have to form impressions from limited experience. The remedy is to hold those impressions loosely and to ask how many cases you've seen, and whether they were typical or just the ones that stood out.
Using a personal story to dismiss data.

"My grandfather smoked a pack a day and lived to 95." It's a true story, and it may even be dear to you. But one case can't outweigh studies of millions, because there are always some people who beat the odds. Personal stories are vivid and memorable, and that's exactly why they can feel stronger than they are. Stories are a good way to start asking a question, but a poor way to answer it.
Assuming the truth must lie halfway between two positions.

If one person says the Earth is round and another says it's flat, the truth isn't that it's slightly curved. The middle ground fallacy assumes that when two sides disagree, the right answer must sit halfway between them. Sometimes a compromise is wise, as with splitting a bill. But on factual questions, one side can simply be right, and splitting the difference then just means being half wrong.
Rejecting a solution because it is not perfect.

A seat belt doesn't save everyone in a crash. That's true, and it's no reason to skip it. The nirvana fallacy rejects a good-enough solution because it's not perfect, comparing it to an imaginary ideal instead of to the real alternatives. The useful comparison is between the options you actually have. A policy, a diet or a plan doesn't need to solve everything to be worth doing, only to be better than the alternative.
A question with an assumption built into it.

"Have you stopped cheating on your taxes?" Whether you answer yes or no, you've admitted to cheating. The question has an assumption built into it, and it traps the answerer. A courtroom lawyer might use one on purpose, and it can happen in everyday conversation by accident. The best response is to refuse the premise. You might say, "I haven't cheated on my taxes, so the question doesn't apply," before answering anything else.
Applying a rule to everyone except yourself without a good reason.

Someone says that rules about being on time are important, except in their own case, where they have good reasons. Maybe they do. But special pleading skips the step of showing why this case is different. It's easy to spot in others and hard to spot in ourselves, because our own circumstances always feel unusual to us. A fair test is to ask whether you'd accept the same excuse from someone else.
Changing the standard of proof after it has been met.

Someone says, "Show me one study that proves it." You find one. "Well, I meant a large study." You find a large one. "I meant a randomized trial." Each time the evidence is delivered, the standard shifts. If nothing could satisfy the person, then the question was never really about evidence. A good-faith discussion starts by agreeing on what would change each person's mind, before looking for it.
Discrediting a source in advance so nothing it says will be heard.

Before you've heard a word from a speaker, someone says, "Don't listen to him, he's a liar." That can make everything the person says afterwards sound suspect. Even if the charge were true, though, what he says next still has to be judged on its own. The harm is done in advance, which is why it works. When someone tries to discredit a source before you've heard it, ask for the specific points to check.
Showing only the evidence that supports your side.

Say there are thirty studies on a question and three found an effect. A person who wants you to believe in it cites just those three. Each citation is accurate, but the picture is misleading. Cherry-picking can hide inside honest facts, so it's hard to catch by checking individual claims. The better question is "What does all the evidence say?" That's the reason reviews that pool many studies are worth more than any single one.
Using group-level data to draw conclusions about individuals.

Looking at countries, you might find that places with higher average income also have higher rates of some disease. It's tempting to conclude that richer people get the disease more. But within each country the wealthy could actually be healthier. A pattern across groups doesn't have to hold for the individuals in them. Statistics about averages describe populations, and they can mislead when we apply them to a single person.
Confusing "how likely is this evidence if innocent" with "how likely is innocence given this evidence".

In 1999 Sally Clark, a British solicitor, was convicted of murdering her two baby sons, who had died suddenly. A pediatrician told the court that the chance of two such deaths in one family was 1 in 73 million. The number was wrongly calculated, and it also confused two different questions: how rare the evidence is if she were innocent, and how likely she is to be innocent given the evidence. Her conviction was overturned in 2003.
Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or the reverse.

"Nobody has shown that ghosts don't exist, so they must." The lack of proof against something isn't proof for it. You can reverse it as well: "No one has proven it's real, so it isn't." There's a subtle exception. If you've searched properly in the places where evidence would show up, and found none, that absence does count for something. A thorough search that finds nothing is informative. An absence of looking isn't.
"I can't imagine how this could be true, so it isn't."

"I just can't imagine how that could be true, so it can't be." The limit of one person's imagination isn't a law of nature. Quantum mechanics is hard to picture, and so is the size of the universe, or how a single cell becomes a human. They are all true anyway. Finding something hard to believe is a signal to learn more, and to check, but it isn't a reason to conclude that the claim is wrong.
Answering a criticism with a different one.

Someone criticizes one action, and the reply is "But what about when your side did it?" It shifts the discussion from the topic to the other person's record. Both things might be wrong, or one might be worse, or they might be quite different. Pointing at someone else's fault doesn't make the first complaint go away. If you hear it, you can say, "Maybe so, and we can talk about that too. Right now, we're discussing this."
Treating two things as equal when they differ greatly in size or kind.

Two things are described as the same because they share one feature, though they differ enormously in scale or kind. Treating a small slip and a deliberate fraud as equivalent because both are "mistakes" is an example. The comparison hides the difference that matters most. A good check is to ask how they compare in size, intent and consequences, not just whether the same word applies.
Deciding a claim is false because someone argued for it badly.

Imagine someone argues for a true conclusion with a bad argument. You point out the flaw. Did you just prove that the conclusion is false? No. A bad argument for something doesn't make it untrue. It only means that this particular reasoning doesn't establish it. Someone can be right for the wrong reasons. The fair response is to say the argument fails, then look for better evidence on both sides.
Assuming something is better because it is new.

A new treatment, gadget or idea is sometimes sold on being new alone, as if newer meant better. Newness tells you nothing about quality. Many new things are improvements and many aren't. The old way might be old because it works. The right test is the same one used for anything else: what's the evidence that it works, and compared with what?
Deciding what is true by what you wish were true.

"There has to be an afterlife, or life would be pointless." That moves from how we'd like things to be to how they are. Wanting an answer to be true, or fearing what follows if it's false, tells us nothing about whether it's correct. The world doesn't owe us comfortable facts. It can be a tough habit to notice, since the wish feels like a reason, and it's worth asking what the evidence says if you set the wish aside.
"If P then Q. Q. Therefore P."

The pattern goes: if it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. Therefore it rained. It sounds right, but a sprinkler, a street-cleaning truck or a burst pipe would also leave a wet street. The "if" gave one route to a result, and the result can have many causes. Doctors, detectives and scientists all have to watch for this one. Seeing the effect doesn't tell you which cause produced it.
"If P then Q. Not P. Therefore not Q."

"If you study, you'll pass. You didn't study, so you won't pass." That doesn't follow, because you might pass anyway: the test could be easy, or you could already know the material. The "if" described one way to reach the outcome, not the only way. It's the mirror image of affirming the consequent, and it's just as easy to slip into when you're thinking fast.
If P then Q, and P, so Q: the basic valid pattern.

This is the basic pattern of valid reasoning. "If it's raining, the ground is wet. It's raining. Therefore the ground is wet." If both of the first two statements are true, the conclusion has to be true. Logic calls an argument valid when its conclusion follows from its premises, whether or not the premises are actually true. The Latin means "the way that affirms." Nearly all everyday deduction runs on it.
If P then Q, and not Q, so not P: the logic of disproof.

The pattern here runs backward: "If the theory is right, the planet will appear at this spot. It didn't. So the theory is wrong." It's the logic of disproof, and Karl Popper built his picture of science on it. A theory can never be completely proven by confirming cases, but one clear failure can sink it. It explains why scientists look hard for results that would contradict their ideas.
Valid: the conclusion follows from the premises. Sound: it is valid and the premises are actually true.

"All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. Therefore penguins can fly." The reasoning is valid, meaning the conclusion follows if the premises are true. But the first premise is false, so the argument isn't sound. A sound argument is valid and also has true premises. When you check an argument, you have to ask two questions: does the conclusion follow, and are the starting facts correct?
Deduction guarantees its conclusion; induction only makes it likely.

Deduction guarantees its conclusion if the premises are true: all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal. Induction only makes a conclusion likely: the Sun has risen every day so far, so it will probably rise tomorrow. Most of science and daily life runs on induction, because we can rarely be certain. It's the reason that we talk about evidence building up, not proof. And one surprising case can overturn an inductive rule.
A claim is scientific only if some possible observation could show it to be wrong.

In 1934 the philosopher Karl Popper suggested that what makes a claim scientific is that it could, in principle, be shown wrong by some observation. A theory that fits whatever happens, like a horoscope, doesn't say much. Philosophers still argue about exactly where to draw the line, but the habit it teaches is useful. Ask yourself what result would change your mind, and if the answer is nothing, then notice that.
What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.

Christopher Hitchens, the writer, put it this way in 2007: what can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence. It places the burden on the person making a claim, and it gives you permission not to take a bare assertion seriously. It's a rule of thumb, though. Dismissing something doesn't prove it false. It just means you've no reason yet to believe it, which is a different thing.

Carl Sagan popularized the idea that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. The more a claim conflicts with what we already know, the stronger the evidence needs to be. If your neighbor says he has a dog, you'd accept that easily. If he says he has a dragon in the garage, you'd want to see it. It isn't a bar set to be impossible. It's a way of matching your trust to how surprising the claim is.
Making a position look silly instead of answering it.

Someone describes an opposing idea in a cartoonish way, and the audience laughs. A laugh isn't a rebuttal, though, and a funny version of an idea isn't the idea. Many true ideas were laughed at at first, including continental drift, which was mocked for decades before the evidence won. Be cautious when mockery has replaced an argument, especially when you find yourself enjoying it.
Rejecting an idea because a disliked person or group also holds it.

"Hitler liked dogs, so liking dogs is bad." It sounds absurd, but the same move is made in subtler ways all the time: rejecting an idea because a disliked person or group believes it. A claim stands or falls on its own evidence, no matter who else agrees with it. A stopped clock is right twice a day, and even a villain can be right about the weather.
Assuming someone is wrong and then explaining their mistake by their motives.

C. S. Lewis named this one, after an invented person called Ezekiel Bulver. Bulver, at the age of five, hears his mother say to his father, "Oh, you say that because you are a man." Bulver realizes that you can dismiss anything by explaining why the person says it. Lewis's point was that you must first show a claim is wrong. Only then does it become interesting to ask why someone believed it.
Vague phrases that sound like evidence but commit to nothing.

"Studies show," "many experts agree," "some people say." These phrases sound like evidence while committing to nothing. Which studies? How many experts, out of how many? Who are the "some people"? If the writer can't name them, then nothing has really been claimed that you can check. They're common in advertising and in news headlines, and a good habit is to ask who exactly is being referred to.
Defending a modest claim when challenged, then acting as if a bolder one was proven.

In medieval castles, the motte was a fortified hill you could retreat to, and the bailey was the more comfortable but harder-to-defend courtyard. In arguments, the bailey is the bold claim someone really wants to make, and the motte is a modest, easy-to-defend claim they fall back on when challenged. Once the challenge passes, they go back to the bold one. If someone keeps switching, ask which claim they're actually defending.
Overwhelming an opponent with so many weak points that none can be answered in time.

It's named for the debater Duane Gish, who would fire off a rapid string of weak arguments, so many that his opponent couldn't answer them all in the time available. It works because it takes much longer to refute a claim than to make one. In a long list, unanswered points can look like points conceded. A sensible response is to pick the two or three strongest and handle those properly, or to say the list can't be fairly answered at that speed.
Treating real life as a casino where the odds are known.

Nassim Taleb coined this term, from the Latin for "game," in his 2007 book The Black Swan. It's the mistake of treating real life as if it were a casino, where the odds are known and the rules are fixed. Neat probability models are built on assumptions, and the real world can break them. The risks that hurt most are often the ones nobody put in the model. A model is a good tool for thinking, and a poor guarantee.
We turn random events into a neat story with causes.

After a company succeeds, we tell a story about the founder's grit and vision, and it all seems to fit together. The story is tidy, and it feels like an explanation. But luck may have done much of the work, and the same story could be told about the founders who failed. Taleb warned us to be careful of stories that explain too neatly. A good one makes you feel you understand, and that feeling isn't evidence.
Two numbers can move together by pure coincidence.

The author Tyler Vigen collects charts of numbers that move together by pure chance. One of them shows that per-person cheese consumption in America tracked, over ten years, the number of people who died tangled in their bedsheets. The match is striking and it means nothing. If you compare enough data sets, some will line up by accident. A correlation needs a plausible reason, and ideally a repeat on new data, before it means anything.
Break a problem down to what is surely true, then build up from there instead of copying how it is usually done.

Aristotle described a first principle as "the first basis from which a thing is known": something you can't break down any further. The habit is to ask what you actually know to be true about a problem, set aside what everyone assumes, and build your answer up from there. Most of us reason by analogy, copying what others do with small tweaks. That's usually fine and efficient. When you're stuck, though, going back to the basics is how you find options that no one else was looking at.
Solve a problem backward: ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid that.

The mathematician Carl Jacobi used to say "invert, always invert," meaning that a hard problem can often be solved by turning it around. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure and then avoid it. The investor Charlie Munger loved this approach and liked to quote the line "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there." It's simple, and it works well for decisions where the ways to fail are easier to list than the ways to win.
Ask "and then what?" about the consequences of the consequences.

The first effect of a choice is usually easy to see. The second effect, which is what happens after that, is the one people miss. In 1902, the French colonial government in Hanoi tried to fight rats by paying a bounty for each rat tail. Some people started breeding rats for the money, and others cut off tails and let the rats go. The rat problem grew. Before acting, ask yourself "and then what?" at least twice.
When two explanations fit the facts equally well, test the simpler one first.

When two explanations account for the facts equally well, try the simpler one first. William of Ockham was a 14th-century English friar, though the popular wording about not multiplying "entities" came later. It's worth remembering what the razor is not. It isn't a law of nature, and the world isn't always simple. It's guidance about where to begin looking. The simple explanation is usually quicker to test, and if it fails, you can move on to a more complicated one.
Do not blame malice for what carelessness or confusion explains.

The advice is not to blame malice for what can be explained by carelessness, distraction or confusion. A friend doesn't answer your message, and a colleague sends a curt email. It's very tempting to assume the worst, but far more often they're busy, tired or didn't realize how it would read. The saying appeared in print in 1980 in a book of Murphy's Law variations, credited to a Robert Hanlon. It tends to save relationships a lot of unnecessary grief.
Before you tear down a fence, find out why it was put up.

In 1929 the writer G. K. Chesterton gave a little parable. Imagine you come across a fence across a road, and you can't see any reason for it. A reformer says, "Let's clear it away." A wiser reformer says, "If you don't see the use of it, I certainly won't let you clear it away. Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it." The point isn't that nothing should change, but that you should understand why something exists before you remove it.
The true cost of something is the best alternative you gave up for it.

The true cost of something isn't only the price you pay, but the best alternative you gave up to get it. The French economist Frédéric Bastiat made the point in 1850 with an essay about "what is seen and what is not seen." We notice what a purchase gets us. We rarely notice what the same money or the same hour would have done somewhere else. Asking "instead of what?" is a small habit that changes a lot of decisions.
Leave a buffer for what you cannot foresee.

When engineers design a bridge, they don't build it to carry exactly the load they expect. They build it to carry several times that, because the future always holds surprises. The investor Benjamin Graham borrowed the idea for his book The Intelligent Investor in 1949. He advised buying only when a price is well below what you think a thing is worth. It applies to ordinary life too: leave extra time for the trip, extra money in the account, and extra room in the schedule.
Know the edge of what you truly understand and stay careful beyond it.

Everyone understands some things well and others hardly at all. Warren Buffett has said that what matters isn't how big your circle of competence is, but how well you know where it ends. Most expensive mistakes happen just outside the edge, where we know enough to feel confident and not enough to be careful. A useful habit is to say plainly, "That's outside what I know," and to find someone who knows it when the stakes are high.
The map is not the territory
A model of reality is a simplification, and it can mislead if mistaken for the real thing.

In 1931 the scholar Alfred Korzybski pointed out that a map isn't the land it describes. A subway map is very useful precisely because it leaves out almost everything: the real distances, the streets above, the hills. But try to find a particular building with it and you'll see how little it tells you. Every model, chart, theory and statistic is a map. It helps you think. It goes wrong when you forget that there's a real, messier world behind it.
A small share of causes often produces most of the results.

Around 1896 the economist Vilfredo Pareto noticed that roughly 80% of the land in Italy was owned by about 20% of the people. The 80/20 split isn't a law, and the real numbers vary. The lasting lesson is that outcomes are often unevenly spread. A handful of customers, bugs or tasks can account for most of the results, so it helps to find which ones.
For ideas and books, the longer something has lasted, the longer it may keep lasting.

The idea, popularized by Nassim Taleb, is that for things that don't age like living creatures, such as books, ideas and technologies, the longer they've survived, the longer they're likely to last. A book that has stayed in print for a hundred years is a better bet to still be read in another hundred than this week's bestseller. Time acts as a filter. It's a rough rule, and it doesn't apply to people or to things that wear out.
Get a rough answer by breaking a question into pieces you can guess.

The physicist Enrico Fermi was known for getting reasonable answers to questions that seem impossible. A classic example is: how many piano tuners work in Chicago? You guess the city's population, the share of households with a piano, how often a piano gets tuned, and how many tunings one person can do in a day. Each guess may be off, but the errors tend to partly cancel. The answer usually lands within a factor of two or three, which is often good enough to decide something.
A rare event with huge impact that we explain as obvious only after it happens.

For centuries Europeans took it for granted that all swans were white, because every swan they'd ever seen was. Then in 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh saw black swans in Western Australia. Nassim Taleb uses the phrase for rare, high-impact events that nobody expected and that we then explain as if they'd been obvious all along. It's a warning about how much weight to put on a record of calm. One surprise can overturn thousands of ordinary days.
Some things gain from shocks: muscles, bones, immune systems.

Some things are fragile and break under stress. Others are robust and just hold up. Nassim Taleb's word "antifragile" describes things that get stronger when they're stressed, like muscles under a workout, bones under load, or immune systems exposed to germs. It's a helpful way of looking at systems, including our own habits. As a full scientific theory it's more a framework than something tested in detail, but the main idea, that some stress is useful, rings true in many places.
A small dose of a stressor can help, while a large dose harms.

Many things are harmful in large amounts and beneficial in small ones, a pattern called hormesis. Exercise is an example: a moderate workout makes you stronger, while too much breaks you down. Some researchers suggest fasting and sun exposure follow the same curve. In toxicology, scientists still debate whether low doses of things like poisons or radiation can actually help. So the idea is well supported in some areas, and still argued over in others.
Actions have effects nobody planned or wanted.

In 1936 the sociologist Robert Merton published a short paper listing why actions so often have effects nobody planned. He pointed to ignorance of how things interact, mistakes in analysis, and what he called the "imperious immediacy of interest," meaning that people focus on the short term. Policies, products and personal decisions all show it. The takeaway isn't to avoid acting, but to spend a little time on the second and third effects, and to try things small before scaling them.
Work expands to fill the time available.

"Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that line in a humorous 1955 essay in The Economist. He had noticed that the British Admiralty kept adding administrators even as the navy shrank. It rings true on a smaller scale. A task you're given a week for tends to take a week, though it might have taken an afternoon. A shorter deadline sometimes gets the same job done with less fuss.
It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter's law into account.

Douglas Hofstadter wrote in his 1979 book Gödel, Escher, Bach: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law." He was describing how long it would take computers to play chess at a high level. The joke is a recursion, but it reflects a serious habit known as the planning fallacy. Our estimates are usually too hopeful. A good rule is to pad your first guess, then look at how long similar jobs have actually taken.
Adding people to a late software project makes it later.

Fred Brooks managed the huge IBM System/360 software project, and in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month he wrote that adding people to a late software project makes it later. New people have to be taught, which takes time from the people who already know the work. And every extra person adds more lines of communication. As he put it, nine women can't make a baby in one month. Some work simply can't be divided up.
In a hierarchy, people tend to be promoted until they reach a job they can't do well.

In 1969 Laurence Peter, an educator, wrote a funny book arguing that people in an organization get promoted for doing well until they reach a job they can't do well, and there they stay. In 2019 economists studied sales data on 53,000 workers at 214 firms and found a version of it. Companies tended to promote the best salespeople into management, where selling skills matter little. Good performance in one role doesn't guarantee it in the next.
Each extra unit of effort or money adds a little less than the last.

The first hour of study usually teaches you a lot. The tenth hour of the same day teaches far less. Each extra unit of effort, money or time tends to add a bit less than the one before. The French economist Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot described it for farming in 1767: extra labor on a given plot yields smaller and smaller extra crops. It's a good reason to stop polishing at some point and to spread your effort across more than one thing.
Choose the rules of a society as if you did not know who you would be in it.

The philosopher John Rawls proposed a thought experiment in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice. Imagine you're designing the rules of a society, but you don't know who you'll be in it: rich or poor, healthy or sick, talented or not, any race or gender. Rawls argued you'd then choose rules that are fair to everyone, since you could end up anywhere. It's a handy test for any rule. Would you still endorse it if you didn't know which side of it you'd be on?
Would you pull a lever to divert a runaway trolley, killing one person to save five?

A runaway trolley is heading toward five people on a track. You can pull a lever to divert it to a side track where it will kill one person instead. Philippa Foot posed the puzzle in 1967, and in 1976 Judith Jarvis Thomson added a version where you'd have to push a large man off a footbridge to stop it. Most people say they'd pull the lever and won't push the man, though the numbers are the same. Philosophers still argue about why.
If every plank of a ship is replaced, is it still the same ship?

The Greek writer Plutarch told of the ship in which the hero Theseus sailed home to Athens. The Athenians kept it for centuries, and as planks rotted they replaced them with new ones. Eventually every plank had been replaced. Was it still the same ship? It's a puzzle about what makes something the same thing over time. Your own body is a version of it, since most of your cells are replaced over the years, and you still feel like you.
Rules for testing claims: get independent confirmation, consider alternatives, and welcome tests that could prove you wrong.

In his 1995 book The Demon-Haunted World, Carl Sagan gave readers a toolkit for spotting bad arguments. It includes seeking independent confirmation of the facts, considering more than one hypothesis, and asking whether a claim could in principle be proven false. One of his tips is to avoid getting too attached to a hypothesis just because it's yours. He thought the tools should be used on yourself as well as on others, since the first person you're most likely to fool is you.
Arguing the other side on purpose to test an idea.

The phrase comes from a real job. When the Catholic Church was considering someone for sainthood, it appointed an official called the advocatus diaboli, who had to argue against the case and look for flaws. The role was ended by Pope John Paul II in 1983. The idea is still useful. Before a big decision, ask someone to argue the opposite on purpose. If the plan survives a serious attack, you can trust it more, and if it doesn't, you've saved yourself a lot of trouble.
Assigning a team to attack your plan to find where it breaks.

A red team is a group whose job is to attack your plan, system or idea to see where it breaks. Militaries use them in war games, and companies use them to test their security by trying to break in. The reason it works is that the people who built something are blind to its flaws, because they know how it's supposed to work. It helps to hire a friendly skeptic. You can use a small version of it at home: ask someone to find the three biggest holes in your plan.
A short list of steps can prevent errors that experts still make.

Experts make mistakes, not because they don't know enough but because complicated jobs have too many steps to hold in your head. In 2006 a team at Johns Hopkins introduced a simple five-step checklist for inserting central lines in Michigan intensive care units, covering things like washing hands and cleaning the skin. Within three months, the median rate of line infections fell from 2.7 per 1,000 catheter-days to zero. A short list can beat expertise alone.
Sort tasks by urgent and important; do, schedule, delegate or drop.

President Eisenhower, in a 1954 speech, quoted a college president who had said, "The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent." From that, people built a simple grid for sorting tasks into urgent or not, and important or not. The most valuable box is the one for things that matter but have no deadline, like your health, your relationships and your long-term work. They're the easiest to put off, because nothing pushes you to do them.
Write down what you decided and why, before you know how it turned out.

Before you know how something turned out, write down what you decided, what you expected, and why. It takes a few minutes. Later, when the result is in, you can separate your reasoning from your luck. You also can't tell yourself that you knew it all along, because the page says otherwise. It works directly against hindsight bias. Over months it shows you the kinds of decisions you tend to get right and the ones where you're too sure.
Judging a decision by its outcome rather than by how well it was made.

The poker player Annie Duke uses the word "resulting" for judging a decision purely by how it turned out. A sensible bet can lose, and a reckless one can win. If you only look at results, you'll learn the wrong lessons: you'll repeat a lucky blunder and abandon a good plan after one bad break. A better question is "given what I knew then, was it a good decision?" That's harder to answer, but it's the one that actually helps you improve.
Take the first option that is good enough instead of searching for the best.

In 1956 the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon pointed out that people rarely find the best option. They find one that is good enough and stop. He called that satisficing, a blend of "satisfy" and "suffice." Later, Barry Schwartz and colleagues found that people who try to find the best, whom they called maximizers, often feel less satisfied with their choices and more regret. Not every study agrees, but "good enough" is often a wise place to stop.
Ask how you will feel about a choice in 10 minutes, in 10 months and in 10 years.

When you're stuck on a decision, imagine how you'll feel about it in ten minutes, ten months and ten years. The writer Suzy Welch popularized the method in 2009. It pulls your attention out of the heat of the moment. The urge to send an angry message may feel overwhelming in ten minutes, and in ten months it may seem trivial. The choice between two job offers might look different over ten years. It's a quick way to check your priorities.
Move fast on decisions you can undo, slowly on the ones you cannot.

In a letter to shareholders, Jeff Bezos described two kinds of decisions. Some are one-way doors, which are hard or impossible to undo. Others are two-way doors: if you walk through and don't like it, you can go back. Most decisions are the second kind, and they can be made quickly, with less than complete information. Save your slow, careful thinking for the one-way doors, and try not to treat every choice as though it were permanent.
Different experts, or the same one on different days, give different answers to the same case.

We usually think about bias, which is when judgments are off in the same direction. Noise is something different: scatter, when different people, or the same person on different days, make different calls on identical cases. In a study at an insurance company, underwriters were asked to price the same case. Their quotes differed by 55% on average, and the executives had expected around 10%. The cost of that scatter is large, and it's hard to see, since each person only sees their own judgment.
The average of many independent guesses is often better than most individual guesses.

In 1907 the statistician Francis Galton visited a fair where people guessed the weight of an ox. He collected the 787 entries and found that the middle guess, 1,207 pounds, was within a percent of the true weight of 1,198. The crowd was better than almost any individual. It works under certain conditions: people have to guess independently and bring different information. If they copy each other, or a loud voice sways the room, the effect disappears.
Estimate by looking at how similar cases turned out, not just at the details of yours.

When we plan a project, we naturally focus on its details and how things will go this time. Daniel Kahneman and Dan Lovallo called that the inside view. The outside view asks a different question: how did similar projects turn out? Bent Flyvbjerg's research on large infrastructure projects found that most go over budget and take longer than planned. So before you trust your own timeline, look up how long comparable jobs have really taken.
Some people predict events well because of how they think, not because they know more.

The political scientist Philip Tetlock ran forecasting tournaments in which thousands of ordinary people predicted world events. A small group did consistently better than the rest, and better than many experts. They weren't geniuses. They broke big questions into smaller ones, thought in probabilities rather than yes or no, and updated their views as evidence came in. The skill seems to come from habits of thinking, and it can be learned.
A way to measure how good probability forecasts are.

How do you grade a weather forecaster who says "70% chance of rain"? If it rains, were they right? If it doesn't, were they wrong? The meteorologist Glenn Brier devised a score in 1950 that fixes this. Over many forecasts, a person who says 70% should be right about seven times in ten. The score rewards being well calibrated, and it punishes being very sure and wrong. It's a standard tool for judging forecasts of all kinds.
Ninety percent of everything is rubbish.

The science fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon is said to have been told, in the 1950s, that ninety percent of science fiction is crud. His reply was that ninety percent of everything is crud. It's a joke, and also a useful reminder. When you judge a whole field by its average, you'll be disappointed. Judge it by its best, and you'll find what draws people to it. The same goes for books, movies, music and even your own ideas.
People give the most attention to the issues they understand best, which are often the least important.

C. Northcote Parkinson imagined a committee with a short agenda. It approves a huge nuclear reactor in a couple of minutes, since few members understand it well enough to object. Then it spends an hour arguing about the bicycle shed, because everyone has an opinion on that. People devote most attention to the matters they feel competent about, which are often the least important. In a meeting, it's worth asking whether the time spent matches the stakes.
Interpret others in the most sensible way their words allow before you reply.

When you're about to disagree with someone, first read their words in the most sensible way they allow. Philosophers use the principle so that they argue against the strongest version of a view, not a weak one. Neil Wilson named it in 1959, and Donald Davidson developed it. It also saves a lot of needless fights in ordinary life. Assume the person is reasonable until the evidence shows otherwise, and you'll often find they meant something different from what you first heard.
The range of ideas the public will accept at a given time.

Joseph Overton was a policy analyst at a think tank in Michigan. He observed that at any time there is a range of ideas the public will accept as reasonable, and that politicians generally stay inside it. Ideas outside the window seem too extreme. The window shifts over time, and activists often work by pushing at its edges so what was unthinkable becomes debated. It's a helpful way of seeing why some policies are discussed and others aren't.
If all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

If the only tool you have is a hammer, it's tempting to treat everything as if it were a nail. Abraham Kaplan wrote in 1964 that "give a small boy a hammer, and he will find that everything he encounters needs pounding." Experts do the same: the person trained in one method tends to see problems that method can solve. It's worth asking, when you're stuck, what other tools exist, and whether you picked this one because it fits or only because it's the one in your hand.
Looking for something where it is easy to look, not where it probably is.

A man is on his hands and knees under a streetlight looking for his keys. A passerby asks where he lost them. "Over there in the park," he says, "but the light is better here." We do something like it all the time. Researchers measure what's easy to measure, managers track what's easy to count, and we look for answers where it's convenient. If you notice that you're searching where it's easy, ask whether the thing you want is probably somewhere else.
Copying the forms of science without its honesty.

In a 1974 commencement speech at Caltech, Richard Feynman described islanders in the South Pacific who, after the war, built runways and wooden control towers and waited for cargo planes, as the military had done. They copied the form of what they'd seen and none of the substance, so no planes came. He said some research is like that. It looks like science but lacks a kind of utter honesty, including reporting anything that might show you're wrong.
You are the easiest person to fool
The first rule of science is not to fool yourself.

In the same 1974 Caltech speech, Richard Feynman said: "The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool." It's the heart of how he thought science should work. You have to be harder on your own ideas than you'd be on anyone else's, because you want them to be true. In practice, that means looking for how you might be wrong first, and being glad when you find out.
Memorize a list by placing each item in a familiar place, then mentally walking through the place.

Greek and Roman speakers who had to deliver long speeches with no notes used this trick, and it's still the one memory champions rely on. You pick a place you know well, like your house, and place each thing to remember at a spot along a route through it, ideally as a vivid, odd image. To recall the list, you walk the route in your mind. In a 2017 study, people trained for six weeks went from remembering about 26 of 72 words to about 62.
Grouping items into meaningful units lets you hold more in mind at once.

Working memory can only hold a few items at once, so the trick is to make each item bigger. A phone number grouped as 555-0142 is easier than seven loose digits. In a classic study, chess masters could recall the pieces on a board from a real game far better than beginners, but they were no better with pieces placed randomly. They weren't remembering more pieces. They were seeing familiar patterns, and each pattern counted as one item.
Words together with a picture give memory two routes in.

In 1971 the psychologist Allan Paivio proposed that we store words and pictures in two linked systems. If you learn something both ways, you've got two routes back to it. That's why it helps to sketch a diagram of what you've read, or to picture an idea, instead of only rereading the words. The picture doesn't need to be good. Making it forces you to think about what the thing means, which is half the benefit.
Thinking about meaning makes a stronger memory than noticing how something looks or sounds.

In 1975 Fergus Craik and Endel Tulving showed people words and asked one of three kinds of question: does it appear in capitals, does it rhyme with something, or does it fit in a sentence? Later, those who had thought about meaning remembered far more words than those who had only looked at the letters or the sound. The deeper you think about what something means, the better it sticks. Rereading is shallow, and explaining is deep.
We remember what we link to ourselves better than what we link to others.

A 1977 study asked people to judge words in different ways. One question was "Does this word describe you?" The people who had asked themselves that question later remembered more of the words than those who had asked about the word's meaning, or whether it described someone else. Linking new information to your own life is a strong aid to memory. When you study, ask yourself how an idea connects to something you've lived or done.
A memory is easiest to retrieve when the cues at recall match those at learning.

Endel Tulving and Donald Thomson found in 1973 that memory works best when the situation at recall resembles the situation at learning. In their experiments, a cue word that was present when someone learned a word helped them recall it better than a strong cue they hadn't seen before. It suggests that you should practice under conditions like the test. Studying while sitting at a desk, with silence, may serve you better than studying lying on a couch if the exam is in a quiet room.
Do you recall better in the place where you learned?

In 1975 Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley had scuba divers learn lists of words either on a beach or underwater, then recall them either in the same place or in the other one. The divers did better when they were in the same setting where they'd learned. It sounds appealing, but later attempts to repeat it have found the effect is small and doesn't always show up. It's more reliable when the place actually shapes what you were thinking about at the time.
Recalling one memory can make related ones harder to recall.

Practicing some of what you know can make you worse at related things you didn't practice. In a 1994 experiment, Michael Anderson and colleagues had people practice recalling some items from a category, like fruits. Later they were worse at remembering the other fruits than they were at items from categories they hadn't practiced at all. The idea is that when your mind picks one memory, it suppresses its competitors. It's a reason to review all the material, not just the parts you find easy.
Information that arrives after an event can change how we remember it.

In 1974 Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed people films of car accidents. They asked how fast the cars were going when they "smashed into" each other, or "hit" each other. The "smashed" group gave higher speeds, an average of 40.8 miles per hour versus 34.0. A week later, they were also more likely to say they'd seen broken glass, though there wasn't any. A single word in a question changed what they remembered.
A detailed memory of something that never happened can be created by suggestion.

In 1995 Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell asked adults to read four short stories about their own childhoods, written with help from their relatives. Three were true, and one was invented: that they'd been lost in a shopping mall as a child. About a quarter of the participants came to remember the made-up event, and some added details of their own. Vivid, detailed memories feel reliable, but a detailed memory can still be wrong.
Memories of shocking events feel vivid and exact but change like others.

When something shocking happens, we feel we'll never forget exactly where we were. In 1986, the day after the Challenger explosion, Ulric Neisser and Nicole Harsch asked students to write down how they'd heard. Two and a half years later, they asked again. About a quarter of the later accounts were wrong in nearly every detail, and the students were still very confident. The memory felt vivid, but the details had been rebuilt over time.
We remember a fact but forget where we learned it.
