You can remember a fact and forget where you learned it. Daniel Schacter and colleagues documented it in the 1980s, in patients and in healthy people. It's why a rumor you heard once, from someone you wouldn't have trusted, can seem like common knowledge months later. The content survives, but the tag that says "unreliable source" doesn't. If something seems like it's just something "everyone knows," it's worth asking where you first heard it.
Mistaking something you heard for an idea of your own.

Sometimes you can come up with an idea or a tune that you think is new, and it's something you heard before. In 1976 a US court decided that George Harrison had "subconsciously" copied the melody of the Chiffons' "He's So Fine" when he wrote "My Sweet Lord." The judge didn't think he'd done it on purpose. A stored tune had simply come back to him without the label. Writers and musicians sometimes worry about it, and it's a reason to keep track of where your ideas come from.
You know the word, but it will not come.

You know the word, you can almost taste it, and it won't come. In 1966 Roger Brown and David McNeill studied the state. People in it can often tell you the first letter and how many syllables the word has, showing that memory stores words in pieces. Pushing harder often makes it worse. The usual advice is to move on and let it come back by itself, which it often does a minute later in the shower.
Remembering to do something later is a separate challenge.

Remembering to do something in the future, like taking medicine or sending a message, is a different task from remembering the past. It usually fails because there was no cue at the moment you needed it. The solution is to attach the intention to something you'll definitely encounter, such as "when I pour my morning coffee, I'll take the pill." Psychologists call these implementation intentions, and they work much better than just resolving to remember.
New memories take hours and days to stabilize.

A new memory is fragile at first and takes hours and days to settle. In 1900 Georg Müller and Alfons Pilzecker showed it with a simple experiment. People who learned a list of nonsense syllables and then immediately learned a second list remembered the first one worse than people who got a rest in between. Sleep is one of the periods when memories seem to firm up, which is a good reason not to cram all night.
A recalled memory can become briefly changeable before it is stored again.

The old picture was that once a memory is stored, it stays fixed. In 2000 Karim Nader, Glenn Schafe and Joseph LeDoux gave rats a fear memory, then reminded them of it and blocked protein production in the brain. The memory was weakened, as if it had to be rebuilt each time it was recalled. It suggested that recalling a memory opens a window when it can be changed. Scientists are still working out how far this applies to people.
The man who could not form new memories, yet could learn new skills.

In 1953 a surgeon removed parts of Henry Molaison's brain, including most of the hippocampus on both sides, to treat his severe epilepsy. The seizures eased, but he could no longer form new memories of facts or events. He met his doctors again and again as if for the first time. Yet he could learn a new skill, like tracing a star in a mirror, and he improved day by day without remembering practicing it. It showed that memory has more than one system.
Knowing that is different from knowing how.

You can know that something is the case, like the capital of France, and you can know how to do something, like ride a bicycle. They seem to depend on different brain systems. You might be able to ride perfectly without being able to explain how you balance. Or you might know the steps of a skill and be unable to do it. People with amnesia often keep their skills while losing their memory of learning them.
Memory for events in your life versus memory for facts about the world.

In 1972 Endel Tulving suggested that we have two kinds of long-term memory for information. Episodic memory holds events from your own life, such as your last birthday party, with the feeling of being there. Semantic memory holds facts about the world, such as that Paris is the capital of France, without remembering when you learned them. In some forms of amnesia one is damaged more than the other.
Short-term thinking uses several parts, not one store.

In 1974 Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed that thinking in the moment uses several parts. There's a phonological loop for sounds and words, a visuospatial sketchpad for images and locations, and a central executive that directs attention. The model explains why you can listen to music while reading a map but find it hard to read an email while someone is talking to you. Tasks using the same part compete, and tasks using different parts don't.
Working memory is small, so instruction should not waste it.

John Sweller suggested in the 1980s that because working memory is so small, teaching should avoid wasting it. Making someone hold too much at once leads to confusion and poor learning. One common problem is split attention, such as a diagram on one page and an explanation three pages later, so the learner has to keep flipping back. Putting the explanation right beside the picture lets the learner use their limited memory for learning.
Novices learn more from studying solved problems than from struggling to solve them.

If you're new to a subject, studying solved problems can teach you more than trying to solve them yourself. John Sweller and Graham Cooper showed it in algebra in 1985. Seeing every step frees your mind from searching for a method, and lets you notice the pattern. As you get better, you should switch to solving problems on your own. The best sequence usually starts with an example and moves gradually toward independence.
What helps beginners can slow experts down.

Something that helps a beginner can get in the way of an expert. Step-by-step guidance with detailed explanations supports a novice, but for someone who already knows the material it's redundant and can slow them down. Slava Kalyuga and colleagues described the effect in 2003. It's a reminder that good teaching adapts to the learner. The same worksheet that rescues one student bores another, so it's worth checking where you stand.
The gap between what you can do alone and what you can do with help.

The Russian psychologist Lev Vygotsky, writing in the 1930s, described the distance between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help. He thought the best teaching works in that gap. If a task is too easy, nothing is learned. If it's too hard, the learner gives up. In between, with a little guidance that is gradually withdrawn, is where growth happens.
Temporary support that lets a learner do more than they could alone.

A scaffold on a building holds things up until the structure can stand without it. In 1976 David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross used the word for the support a tutor gives a child. The tutor does the parts the child can't yet manage, such as holding the pieces in place, and hands over more and more as the child improves. Good scaffolding is meant to be temporary. If it never comes down, the learner never learns to stand.
Master each step before moving on.

Benjamin Bloom suggested in 1968 that students should master each step before moving to the next, with extra help and time if they need it, rather than moving on with gaps. In 1984 he reported a "two sigma" finding: students tutored one-on-one with mastery methods did about two standard deviations better than those in a regular class. Later studies have found smaller gains, but the effect is real, and it's why practicing basics until they're solid pays off.
A paper system for spaced flashcards.

In 1972 the German science writer Sebastian Leitner described a simple way to schedule flashcards using a few boxes. All new cards start in box one. When you get one right, it moves up to the next box, which you review less often. When you get one wrong, it goes back to box one. The cards you know well get less of your time, and the ones you struggle with come back more. Many flashcard apps use the same idea.
Does taking notes by hand beat a laptop?

In 2014 Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer found that students who took notes by hand did better on conceptual questions than those who typed. Their explanation was that typists copy more word for word, while writers have to summarize. Later attempts to repeat the study found smaller differences, or none. The result may depend on how you take notes. Typing and thinking about the meaning probably beats handwriting and copying.
Reading much faster than normal costs you understanding.

Courses promise to teach you to read at 1,000 words a minute or more with full understanding. In 2016 a team of reading researchers led by Keith Rayner reviewed the evidence and concluded that it doesn't hold up. There's a trade-off between speed and comprehension. You can skim, and skimming is useful for finding the main points. But it's a different task from reading, and you miss details. A normal speed for adults is about 200 to 300 words a minute.
Reading aloud helps you remember it.

In 2010 Colin MacLeod and his colleagues found that people remembered words better when they read them aloud than when they read them silently. Hearing your own voice adds another feature to the memory, something distinctive about that item. It works best for the things you want to remember, so reading key points aloud, even quietly to yourself, can help. It's an easy trick to try when you're studying alone.
Work in short bursts of 25 minutes with short breaks.

In the late 1980s Francesco Cirillo, then a university student, used a tomato-shaped kitchen timer to break his work into 25-minute blocks with short breaks. The technique, named for the Italian word for tomato, gives a clear start and end to each session and can make it easier to begin. It may help some people focus. But there's little controlled research to show that 25 minutes is the right length, so adjust it to what works for you.
Skills often do not carry over to different tasks.

Does learning one skill help with another? In 1901 Edward Thorndike and Robert Woodworth tested it and found that practicing one kind of judgment, such as estimating the area of rectangles, did little for others. They suggested that transfer happens mostly when two tasks share the same elements. It's a sober point for anyone hoping a hobby, such as chess or Latin, will make them smarter in general. Skills usually carry over only to similar tasks.
Extra practice right after you master something adds little lasting memory.

It seems sensible to keep practicing after you've got something right, to be sure. In a 2005 study by Doug Rohrer and colleagues, students learned geography facts and then either stopped or kept drilling the same ones in the same session. A week later, the extra drilling made no difference to how much they remembered. The better use of time is to come back to the material later, after some forgetting has set in, and practice it again.
Link a foreign word to an English word it sounds like, then picture the two together.

To learn a foreign word, find an English word that sounds like it, then make a picture that connects the two. For the Spanish word "pato," meaning duck, you might imagine a duck wearing a pot on its head. Richard Atkinson and his colleagues tested the method in the 1970s and found that students using it learned vocabulary faster at first. It works best for concrete words, and it's less helpful for abstract ones.
The best memorizers were not born with special brains.

In 2003 Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues scanned the brains of people who rank among the best memorizers in the world. They found no unusual structure. What distinguished them was how they remembered: almost all used the method of loci, imagining a familiar journey and placing items along it. In other words, their results came from technique and practice, not from some special gift.
Old and new memories get in each other's way.

Forgetting isn't always fading. Often one memory gets in the way of another. In 1924 John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had two students learn lists of nonsense syllables and then either sleep or stay awake. After the same number of hours, they remembered more after sleep. When you're asleep, less new material comes in to interfere. Old things can disturb new ones, and new things can disturb old ones, and both happen all the time.
You may recall nothing, yet relearn it faster than before.

Hermann Ebbinghaus, who started the scientific study of memory in the 1880s, noticed something. A list of syllables he could no longer recall at all still took him fewer repetitions to learn a second time. He called the difference "savings." The memory had faded, but not vanished. It's encouraging: if you've studied something before, even years ago, you'll relearn it faster than someone starting from scratch.
You can focus on one stream and miss the others.

In 1953 Colin Cherry studied how people follow one conversation in a noisy room, which became known as the cocktail-party effect. You can concentrate on one speaker and tune out the others. Yet if someone across the room says your name, you often notice. So your attention filters, but not completely. Some of what you're ignoring is still being processed, which is one reason it's hard to concentrate in a busy place.
We can fail to see something obvious when we are focusing on something else.

In the famous invisible gorilla study, people counting basketball passes often failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk through the scene. A similar thing was found in medicine. In 2013 researchers asked radiologists to look for lung nodules in a set of scans. In the last scan, they'd put a picture of a gorilla about 48 times the size of a typical nodule. Most of the radiologists, 83 percent, didn't see it.
We miss big changes to a scene when they happen during a blink or a cut.

We tend to think we'd notice a big change in our surroundings. In a 1998 field study by Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin, an experimenter stopped a pedestrian and asked for directions. While they talked, two men carrying a door walked between them, and the experimenter was swapped with a different person. About half of the pedestrians didn't notice that the person they were talking to had changed.
A second target is missed if it comes about half a second after the first.

If you're watching a fast stream of images and looking for two particular targets, you'll often notice the first but miss the second when it comes within about half a second. In 1992 Jane Raymond, Kimron Shapiro and Karen Arnell described the effect. Processing the first target seems to use up your attention for a moment. It's a fine illustration of how limited our attention is, even when we're alert.
Switching between tasks slows you and adds errors.

People often believe they can do two things at once. Mostly, they're switching rapidly between them, and every switch costs something. In lab experiments, people were slower and made more mistakes on the first trial after a change of task, even when they knew the switch was coming. Doing one task at a time and finishing it generally takes less total time than bouncing between several.
Our minds drift about half the time, and usually not happily.

In 2010 Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert built an app that pinged thousands of people at random moments and asked what they were doing and thinking about. People's minds were wandering in 46.9% of the samples, whatever the activity. They also reported being less happy when their minds wandered than when they were focused on what they were doing. Even when the daydream was pleasant, it didn't make people happier.
A state of full absorption when challenge matches skill.

The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied people who got completely absorbed in activities, such as rock climbers, chess players and surgeons. He called the state flow. It tends to appear when a task is challenging enough to need all your attention but not so hard that it overwhelms you, and when the goals are clear and you get quick feedback. Time seems to disappear. It's one reason that matching difficulty to your skill makes work more enjoyable.
Performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls.

In 1908 Robert Yerkes and John Dodson trained mice to avoid shocks and found that moderate shocks led to the best learning. Too weak or too strong did worse. Psychologists extended the idea into a rule that performance rises with arousal up to a point and then falls. Later work suggests the best level depends on the task: harder tasks do best with lower arousal. It's a rough guide, not a precise law.
Sleep and the next day's learning
Sleep before learning prepares the brain to absorb, and sleep after learning helps keep it.

In 2007 Seung-Schik Yoo, Matthew Walker and colleagues kept some volunteers awake all night and let others sleep, then showed everyone pictures to remember. The next day, the people who'd been up all night remembered about 40 percent fewer of the pictures. Scans showed less activity in the hippocampus, a region important for forming memories. Sleep matters for learning before you study as well as after.
A short sleep in the afternoon can restore learning.

In 2003 Sara Mednick and her colleagues tested people on a visual task that gets better with practice. Those who had a nap of 60 to 90 minutes improved as much as people who'd had a full night's sleep. Those who didn't nap got worse over the day. A well-timed nap can restore some of your ability to learn. A short one of about 20 minutes may be better for just feeling alert.
Do educational videos make babies smarter?

Videos for babies were sold in the 2000s as a way to boost their learning. In 2007 Frederick Zimmerman and colleagues surveyed parents of infants aged 8 to 16 months. For each daily hour of baby videos, the children knew a few fewer words than babies who didn't watch them. Researchers can't be sure the videos caused it. What does help babies learn words is talking, reading and playing with the people around them.
A cue that was linked to the memory when it was formed can bring it back.

Endel Tulving and Zena Pearlstone showed in 1966 that a memory can seem lost until the right cue appears. People who couldn't recall a list of words suddenly could when they were given category names as hints. The memory was there but they couldn't reach it. It's a reason to leave yourself cues when you study, such as a keyword or a note in the margin. A smell or a song can bring back a scene because it was part of the original memory.
After reading something twice, we feel we know it.

In a well-known 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read a passage and then either read it again or take a test on it. The students who had reread felt more prepared. A week later, the ones who'd been tested remembered far more. Rereading creates a feeling of familiarity, which is easy to mistake for knowledge. Testing yourself feels harder, and that's partly why it works.
Getting something wrong and then seeing the right answer can help.

You might think that guessing wrong would plant the wrong answer in your mind. In a 2009 study, Nate Kornell, Matthew Hays and Robert Bjork had people try to guess answers before being shown the correct one. Even when the guesses were wrong, they learned the right answer better than people who just read it. A wrong guess followed by quick feedback seems to prepare the mind to take in the answer.
The more sure you were of a wrong answer, the better you remember the correction.

Surprisingly, the more confident you are in a wrong answer, the more likely you are to remember the correction. In 2001 Brady Butterfield and Janet Metcalfe found that high-confidence mistakes were corrected more often than low-confidence ones. The surprise of learning you were wrong when you were sure seems to grab your attention. So there's no need to feel embarrassed about being wrong. A confident mistake is one of the best ways to learn.
Thoughts, feelings and actions influence each other, so changing one can shift the others.

Aaron Beck was a psychiatrist who started out trying to test a Freudian theory of depression in the early 1960s and ended up noticing something else. His patients had a running stream of negative thoughts they hardly noticed, and those thoughts seemed to drive their mood. He built a short, practical therapy around spotting and testing them. It has been studied in hundreds of trials, and it helps with depression and anxiety. Many of its tools can be learned from a good book.
Write the thought, the evidence for it and against it, then a more balanced thought.

This is one of the core exercises of cognitive therapy, and it's simple. You write down a situation, the thought that came to mind, and how strongly you felt it. Then you list the evidence for the thought and the evidence against, and come up with a more balanced version. The aim isn't to replace a bad thought with a positive one. It's to check whether the first thought was accurate, since it's usually only one of several ways to read what happened.
Seeing things in two categories, perfect or failure.

David Burns, who popularized Beck's ideas in his 1980 book Feeling Good, listed it first among the common thinking traps. Things are either perfect or a failure, with nothing between. "I missed one step in the plan, so the whole day is ruined." Real life is mostly in the gray area, and so is most of what we do. A good habit is to catch words like "always," "never" and "completely," and ask what a more accurate description would be, such as "mostly went well, with one miss."
Jumping to the worst possible outcome.

A headache becomes a brain tumor, a late reply becomes the end of the friendship. Catastrophizing means leaping to the worst possible outcome and treating it as likely. One standard way to deflate it is to ask three questions: what's the worst that could happen, what's the most likely thing, and how would I cope if the worst did happen? Answering them honestly usually shows that the worst case is unlikely, and that you'd manage better than you fear.
Assuming you know what others think of you, with no evidence.

"She didn't text back, so she must be angry with me." We often feel sure we know what others are thinking, especially about us, and the guess is usually negative. In truth, people are busy, distracted and mostly thinking about their own lives. When you notice yourself mind reading, it can help to list other explanations for what you saw, and to ask the person if it matters. A guess is not a fact, even when it feels like one.
Treating a feeling as proof: "I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong."

"I feel guilty, so I must have done something wrong." "I feel anxious, so something bad is about to happen." Emotional reasoning treats a feeling as evidence about the world. Feelings do tell you something, but mostly about your body and your state of mind. Guilt can come from a rule you were taught, and anxiety from tiredness. A helpful move is to name the feeling and then check the facts separately, as if you were a fair-minded friend.
Rigid rules about how you or others must behave.

Words like "should," "must" and "ought" set rigid rules for how we or others have to behave. Aimed at ourselves, they produce guilt: "I should be over this by now." Aimed at others, they produce anger: "They should know better." The psychologist Albert Ellis called it "musturbation." Swapping "should" for "I would like to" or "it would help if" tends to keep the standard but drop the whip.
Describing a whole person by one act: "I'm a failure."

One mistake becomes a whole identity: "I'm a failure," "I'm an idiot," "I'm unlovable." It's an extreme form of overgeneralizing, and it's harsh in a way we'd never be with a friend. It also makes change seem impossible, because you can't change what you are. Instead, describe the behavior: "I made a mistake on that task." A mistake is something you did, and you can learn from what you did.
Taking blame for things that were not yours alone.

When something goes wrong, we may assume it's our fault, even when it wasn't mainly. A child has a bad day at school. A partner is in a mood. A team misses a target. Usually there are many causes: other people's choices, circumstances, luck. One way to see this is to write a pie chart of everything that contributed, and put your own share last. Most people find it's much smaller than the share they'd been blaming themselves for.
An event (A) does not directly cause your feelings (C); your belief about it (B) does.

Albert Ellis taught in the 1950s that what upsets us isn't events themselves but our beliefs about them. A is the activating event, B is the belief, and C is the consequence, the emotion. Two people miss the same train. One thinks, "This is a disaster, I'll be late and in trouble," and feels panic. The other thinks, "Well, time for a coffee," and feels fine. The event was the same, and the beliefs made the difference. Beliefs can be questioned.
When you feel low, do small valued activities first, and the mood follows.

When you're low, it's natural to wait until you feel better to do things. But the lack of activity makes the low mood worse, and a cycle starts. Behavioral activation reverses it: you schedule small activities that matter to you, such as a walk or a phone call, and do them whether or not you feel like it. Mood often follows action. In a 1996 trial, activation alone worked about as well as full cognitive therapy for depression.
Act opposite to what the emotion urges when the emotion doesn't fit the facts.

Marsha Linehan's dialectical behavior therapy includes a skill for when an emotion pushes you to do something that isn't helpful. Sadness says to hide in bed. Anger says to lash out. Fear says to avoid. Opposite action means doing the reverse in small ways: reaching out to a friend, being gentle, approaching what you fear. It works when the feeling is out of proportion to the situation. It isn't meant to override feelings that fit the facts.
Fully accept what has happened, without approving it, and stop fighting reality.

Marsha Linehan draws a line between pain and suffering. Pain is what happens: the loss, the diagnosis, the end of the marriage. Suffering is what we add by fighting the fact that it happened, with "this shouldn't be happening" or "it isn't fair." Radical acceptance means fully acknowledging what is, in your mind and body. It doesn't mean approving, liking it or giving up on changing things. It means no longer spending your energy on the argument with reality.
The overlap of emotional mind and reasonable mind.

In dialectical behavior therapy, there are said to be three states of mind. Emotional mind is driven by feelings and tends to be impulsive. Reasonable mind is driven by facts and logic, and can miss what matters. Wise mind is where they overlap, the place where you know something is right and can feel it too. Linehan teaches people to pause, breathe and ask from that place, "What do I really want to do here?"
Four fast ways to calm a surge of distress: temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired relaxation.

When distress spikes so hard that thinking clearly is out of reach, Linehan's group suggests changing the body first. TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing and Paired muscle relaxation. Cold water on your face, a minute of hard exercise or a long slow exhale quickly shifts your body's alarm state. They're meant for the moments when you're flooded, not for solving the underlying problem, which you can tackle once you're calmer.
Notice a thought as a thought, not a fact.

In acceptance and commitment therapy, you learn to treat thoughts as passing events in the mind, not as truths. Instead of "I'm worthless," you say, "I'm having the thought that I'm worthless." The thought may not vanish, but it loosens its grip, because you're now watching it instead of being it. It can sound like a small trick, but with practice it creates a little space between you and what your mind says, and in that space you can choose how to act.
A goal can be finished; a value is a direction you keep walking in.

In acceptance and commitment therapy, a goal is something you can finish, like attending your child's recital. A value is a direction you keep moving in and never complete, like being a loving parent. Goals can be missed, and then it can feel like failure. Values can always be lived, in some small way, today. When life has been knocked off course, asking what you value, and what one small step fits it, can show you where to go.
An eight-week course of meditation and gentle movement.

In 1979 Jon Kabat-Zinn started a stress clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. Patients came for an eight-week course combining meditation, body awareness and gentle yoga. It has been tested in many trials. A large review in 2014 found moderate evidence that it helps with anxiety, depression and pain, about as much as other active treatments. It's not a cure-all, but it gives many people a skill.
A mindfulness course can help keep depression from returning.

Depression often comes back. Zindel Segal, Mark Williams and John Teasdale developed a version of mindfulness training to help prevent that. In a 2000 trial, people who had had three or more episodes of depression were followed for a year. The relapse rate was 37% for those who took the course and 66% for those who got usual care. For people with fewer episodes, there was no difference.
Writing about a hard experience for 15 to 20 minutes on a few days can help.

In the 1980s James Pennebaker asked people to write about the most upsetting experience of their lives for 15 to 20 minutes on each of several days. Some later showed improvements in health, such as fewer doctor visits. Later reviews found the average effect is small and varies from person to person. Still, it seems safe, and many people find that putting something into words helps them make sense of it.
Set aside 15 to 30 minutes a day to worry, and postpone worries until then.

If you can't stop worrying, one method is to give worry its own appointment. Thomas Borkovec's work in the 1980s led to a technique where you pick a time, say 15 to 30 minutes in the early evening, and postpone worries until then. When one comes up during the day, you note it down and tell yourself "later." Many people find that the urge fades by the time the appointed hour comes.
A style of conversation that helps someone talk themselves into change.

William Miller and Stephen Rollnick developed this style of conversation in the 1980s while working with people with addictions. Arguing for change usually makes people argue back. Instead, the helper asks open questions, listens carefully, and invites the person to talk about both sides of their mixed feelings. When people hear themselves say why they might change, they're more likely to do it. It works well when someone is unsure.
People move through readiness stages before a lasting change.

In the 1980s James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente studied how people quit smoking and described a series of stages. In precontemplation they aren't thinking about it. In contemplation they're weighing it up. Then come preparation, action and maintenance. Relapse is common and counts as part of the cycle, not as failure. Researchers debate whether the stages are truly distinct, but the idea that readiness matters is widely used.
People thrive when three needs are met: autonomy, competence and relatedness.

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan studied what keeps people motivated and found three basic needs. Autonomy is the sense that you're making your own choices. Competence is feeling capable. Relatedness is feeling connected to others. When these needs are met, people are more motivated, more creative and happier. The pattern holds across many cultures. It helps explain why pressure works poorly for long: it takes away autonomy.
Do you believe your results come from you or from outside forces?

In 1966 Julian Rotter described a difference between people who believe their lives are shaped mainly by their own actions, and those who believe it's mainly luck, fate or other people. An "internal" locus tends to go with better coping, health habits and achievement. But the world isn't fully controllable, and an accurate sense of what's in your power matters too. The useful skill is telling the two apart.
Believing you can do a particular task predicts whether you try and keep going.

Albert Bandura introduced the term in 1977 for your belief in your ability to do a specific task. It's different from general confidence. It predicts whether you'll try, how hard you'll work and whether you'll keep going after a setback. It grows mainly from small successes, from watching someone like you succeed, from encouragement and from managing your stress. Setting a goal you can actually reach is a good way to build it.
After uncontrollable pain, animals and people can stop trying.

In the 1960s Martin Seligman and Steven Maier gave dogs shocks they couldn't escape. Later, when the dogs could easily avoid shocks by jumping a barrier, many just lay down. It looked like they'd learned that nothing they did mattered. In 2016 Maier and Seligman revised the theory. Passivity is the brain's default response to pain, and what has to be learned is that you do have control. That's a hopeful reading.
How you explain bad events predicts how you cope.

Martin Seligman found that people differ in how they explain bad events to themselves. Pessimists tend to see causes as permanent, personal and pervasive: "It will always be like this, it's my fault, and it ruins everything." Optimists see them as temporary, specific and partly outside their control. Explanatory style predicted sales success at an insurance company and how people recovered from low mood. It can be changed with practice.
Most people recover well after a loss or trauma.

George Bonanno studied how people cope with losses like the death of a spouse. Many expected most to go through a long period of deep distress. He found that the most common pattern was a short time of grief followed by a return to normal functioning, and a minority did have prolonged difficulty. Being resilient doesn't mean not hurting. It means that people are, on the whole, sturdier than they expect.
The dual process model of grief
Healthy grieving swings between facing the loss and managing the rest of life.

In 1999 Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut proposed that grieving well isn't a straight line. People swing back and forth between two kinds of coping. In loss-oriented moments, they face the pain, think about the person and miss them. In restoration-oriented moments, they deal with daily life and new roles, and take breaks from grief. The back and forth is normal and healthy. Taking a break from sadness isn't avoiding it.
Intense grief that does not ease after a year or more, and gets in the way of living.

Grief is not an illness. Most people find that the sharpest pain eases over time. For some, intense longing and distress continue for a year or more and make daily life difficult. In 2022 the diagnostic manual added prolonged grief disorder for that situation. It is a name for grief that's stuck, not a judgment about how much someone loved. It responds to treatment, which can help people live with the loss.
Some people report new strength or meaning after adversity.

In 1996 Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun described how some people report positive changes after a crisis: closer relationships, a greater appreciation of life, new priorities or a stronger sense of purpose. It's a real experience for many. But not everyone has it, and no one should feel they have to. Researchers also point out that people's own reports of growth don't always match how they're actually doing later.
A divorce is a series of changes over years, not a single event.

Paul Amato, who has studied divorce for decades, describes it as a long series of changes, not a single event. Conflict before the split, the move, the finances, parenting arrangements and new relationships each affect how people cope. Most adults adjust over time. But the path varies a lot, and the stress people feel depends heavily on what follows the separation, so how things go afterward is partly within your influence.
Most children of divorce do fine
The majority of children adapt well, though some face more problems than children in intact families.

E. Mavis Hetherington followed families through divorce for decades in the Virginia Longitudinal Study. About 75 to 80 percent of the children from divorced families were functioning well as adults, compared with about 90 percent of those from intact families. So most children cope, though a minority struggle more. What helped them was steady parenting, low conflict between the parents and a warm relationship with at least one adult.
Having people to lean on softens the harm of hard events.

In 1985 Sheldon Cohen and Thomas Wills reviewed the research on how social support affects health. They found that having people to lean on protects against the harm of high stress. What matters most is the sense that if you needed help, someone would be there. That perception may be as protective as actually receiving help. It's one reason that staying in touch with the people who care about you pays off during hard times.
Weak social ties carry a health risk as large as some well-known ones.

In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues combined 148 studies covering more than 300,000 people. They found that people with strong social relationships had a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up periods. The size of the effect was comparable with quitting smoking, and larger than that of obesity or inactivity. It's not just that the lonely are sicker to begin with. Connection seems to matter for staying well.
Writing down things you are thankful for gives a small mood boost.

Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked people to write weekly about things they were grateful for. In 2003 they reported that, compared with people who wrote about hassles, the gratitude group felt better about their lives. A later review found the average benefit is modest. So it's a helpful habit that costs nothing, though it isn't a cure for depression. It seems to work best if you write about specifics and people, not generalities.
Each night write three good things that happened and why.

Martin Seligman and colleagues asked people to write down three things that went well each day and why, for one week. In a 2005 study, those who did so were happier and less depressed for up to six months. Later studies have found smaller or shorter-lived effects, so the results are mixed. It takes only a few minutes a night, and many people find it shifts their attention toward what's good.
Deliberately attending to a pleasant moment makes it last longer.

Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff, who wrote the book on savoring, describe it as deliberately paying attention to a pleasant experience so that you enjoy it more and it lasts longer. They suggest sharing it with someone, taking mental snapshots, and thinking about it afterward. You can savor the past through memories, the present through full attention, and the future through anticipation. It's a skill that can be practiced.
Standing before something vast can shrink worries and widen your view.

The psychologist Dacher Keltner studies awe, the feeling you get before something vast that changes how you see the world. It could be a mountain range, a piece of music or a big idea. In his research, awe makes people feel smaller in a good way, more connected to others and more generous. It also seems to quiet self-focused worry. You don't need a trip to the Grand Canyon, and walks in nature and looking at the night sky can do it.
People who can describe feelings precisely cope better than those who use only "bad".

Lisa Feldman Barrett found that some people describe their feelings with precision, telling "anxious" from "disappointed" from "ashamed," and others lump everything together as "bad" or "awful." The first group copes with stress more flexibly. They seem to have more options, since a precise label points to a particular response. Building your emotional vocabulary can be as simple as pausing to ask what exactly you're feeling.
The body's alarm makes the heart race and gets muscles ready, whether the danger is a bear or an email.

Walter Cannon, a physiologist at Harvard, described in 1915 how the body prepares for fight or flight. Your heart races, your breathing quickens and your muscles tense. The system evolved for physical danger, but it responds to an urgent email just as well. Freezing is another common response. The good news is that the system can be switched off. Slow breathing, a walk and talking with a friend all tell the body that it's safe to stand down.
Repeated or long stress wears the body down.

Bruce McEwen introduced the term in the 1990s for the wear and tear that builds up when the body's stress systems are working too much, or never switch off. Over time it can show up as higher blood pressure, weakened immunity and sleep problems. It isn't just about how big a stressor is. How long it lasts and how well you recover also matter, so rest and recovery are part of managing stress, not a reward for finishing it.
A state of exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of ineffectiveness, most often from chronic work stress.

Christina Maslach, a psychologist, developed the best-known measure of burnout in the early 1980s. It has three parts: exhaustion, cynicism or detachment from the work, and a feeling of being ineffective. It usually grows out of chronic stress at work, including overload, little control and a lack of recognition. The World Health Organization calls it an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. It's often addressed by changing the conditions, not just the person.
Successful people who believe they are frauds about to be found out.

In 1978 Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described high-achieving women who felt like frauds who'd fooled everyone and were about to be found out. Later work showed it happens to men too, and it's very common. It isn't a diagnosis. People who feel it often attribute success to luck and discount their abilities. One of the best remedies is talking about it with others, since you'll often discover that people you admire feel the same.
Two inhales through the nose and a long exhale through the mouth, for five minutes a day, lifted mood.

The technique is two breaths in through the nose, the second a small top-up, followed by a long slow breath out through the mouth. In a 2023 Stanford trial with 108 people, those who did five minutes of it a day for a month improved their mood and lowered their resting breathing rate more than people who did mindfulness meditation. It's simple to try, and the long exhale seems to be what calms the body.
The average person who receives therapy ends up better off than most who don't.

In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass combined the results of 375 studies of psychotherapy in one of the first meta-analyses. They found that the average person who had therapy ended up better off than about 75 percent of people who hadn't. Later reviews have reached similar conclusions. It doesn't mean every therapy works for every person. It does mean that, on average, talking with a trained person helps.
The bond between client and therapist predicts results across kinds of therapy.

Researchers have found that the quality of the bond between client and therapist, including agreement on the goals and the tasks of therapy, predicts how well the treatment works. A 2018 review of nearly 300 studies found a consistent link, whatever the type of therapy. So if you're thinking about seeing someone, it matters that you feel understood and comfortable. It's fine to try a different therapist if the first isn't a good fit.
Different therapies often work about equally well.

In Alice in Wonderland, after a race, the Dodo declares, "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1936 Saul Rosenzweig borrowed the line to describe a puzzling finding that different forms of psychotherapy seem to work about equally well. Later researchers, including Lester Luborsky, found similar results. Not everyone agrees. For some conditions, such as phobias, particular treatments do better. But the overall similarity suggests that shared ingredients, such as the relationship, matter a lot.
Mental habits that protect us from painful feelings.

In 1936 Anna Freud, Sigmund's daughter, described the mind's habits for protecting us from painful feelings, such as denial, projection, displacement and rationalization. The psychiatrist George Vaillant later ranked them from immature, like denial, to mature, like humor and sublimation. The ideas are useful for describing how people cope, and many therapists use them. But the research behind them is mostly observation, not controlled experiment.
Taking frustration out on a safer target.

When we can't safely express a feeling at its source, we sometimes aim it at someone safer. A man is humiliated by his boss, says nothing, and then snaps at his family when he gets home. It's one of the classic defense mechanisms. Spotting it can help. When your reaction seems bigger than the situation, ask yourself who or what the feeling is really about. Often the answer is somewhere else.
Freud shaped how we talk about the mind, but most of his specific theories are not supported.

Sigmund Freud shaped the vocabulary of psychology, and we still talk about the unconscious, repression and the importance of early childhood. Some of those ideas hold up in modified forms. Others, such as the Oedipus complex or the idea that dreams are disguised wishes, have not been supported. A big problem is that many of his claims can't be tested, since any result can be explained within the theory. He's more important as a historical figure than as a scientific authority.
Sorts people into 16 types, but it is not a reliable scientific tool.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator sorts people into 16 types, such as INFJ or ESTP, from four either-or choices. It's very popular in workplaces. But scientists generally don't regard it as reliable. In some studies, about half of people got a different type when they retook the test five weeks later. The reason is that traits like introversion fall along a continuum, and the test cuts it in the middle. The Big Five model has a much better record.
Five broad personality traits: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.

After decades of research, many personality psychologists settled on five broad dimensions: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Researchers have found the same five in many countries and languages. They stay fairly stable through adult life and predict real outcomes, such as job performance, relationship satisfaction and health. Unlike the Myers-Briggs types, each is measured on a scale, so most people are somewhere in the middle.
About half of the differences in personality and many behaviors trace to genes.

In 2015 Tinca Polderman and colleagues combined nearly fifty years of twin studies, covering over 14 million pairs of twins. Across all the traits measured, about 49 percent of the differences between people could be traced to genes. The other half came from the environment, mostly the kind that siblings in the same family don't share. It means neither genes nor upbringing alone decide who we become.
Average IQ scores rose about 3 points per decade through the 20th century.

James Flynn discovered that the average score on IQ tests rose about three points every decade through most of the 20th century, in many countries. That's a big change in a few generations, too fast to be genetic. Possible causes include more schooling, better nutrition, and growing familiarity with abstract thinking and tests. In some countries, scores have stopped rising or have even gone down in recent years, and experts aren't sure why.
Howard Gardner proposed several separate types of intelligence.

In 1983 the psychologist Howard Gardner proposed that people have several separate kinds of intelligence, such as musical, bodily, interpersonal and logical. The theory is very popular among teachers. But researchers haven't found good evidence that the types are independent. People who score high on one kind of mental test tend to score higher on others, which supports the idea of a general factor. The ideas are better seen as a way of appreciating different strengths.
Did a child's wait for a second marshmallow predict their success?

In the 1960s and 70s Walter Mischel offered young children a choice: one marshmallow now, or two if they waited. Follow-up studies suggested that the ones who waited did better in life. In 2018 Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan repeated it with a larger and more varied group. After controlling for family background, the link was about half as strong, and mostly disappeared. Waiting seems to reflect circumstances as much as willpower.
Passion and perseverance for long-term goals.

In 2007 Angela Duckworth and colleagues defined grit as passion and perseverance for long-term goals, and found it predicted who stayed at West Point and who won the national spelling bee. Later reviews found that grit overlaps a lot with conscientiousness, a long-known trait, and predicts success only modestly. Perseverance does matter, but the idea that grit is a separate and powerful predictor has been oversold.
Needs from food and safety up to meaning, arranged as a pyramid.

In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed that human needs form a pyramid, from physical needs and safety at the bottom to belonging, esteem and self-fulfillment at the top. The idea that needs matter is useful. The strict order isn't supported. A survey across more than 120 countries found that people pursue love and purpose even when basic needs aren't fully met. The pyramid is better thought of as a rough guide.
Boosting self-esteem does not by itself improve grades or performance.

In the 1980s and 90s it was widely believed that raising children's self-esteem would improve grades and behavior. In 2003 Roy Baumeister and colleagues reviewed the research. They found self-esteem tends to follow success more than cause it, and boosting it directly did little for performance. Praise for effort and strategy works better than praise for being smart, because it teaches that the outcome depends on what you do.
Ordinary people obeyed instructions to give what they thought were painful shocks.

In 1961 Stanley Milgram, at Yale, had volunteers play the part of a teacher who gave electric shocks to a "learner" for wrong answers, with the shocks increasing to a dangerous 450 volts. The shocks were fake, and the learner was an actor. In the baseline version, 65 percent of participants went all the way to the maximum. Later analyses question how realistic the setup was. Still, it showed how far ordinary people may go under instruction from an authority.
People gave obviously wrong answers to match a group.

In the early 1950s Solomon Asch asked people to say which of three lines matched a standard line, an easy task. But everyone else in the room was an actor and had been told to give the wrong answer. About 75 percent of the participants went along with the group at least once, and about a third of all their answers conformed. If one other person gave the right answer, conformity dropped sharply. A single ally makes it easier to speak up.
A famous 1971 study said roles turn ordinary students into cruel guards.

In 1971 Philip Zimbardo had college students play guards and prisoners in a mock prison in a basement. It was said to show that the situation turns ordinary people cruel. But later evidence showed that the guards were coached on how to behave, and some participants were acting. Most psychologists now regard it as a vivid demonstration, not proof of what happens naturally. It shows how powerful a setup can be, but it's a shaky basis for conclusions.
Two groups of boys at a camp became hostile; shared goals ended it.

In 1954 Muzafer Sherif ran a summer camp for twenty-two boys in Oklahoma. He split them into two groups, the Rattlers and the Eagles, and set up competitions with prizes. Hostility rose quickly. Later he created problems that could only be solved by working together, such as fixing the water supply, and the animosity eased. The study suggests that rivalry creates conflict and shared goals reduce it.
People who agree to a small request are more likely to agree to a larger one later.

In 1966 Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser asked homeowners to put a large, ugly "Drive Carefully" sign on their lawns. Only about 17 percent agreed. But when another group had earlier been asked to display a small sign, and had agreed, 76 percent said yes to the large one. A small yes changes how you see yourself, as someone who helps with this kind of thing, and it makes the next request easier.
After refusing a big request, people are more likely to agree to a smaller one.

In 1975 Robert Cialdini and his colleagues asked college students to spend two years as volunteer counselors for juvenile offenders. Almost everyone said no. When the same students were then asked to spend two hours taking the kids to the zoo, about half agreed, compared with 17 percent of students who were asked only about the zoo trip. After turning down a big request, people feel a pull to meet you partway.
Six levers of influence: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity.

In his 1984 book Influence, Robert Cialdini described six levers that make people say yes: reciprocity (we repay favors), commitment (we stay consistent), social proof (we follow others), authority, liking and scarcity. He worked out the list by training with salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers. Knowing them doesn't make you immune. But it helps you notice when someone is pulling one, and ask yourself whether you'd agree without it.
People change their behavior when they know they are watched.

The name comes from experiments in the 1920s and 30s at the Hawthorne Works, a Western Electric factory near Chicago. Workers' output seemed to rise when lighting was changed, whichever way, which was taken to mean people work harder when they're being watched. In 2011 Steven Levitt and John List went back to the original data and found little evidence of such an effect in those studies. Being observed may change behavior, but this famous example isn't solid.
A 1973 study claimed healthy people faked symptoms to enter psychiatric hospitals and were not detected.

In 1973 David Rosenhan published "On Being Sane in Insane Places." He said that eight healthy people faked a symptom, hearing voices, to be admitted to psychiatric hospitals, and then acted normally but weren't discovered. A 2019 investigation by the journalist Susannah Cahalan found evidence that he misreported some of the data and details. Doubts about how reliably psychiatric diagnosis was made then were reasonable, but the study itself isn't trustworthy.
Baby monkeys preferred a soft cloth mother to a wire one that gave milk.

In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised baby rhesus monkeys with two artificial mothers: one made of wire that held a bottle, and one covered in soft cloth that didn't. The babies clung to the cloth mother and went to the wire one only to feed. It showed that attachment grows from comfort and contact, not just from food. It changed how child-care experts thought about babies, though the experiments were cruel and would not be done today.
A short lab procedure that shows a baby's attachment style.

In the 1970s Mary Ainsworth devised a short laboratory test. A one-year-old is in a playroom with a parent, then a stranger comes in, the parent leaves, and then comes back. What the baby does at the reunion shows a pattern. About 65 percent were securely attached, upset when the parent left and quickly comforted on return. The rest showed avoidant or anxious patterns. The test has been used for decades to study attachment.
Attachment patterns may show up in how we handle closeness as adults.

In 1987 Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver proposed that adult romantic relationships follow the same patterns as the bond between a baby and a caregiver. People are described as secure, anxious or avoidant in how they handle closeness. Attachment styles are partly stable but not fixed, and they can change with new relationships or therapy. Researchers now measure them on spectrums, not as fixed types.
Early severe deprivation harms development, and earlier rescue helps more.

After the fall of the Ceaușescu regime in 1989, thousands of Romanian children were found in overcrowded orphanages with very little care. The English and Romanian Adoptees study followed those who were adopted into British families. Children adopted before six months of age mostly caught up. Those adopted later had more lasting difficulties with attention, relationships and thinking. It showed that severe early neglect has real effects, and that earlier rescue helps.
A neutral signal that is paired with something that matters comes to trigger the same response.

Ivan Pavlov, a Russian physiologist studying digestion, noticed that his dogs started to salivate when they heard the footsteps of the assistant who fed them. He then paired a bell with food and found the bell alone would produce salivation. A neutral signal that's linked with something meaningful comes to trigger the same response. The same thing happens in people: a song linked to a memory can bring back the feeling.
Behavior followed by reward becomes more likely; followed by punishment, less likely.

In 1898 Edward Thorndike put cats in puzzle boxes and found that actions that led to escape were repeated. He called it the law of effect. B. F. Skinner developed the idea in the 1930s with his "Skinner box." Behavior that's followed by something rewarding becomes more likely, and behavior followed by something unpleasant becomes less likely. Rewards usually change behavior faster and more lastingly than punishment does.
Unpredictable rewards produce the most persistent habits.

B. F. Skinner found that how often you reward matters. When rewards come on an unpredictable schedule, like a slot machine, animals keep pressing the lever the longest, even after the rewards stop altogether. We can see the same thing in many places: checking your phone to see whether anything new has arrived, or pulling to refresh a feed. The unpredictability makes the habit stick, which is why it's so hard to break.
A learned response fades when the reward or the pairing stops, but it can come back.

When a learned response stops being rewarded, it fades. A dog stops salivating to a bell that no longer predicts food. But it's not erased. After a rest, it often returns, which is called spontaneous recovery. In people, a fear or habit that has faded can return with stress or in a new place. Researchers like Mark Bouton find that practicing the new learning in many settings makes it last longer.
A 1920 experiment on conditioning fear in an infant.

In 1920 John Watson and Rosalie Rayner at Johns Hopkins showed a nine-month-old baby a white rat while making a loud noise behind him. After several pairings, the baby cried at the sight of the rat, and at other furry things. It's a famous example of conditioned fear. It's also an ethically troubling study with weak methods, and later accounts of what it proved are often exaggerated. It wouldn't be allowed now.
Children copied adults' aggression toward an inflatable doll.

In 1961 Albert Bandura and his colleagues showed nursery-school children an adult either hitting a large inflatable doll or ignoring it. When the children were later left alone with the doll, those who had seen the adult attack it copied the same actions and even the same words. The study showed that children can learn by watching, without being rewarded themselves. It started a long debate on media violence.
Rats and people build mental maps, not just chains of habits.

In 1948 Edward Tolman showed that rats don't simply learn a chain of left and right turns. After they'd learned a maze, he blocked the usual route. Instead of getting confused, they chose a new route in the direction of the goal, as if they had a map in their heads. The finding was important because it showed that animals, and so people, build mental representations of space and not only habits.
We learn without any reward and show it only when it is useful.

In 1930 Edward Tolman and Charles Honzik put hungry rats in a maze. One group was fed at the end every time and got better quickly. A second group was never fed. A third wasn't fed until the eleventh day, and then suddenly performed as well as the rewarded rats. They had been learning the layout all along but showed it only when it became worth showing. We learn a lot without reward.
Warm touch lowers stress responses in people.

In 2006 James Coan and colleagues put married women in a brain scanner and told them they might get a mild electric shock. Those who held their husband's hand showed less activity in brain areas linked with threat than those who held a stranger's hand or no one's. Physical contact with someone you trust seems to calm the body's alarm system, and the effect was bigger in happier marriages.
The human brain has about 86 billion neurons.

For a long time, textbooks said the human brain has 100 billion neurons, a round number nobody had really counted. In 2009 the Brazilian scientist Suzana Herculano-Houzel and her colleagues did it a different way: they dissolved brain tissue into a uniform soup of cell nuclei and counted samples under the microscope. They arrived at about 86 billion neurons, and roughly the same number of other cells. It's a smaller number than the legend, and it's still more than enough to be astonishing.
A tiny gap where one neuron sends a chemical message to the next.

Neurons don't touch. At the junction, called a synapse, there's a tiny gap, and when a signal arrives, the first cell releases chemical messengers that cross the gap and tell the next cell whether to fire. A single neuron can receive thousands of these connections. Learning works partly by strengthening some synapses and letting others fade, so what you do with your brain changes its physical wiring. That's how a skill you practice turns into something your body just knows.
A neuron's signal is an all-or-nothing electrical spike.

A neuron's signal is a spike of electricity that either happens fully or doesn't happen at all. In 1952 Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley worked out how it travels, using the huge nerve fiber of a squid, which was big enough to put electrodes inside. A stronger stimulus doesn't make a bigger spike. It makes more spikes per second. So the brain's code for "louder" or "brighter" is "faster," like a Geiger counter clicking more rapidly.
A fatty sheath around nerve fibers that makes signals travel much faster.

Many of your nerve fibers are wrapped in a fatty coating called myelin, the way electrical wire has insulation. It makes signals travel dramatically faster, over 100 meters per second in the fastest fibers, compared with about a meter per second in bare ones. In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks the myelin, and messages slow down or stop getting through. It's why the disease can cause weakness, numbness and vision trouble.
Brain cells that are not neurons but do essential work.

Neurons get the attention, but the brain has about as many other cells, called glia, and they do vital work. Astrocytes feed neurons and tidy up their chemical surroundings. Oligodendrocytes make myelin. Microglia act as the brain's cleaners and defenders. "Glia" comes from the Greek for glue, since early anatomists thought that's all they were. It's now known they help shape how circuits work, and they're a very active area of research.
The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of the body's energy.

Your brain is only about 2 percent of your body's weight, but it uses roughly 20 percent of its energy, whether you're thinking hard or lying on the couch. Much of that goes to keeping neurons ready to fire, like an engine idling. Hard concentration adds only a small amount to the constant bill. So "thinking burns lots of calories" is mostly a myth, since your brain is expensive just for being on.
The brain's main accelerator and brake.

Most of the brain's signaling comes down to a push and a pull. Glutamate is the main excitatory messenger, telling neurons to fire. GABA is the main inhibitory one, telling them to calm down. The balance between them matters a great deal, and a lot of medicines work by shifting it. Alcohol and many anti-anxiety drugs, for instance, partly work by boosting the effect of GABA, which is why they feel calming.
A chemical messenger linked to mood, sleep and digestion, made mostly in the gut.

Serotonin is often called the mood chemical, but most of it, about 90 percent, is actually in your gut, where it helps regulate digestion. It doesn't cross from the gut into the brain, which makes its own supply. For decades people said depression comes from low serotonin. A big review in 2022 found no consistent evidence for that simple idea. Serotonin matters for mood, but the story is much more complicated than a single chemical running low.
Dopamine is also needed to start movement.

Dopamine has a reputation as the pleasure chemical, but one of its most important jobs is helping you move. In Parkinson's disease, the cells that make dopamine in a deep part of the brain gradually die. People develop tremors and slowness, and find it hard to start movements. A drug called L-dopa, which the brain turns into dopamine, can restore movement for a time, and it was one of the first great successes of brain chemistry.
A messenger used at the muscles and for attention and memory.

Acetylcholine is the messenger a nerve uses to tell a muscle to contract, so every step you take depends on it. It also plays a role in attention and memory in the brain. Some medicines for Alzheimer's disease try to keep its levels up. And botulinum toxin, the active ingredient in Botox, works by blocking its release, which is why it relaxes muscles and smooths wrinkles.

In the early 1970s scientists found that the brain has receptors that fit opium, which seemed odd. Why would we have receptors for a plant drug? The answer came in 1975, when John Hughes and Hans Kosterlitz isolated the body's own opioid-like molecules, which they named enkephalins. Endorphins are the broader family. They're released during hard exercise, laughter and pain, and they may be part of why a good run can feel wonderful.
A hormone that affects bonding and trust, but not as simply as its "love hormone" nickname suggests.

The "love hormone" or "cuddle hormone" has a lot of press. Oxytocin does help with childbirth and breastfeeding, and it plays a role in bonding. But the claims about nasal sprays making people more trusting have been hard to repeat, and some studies found that it can also increase favoritism toward your own group. Its effects depend heavily on the situation and the person, so the nickname oversimplifies.
The body's main stress hormone, which also follows a daily rhythm.

Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone, but it's not just for emergencies. It follows a daily rhythm, peaking about 30 minutes after you wake up, which helps you get going, and dropping to its lowest at night. Short bursts of it are helpful. When levels stay high for a long time, it can harm memory, immune function and sleep. Both the spike and the recovery matter.
The surge hormone behind a pounding heart and sharp focus.

When you sense danger, your adrenal glands, which sit on top of your kidneys, release adrenaline within seconds. It makes your heart pound, widens your airways, sends blood to your muscles and sharpens your senses, preparing you to fight or flee. In the United States, it's often called epinephrine, which is the same chemical. It's the same one that is in an auto-injector for severe allergic reactions.
The front part of the brain handles planning, impulse control and weighing consequences.

The front part of your brain, behind your forehead, is where planning, impulse control, and weighing consequences largely happen. It's among the last areas to mature, continuing to develop into your mid-twenties, which helps explain teenage risk-taking. Damage to it can leave a person's knowledge and intelligence intact, but make it very hard to plan, to hold back impulses and to carry things through.
An almond-shaped region that tags things as important, especially threats.

The amygdala is a pair of almond-shaped clusters deep in the brain that tag things as important, especially possible threats. A woman with damage to hers, known in the research as S.M., felt almost no fear and had trouble recognizing fear on faces. But it isn't only about fear. The amygdala also responds to what's new, surprising or emotionally charged, whether it's good or bad.
A seahorse-shaped region needed to form new memories and navigate.

The hippocampus, named for its seahorse shape, is crucial for forming new memories and for finding your way around. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire scanned London taxi drivers, who have to memorize thousands of streets, and found that the rear part of their hippocampus was larger than in other people. The more years they'd driven, the bigger it was. It's also one of the first regions affected in Alzheimer's disease.
The "little brain" at the back, with most of the brain's neurons.

The cerebellum sits at the back of the brain and means "little brain." It's small, about 10 percent of the brain's volume, but it contains about 80 percent of its neurons. It smooths and times your movements, keeps your balance and helps you learn skills like riding a bike. Researchers have also found it takes part in language and thinking, so it does more than coordinate muscles.
The brain's relay station for the senses.

Think of the thalamus as a switchboard in the middle of your brain. Almost all of the signals from your senses, except smell, stop there on the way to the outer cortex. It helps decide what gets through. It also plays a part in regulating attention and sleep, so when it's damaged, people can have trouble staying alert or may lose awareness altogether.
A tiny region that keeps the body's internal balance.

The hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond, but it keeps your body in balance. It monitors and adjusts body temperature, thirst, hunger, sleep cycles and the release of many hormones. It's also the link between the brain and the hormone system, directing the pituitary gland. When you shiver, feel hungry, or get sleepy in the evening, the hypothalamus is involved.
Deep brain structures that help select actions and build habits.

Deep in the brain, the basal ganglia help you choose which action to take and when. They're involved in starting and stopping movements, and in turning repeated behavior into habit. Ann Graybiel's work showed that as a routine becomes automatic, these structures change their activity. They're affected in Parkinson's disease, where movement is hard to start, and in Huntington's disease, which causes unwanted movements.
A bundle of about 200 million fibers connecting the two hemispheres.

The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of about 200 million nerve fibers that connects the left and right halves of the brain and lets them share information. In the mid-twentieth century, doctors began cutting it in some people with severe epilepsy, to stop seizures from spreading across the brain. These patients became the subjects of the famous split-brain studies, which taught us a lot about how the two sides work.
A fold deep in the cortex that tracks signals from inside the body.

The insula is a fold of cortex tucked deep inside, and it listens to your body. It's active when you notice your heartbeat, feel nauseated, sense pain or experience disgust. Many scientists think it helps turn raw signals from your body into emotions. A gut feeling, in a literal sense, may involve your insula.
A region that notices conflict and errors.

This region sits in the middle of the brain, curving around the front of the corpus callosum. It's a kind of conflict monitor. It becomes active when two responses compete, as when you have to name the ink color of the word "red" printed in blue. It also lights up when you realize you've made a mistake, and when you feel social pain, such as being excluded. It seems to signal that something needs attention.
The stalk that keeps breathing, heartbeat and alertness going.

The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord, and it runs the basics: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, and the cycle of sleeping and waking. You don't have to think about any of it. That's also why damage to the brainstem is so often fatal. A small injury here can be more serious than a much larger injury in the outer parts of the brain.
A map of the body along the surface of the brain's motor strip.

In the 1930s the neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield, operating on patients who were awake, stimulated the surface of the brain with a small electrode and noted which part of the body moved. He mapped a strip of cortex where each body part has its own patch. When drawn as a figure, it looks like a distorted little person with huge hands, lips and tongue, because those parts need the most precise control.
A region in the left frontal lobe linked to producing speech.

In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca treated a man nicknamed "Tan," because that was nearly the only word he could say, although he could understand speech. After the man died, Broca examined his brain and found damage in a spot in the left frontal lobe. People with damage there still understand language but speak slowly and with effort. It was one of the first clear links between a brain region and a mental function.
A region in the left temporal lobe linked to understanding language.

In 1874 the German doctor Carl Wernicke described patients who had a different problem from Broca's. They could speak fluently, but what they said made little sense, and they had trouble understanding others. Their damage was in a part of the left temporal lobe. The two language areas are linked by a bundle of fibers, and the pair showed that language depends on a network, not on one spot.
When the two halves are disconnected, each can act without the other knowing.

When the connection between the two hemispheres is cut, strange things happen. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga tested these patients in the 1960s. If a word was flashed to the right hemisphere, which can't speak, the patient said they'd seen nothing, yet their left hand could pick out the matching object. Each half seemed to have its own knowledge. Sperry won a Nobel Prize in 1981 for the work.
A railroad worker survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe in 1848.

In 1848 a railroad worker named Phineas Gage was packing explosive powder when it went off and drove an iron rod through the front of his skull. He survived, and a doctor reported that he changed from a responsible man into an impulsive, profane one. Later historians found the story had been exaggerated over time. Gage recovered much of his ability, and spent years working as a stagecoach driver, so the full tale is more complicated.

In some animals, the hippocampus keeps making new neurons through adulthood. Whether people do is hotly debated. In 2018 one team reported that new neurons in the human hippocampus stop forming in childhood, and another team in the same year found evidence that they continue into old age. The different results may come from how brain samples were handled. So the answer, for now, is that nobody is sure.
The brain trims connections it uses less.

A baby's brain has a burst of connection-building, and the number of synapses peaks in early childhood. Then, through adolescence and into early adulthood, the brain trims many of them, keeping the ones that are used. It may sound like a loss, but it makes the circuits more efficient. Pruning is a bit like trimming a hedge. What you're left with is shaped by experience.
A night of sleep cycles through light, deep and REM sleep about every 90 minutes.

A night of sleep isn't one steady state. Over about 90 minutes you go from light sleep into deep sleep and then into REM sleep, and then the cycle repeats four or five times. Deep sleep is concentrated in the first half of the night, and REM sleep gets longer toward morning. That's why cutting your sleep short on the end loses most of your REM, and it may be one reason you feel foggy.
The stage where most vivid dreaming happens.

In 1953 Eugene Aserinsky, a graduate student, and his professor Nathaniel Kleitman noticed that sleepers' eyes darted back and forth under their lids at certain times in the night. When they woke people during that phase, they often reported vivid dreams. It's called rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. In REM, your body's muscles are mostly paralyzed, which keeps you from acting out your dreams.
The brain clears waste more during sleep.

In 2013 Maiken Nedergaard's lab at the University of Rochester reported that in mice, the spaces between brain cells expanded by about 60 percent during sleep, letting cerebrospinal fluid wash through and carry away waste, including proteins linked to Alzheimer's. It suggested that one function of sleep is cleaning house. The evidence in people is still developing, and scientists are debating the details.
Most adults need seven or more hours a night.

In 2015 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society issued a consensus statement based on a panel of experts reviewing the research. It said adults should regularly sleep at least seven hours a night for good health. Needs vary a little from person to person, and a few people truly do well on less. But if you rely on caffeine to get through the day, you're probably not getting enough.
Sleep loss feels like being drunk
Going without sleep impairs you like alcohol.

In studies from the late 1990s, researchers compared the effects of staying awake with the effects of alcohol. After 17 to 19 hours without sleep, people's performance on tests of reaction time and coordination was as poor as at a blood alcohol level of 0.05 percent. After 24 hours it was like 0.10 percent, over the legal driving limit in the United States. Drowsy driving is a real danger.
The mismatch between your body clock and the schedule you keep.

Till Roenneberg, a German chronobiologist, found that many people sleep much later on weekends than on workdays. He called the mismatch "social jetlag," because it's like flying a few time zones west on Friday night and back east on Monday morning. People with a bigger gap tend to be more tired and in a worse mood, and to have more health problems. Keeping a regular wake-up time helps.
The body clock is not exactly 24 hours
