Most people's internal day is about 24 hours and 10 minutes.

Your internal clock runs slightly longer than a day. In 1999 Charles Czeisler and colleagues kept volunteers in dim light for weeks, with no clocks and no daylight cues, and measured an average internal day of 24 hours and 11 minutes. Each morning, light resets the clock to the 24-hour day. That's why a bright morning can make you feel better, and why jet lag takes days to clear.
During puberty the body clock moves later.

During puberty, the body clock moves later. Mary Carskadon at Brown University found that teenagers don't get sleepy until later in the evening, and naturally want to wake later in the morning, and it isn't just laziness. When schools have started later, studies have found that students got more sleep and had better attendance. A 7:30 start asks a teenager to wake at what feels like the middle of their night.
The eye has two kinds of light sensors: rods for dim light and cones for color.

The retina of each eye has two kinds of light sensors. Rods, about 120 million of them, work in dim light but can't see color, which is why the world looks gray at night. Cones, about 6 million, work in bright light and give you color and fine detail. They're concentrated in the center of your vision, where you focus. The two systems together let us see in both starlight and sunshine.
Each eye has a spot with no sensors where the nerve leaves the eye.

Each eye has a place where the optic nerve leaves the back of the eye, and there are no light sensors there. So each of us has a small hole in our vision. We don't notice it, because the brain fills it in using the surroundings and the other eye. You can find yours: close your left eye, look at a mark on the left side of a page with your right eye, and move the page slowly toward you until a second mark to its right disappears.
The eyes do not glide; they jump about three times a second.

Your eyes don't glide smoothly across a scene. They hop about three times a second, in quick jumps called saccades, and stop to take in information between them. During each jump, your vision is briefly suppressed, so you don't see the blur. What feels like a smooth, continuous view is in fact built from many snapshots stitched together by your brain.
Color comes from three types of cone cells, each tuned to a range of light.

Thomas Young proposed in 1802 that the eye has three kinds of color receptors, and later experiments confirmed it. Each type of cone responds best to a different range of light, roughly red, green and blue, and your brain compares their signals to give you the full range of colors. About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a form of color blindness, because the genes involved are on the X chromosome.
A snail-shaped organ where sound becomes nerve signals.

The cochlea, a coiled tube in the inner ear that looks like a snail shell, is where sound turns into nerve signals. It's lined with thousands of tiny hair cells, each tuned to a certain pitch. In humans, once those cells are destroyed, they don't grow back, which is why damage from loud noise is permanent. Young people can hear from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, and the upper range shrinks with age.
Sounds at 85 decibels or above can harm hearing over hours.

Sounds at 85 decibels, about as loud as heavy city traffic, can damage hearing if you hear them for hours. For every 3 decibels louder, the safe time is cut in half. So a rock concert at 100 decibels is safe for only about 15 minutes without protection. Hearing loss from noise builds up silently and permanently, and a pair of cheap foam earplugs makes a real difference.
The tongue detects sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

Your tongue detects five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. The Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified umami in 1908, when he worked out what made seaweed broth so savory. It's the taste of glutamate, found in broth, cheese and ripe tomatoes. You may have seen a "tongue map" with different zones for each taste. It's a myth, and every area of the tongue can detect all five.
Smell has a quick route to the brain's memory and emotion centers.

The sense of smell has a more direct route to the brain's emotional and memory areas than other senses. Scent signals reach the amygdala and hippocampus after only a couple of connections. That may be why a smell, like a perfume or a kitchen, can suddenly bring back a vivid scene from childhood. Studies find that odor-evoked memories tend to be more emotional, though they aren't necessarily more accurate.
A 2014 study said people can tell apart over a trillion odors.

In 2014 a study in Science claimed that humans can tell apart more than a trillion different odors, a number that got a lot of press. Other scientists looked at the math and said the conclusion didn't follow from the data, and the true number could be far lower. We still don't know how many smells people can really distinguish.
The gate control theory of pain
The spinal cord can turn pain signals up or down before they reach the brain.

In 1965 Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed that the spinal cord has a kind of gate that can let pain signals through or block them. Signals from touch, for example, can close the gate, which is why rubbing a bumped elbow helps. Signals from the brain can also open or close it, so your attention, mood and expectations change how much a given injury hurts.
People who lose a limb can still feel it.

After an amputation, many people go on feeling the missing limb, sometimes with pain. V. S. Ramachandran invented a mirror box in the 1990s. A patient puts the intact hand in one side so that its reflection looks like the missing one, then moves it, and some felt relief from the pain. Later trials have had mixed results, so it's an interesting idea that works for some people and not others.
Your sense of where your body is without looking.

Close your eyes and touch your nose. You can do it because of a sense you rarely notice, proprioception, which tells you where your limbs are. In 1906 the physiologist Charles Sherrington gave it the name. Stretch sensors in your muscles, tendons and joints send constant information to the brain. People who lose it, from nerve disease, have to watch their limbs to move them at all.
The inner-ear sensors for balance and head motion.

Deep in each inner ear are three fluid-filled loops that sense rotation of the head, and two small organs that sense tilt and acceleration. Together they're the vestibular system, which keeps you balanced and your gaze steady as you move. Motion sickness happens when the signals from this system don't match what your eyes see, as when you read in a moving car, so your brain gets conflicting reports.
It beats about 100,000 times a day.

Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day without a break. At rest it pumps about five liters of blood around the body each minute, and that's roughly all the blood you have, so a drop of blood makes a complete trip in about a minute. Over a long lifetime it will beat more than 2.5 billion times. It's a muscle, and regular exercise makes it stronger and more efficient.

Skin is the body's largest organ, covering about two square meters in an adult. It keeps water in and germs out, helps regulate your temperature, makes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight, and gives you the sense of touch. The outer layer constantly sheds and replaces itself, about once a month, so some of the dust in a home is shed skin.
The only internal organ that can regrow.

The liver can do something no other internal organ does: regrow. If part of it is removed, as in surgery or in a living donation, the remainder can grow back to nearly the original size within weeks. It's also a chemical workhorse that filters the blood, makes bile for digesting fat, stores sugar and breaks down drugs and toxins. It's why living-donor liver transplants are possible.
Two organs that filter about 180 liters of blood fluid a day.

Your two kidneys filter about 180 liters of fluid from your blood each day, far more than the volume of fluid in the body. Almost all of it is reclaimed, leaving about 1.5 liters to leave as urine. The kidneys keep the balance of salts and water just right, and help control blood pressure. People can live a healthy life with just one, which is why living kidney donation works.
An adult has 206 bones; a baby has about 300.

An adult has 206 bones, but a newborn has around 300. Many of a baby's bones fuse together as it grows, such as the separate plates of the skull and the bones at the base of the spine. Bone isn't dead. It's living tissue that constantly rebuilds itself, with old bone absorbed and new bone laid down, and it gets stronger with weight-bearing exercise.
A muscle can only pull, never push.

A muscle can only contract. It can pull, but it can never push. That's why muscles work in pairs on either side of a joint: one bends your elbow and its partner straightens it. The body has more than 600 muscles. The heart is a special kind, which works without ever stopping. Moving the body well is a matter of timing and coordination between them.
The body holds about as many bacteria as human cells.

The human body hosts trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria in the gut. For years, it was said that they outnumbered our own cells ten to one. In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo recalculated and found about 38 trillion bacteria and about 30 trillion human cells, closer to even. They help digest food, make some vitamins and train the immune system, and scientists are still learning how much they affect health.
The gut and brain send signals both ways, mainly through the vagus nerve.

Your gut and your brain are in constant conversation, mostly along the vagus nerve, a long nerve that runs between them. It's why stress can upset your stomach and why anxiety can make your gut feel tight. In animal studies, changes in gut bacteria change behavior. How much this affects human mood is still being worked out, and claims made for probiotics are ahead of the evidence.
The body has a fast, general defense and a slower, specific one.

The immune system has two parts. The innate part is fast and general: within hours, cells such as macrophages attack anything that looks foreign. The adaptive part is slower but precise. T cells and B cells learn the particular shape of a germ over days, and make antibodies. Afterward, memory cells remember it, sometimes for decades, which is the principle behind vaccines.
A raised temperature is a defense, not just a symptom.

A fever feels miserable, but it's part of the body's defense. A higher temperature slows the growth of many germs and helps your immune cells work faster. Treating a mild fever is mainly for comfort, and it isn't always necessary. A very high fever, or any fever in a young infant, is a reason to see a doctor, since it can signal a serious infection.
"Boosting" immunity is not a scientific idea.

You see "immune boosting" on supplement labels, but scientifically it isn't a meaningful idea. The immune system isn't a muscle that gets stronger the more it's stimulated. It's a balance, and an overactive one is what causes allergies and autoimmune diseases. What actually supports it is plain: enough sleep, regular exercise, a balanced diet, vaccination, not smoking and managing stress.
The immune system reacts to a harmless thing as if it were dangerous.

An allergy is when the immune system treats something harmless, such as pollen or peanut, as a threat and produces antibodies called IgE against it. The next exposure triggers sneezing, itching or, in serious cases, anaphylaxis. For years parents were told to keep peanuts away from babies. In 2015 the LEAP trial showed the opposite: giving peanut foods early to infants at high risk cut their chance of a peanut allergy by about 80 percent.
The hormone that moves sugar from blood into cells.

Insulin is the hormone that tells your cells to take up sugar from the blood. In 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in a Toronto lab, isolated it, and in January 1922 a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson, who was dying of type 1 diabetes, got the first injection. Within a year, people who would have died within months were being kept alive. It's one of the great stories of modern medicine.
A hormone from fat cells that tells the brain how much energy is stored.

In 1994 Jeffrey Friedman's team at Rockefeller University discovered leptin, a hormone made by fat cells that signals to the brain how much energy is stored. Mice that lack it eat constantly and become very obese, and so do rare people with the same genetic fault. Most people with obesity, however, have high levels of leptin and the brain has become less responsive to it. It showed that body weight is regulated by hormones.
About 3 billion letters long, and 99.9% the same as anyone else's.

The human genome is about 3 billion letters long, and any two people share about 99.9 percent of them. There are around 20,000 genes that code for proteins, but they make up only 1 or 2 percent of the sequence. The rest includes regulatory regions and a lot we're still learning about. Small differences in those letters help explain why people differ in traits and in disease risk.
Exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, in empty space.

Light in empty space travels at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second. It's exact because we define it that way. Since 1983 the meter has been defined as the distance light covers in 1/299,792,458 of a second, so the speed fixes the length. It's also the same for every observer, however fast they're moving, which is the strange fact that Einstein built relativity on. Nothing that has mass can ever reach it.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us.

Light takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to get from the Sun to Earth. So when you look at the Sun, which you shouldn't do directly, you're seeing it as it was a little over eight minutes ago. If the Sun disappeared, we wouldn't know for those eight minutes. The next-nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is just over four light-years away, so its light shows you the star as it was more than four years ago.
Things keep their motion, force makes them accelerate, and forces come in pairs.

In 1687 Isaac Newton published three rules of motion in his Principia. An object keeps doing what it's doing unless a force acts on it. A force makes an object accelerate, more for a lighter object. And forces come in pairs: when you push on something, it pushes back equally. A rocket works through the third law. It throws gas backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward. It doesn't need air to push against, which is why rockets work in space.
In a vacuum, a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate.

Galileo is said to have shown that heavy and light objects fall together. In 1971, astronaut David Scott tested it on the Moon, where there's no air. He held a geologist's hammer and a falcon feather at shoulder height, let go, and both hit the lunar dust at the same moment, on live television. On Earth, air resistance holds the feather back. Without it, gravity treats everything the same.
Energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. A pendulum swaps motion for height and back. A battery turns chemical energy into electricity and then into light or motion. Several scientists reached the idea in the 1840s, and Hermann von Helmholtz set out the law in its general form in 1847. It's one of the most reliable rules in physics, and no machine that gets energy from nothing has ever worked.
The lowest possible temperature is about -273.15 degrees Celsius, or 0 kelvin.

The lowest temperature there could be is about minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, or zero on the Kelvin scale. At that point, the particles in a substance would have as little motion as physics allows. Scientists have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a degree above it, but the laws of thermodynamics say you can't reach it exactly. The coldest natural place we know of, the Boomerang Nebula, is about one degree above.
Current equals voltage divided by resistance.

In 1827 the German schoolteacher Georg Ohm published what became the first rule of electrical circuits: the current through a conductor equals the voltage across it divided by its resistance. Double the voltage across a fixed resistor, and the current doubles. Double the resistance, and the current halves. It was dismissed at first, and Ohm struggled for years. Now every electrician uses it, and the unit of resistance carries his name.
Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
A lightning bolt heats the air to about 30,000 kelvin.

A bolt of lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 kelvin, roughly five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun, which is about 5,800 kelvin. The heating is so sudden that the air expands faster than the speed of sound, producing a shock wave. That's the thunder you hear. You can estimate how far away a strike was by counting the seconds between the flash and the sound, about five seconds per mile.
The field shields us from charged particles and has flipped many times.

Earth's core acts like a giant magnet, and its field deflects charged particles from the Sun, which helps protect life. The field isn't fixed, though. Rocks record that its direction has reversed many times. The last full flip was about 780,000 years ago, and after one, a compass needle would point south. A reversal takes thousands of years, and nothing suggests one would be a catastrophe, but nobody knows when the next will be.
In air at 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels about 343 meters per second.

In air at 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels at about 343 meters per second, roughly a kilometer every three seconds. It moves faster through liquids and solids: about 1,480 meters per second in water, and over 5,000 in steel. The reason is that denser, stiffer materials pass vibrations along more quickly. It's why you can hear an approaching train by putting an ear to the rail before you hear it in the air.
A moving source's pitch rises as it approaches and falls as it leaves.

When a source of sound moves toward you, the waves are squeezed together and the pitch sounds higher. When it moves away, the waves are stretched and the pitch drops. You hear it when an ambulance passes. Christian Doppler proposed the idea in 1842, and in 1845 the Dutch scientist Buys Ballot tested it with trumpeters playing a steady note on a moving train. Astronomers use the same effect with light to measure how fast distant galaxies are moving.
Why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge fell
The 1940 collapse was caused by wind making the deck twist, not simple resonance.

In November 1940 a new suspension bridge in Washington state twisted wildly in a moderate wind and collapsed. Many physics textbooks used to call it a simple case of resonance. Later analysis showed it was something more subtle, called aerodynamic flutter, in which the twisting motion of the deck changes how the wind pushes on it, which feeds more energy into the motion. Engineers have designed bridges to avoid it since.
White light is a mix of colors, and a prism splits it.

Before Newton, many people thought a prism added colors to white light. In 1666 he showed otherwise. He sent a beam of sunlight through one prism and it spread into a rainbow. Then he sent the colors through a second prism turned the other way, and they came back together as white. So white light is a mixture of all the colors, and the prism only separates them. A rainbow does the same thing using raindrops.
Light and matter behave like waves and particles.

In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw a pattern of bright and dark stripes on a screen behind them, which is what waves do when they overlap. A century later, scientists found that light also comes in particles. Then in 1927 Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer found that electrons behave like waves too. Later experiments sent single electrons, one at a time, through the slits, and the stripes still built up.
You cannot know both a particle's exact position and momentum at once.

In 1927 Werner Heisenberg showed that you can't know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a particle at the same time. The more precisely you pin down one, the fuzzier the other becomes. It's often described as the effect of measuring disturbing the thing measured. But the deeper point is that it's built into nature: a particle simply doesn't have a perfectly sharp position and a perfectly sharp velocity together.
Until measured, a quantum system is described by a combination of possibilities.

In quantum mechanics, a particle can be in a combination of states at once, until it's measured. Erwin Schrödinger found this so strange that in 1935 he made up a thought experiment in which a cat in a box is linked to a quantum event, so that it's both alive and dead until someone opens the box. He meant it as a criticism, to show how odd the idea gets when scaled up. Physicists still debate what a measurement actually does.
Two particles can share a state so that measuring one tells you about the other.

Two particles can be linked so that measuring one instantly tells you something about the other, however far apart they are. Einstein didn't like it and called it "spooky action at a distance." But experiments, from Alain Aspect's in the early 1980s to tests with no loopholes in 2015, have confirmed that it's real. Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work. It doesn't let you send messages faster than light.
Particles can pass through barriers they classically could not.

In everyday life, a ball can't roll through a hill that's higher than its energy. In the quantum world, particles sometimes can. This is called tunneling, and it's how the Sun shines: protons in its core don't have quite enough energy to overcome their mutual repulsion and fuse, but a few tunnel through, enough to keep it burning. The effect is also used in scanning tunneling microscopes, and in the flash memory in phones.
Light knocks electrons from metal only if its frequency is high enough, no matter how bright.

When light hits a metal surface, it can knock electrons loose, but only if its frequency is high enough. A dim blue light does it, while a very bright red light doesn't. Physicists couldn't explain that with waves. In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in packets of energy, later called photons, and each must carry enough energy to free an electron. This, and not relativity, won him the 1921 Nobel Prize.
The nucleus is about 1/100,000 the size of the atom.

In 1911 Ernest Rutherford's team fired particles at thin gold foil and found that most went straight through, but a few bounced right back. He concluded that an atom has a tiny, dense nucleus with mostly empty space around it. The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller than the atom. If the atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea at the center. Things feel solid because of the electric forces between atoms.
Gravity is the bending of space and time by mass and energy.

In 1915 Einstein published a new theory of gravity. Instead of a force, he described it as the bending of space and time by mass and energy. Matter tells space how to curve, and curved space tells matter how to move. In 1919, during a solar eclipse, Arthur Eddington's expeditions measured starlight bending as it passed the Sun, by an amount consistent with Einstein's prediction. It made him world-famous overnight.
Ripples in spacetime, first detected in 2015.

Einstein predicted in 1916 that moving masses would send out ripples in spacetime. They're incredibly faint. On September 14, 2015, the LIGO detectors in Louisiana and Washington picked up a signal from two black holes that had merged 1.3 billion light-years away. The stretching of space they measured was thousands of times smaller than the width of a proton. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish won the 2017 Nobel Prize for it.
Regions where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, escapes.

A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from inside its boundary, called the event horizon. They form when very massive stars collapse. The first image of one, in the galaxy M87, was released in 2019 by the Event Horizon Telescope. In 2022 the same team showed the black hole at the center of our own galaxy, which is about four million times the mass of the Sun.
Black holes slowly lose mass by emitting faint radiation.

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that, thanks to quantum effects near the event horizon, black holes should slowly lose mass by emitting a faint glow of radiation. It means they aren't completely black, and that they can eventually evaporate. For a black hole of the size we know, the process would take far, far longer than the current age of the universe. No one has ever detected the radiation, since it's far too weak.
Clocks tick slower where gravity is stronger.

General relativity predicts that time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. A clock at sea level ticks slightly slower than one on a mountain top. In 2010 researchers at NIST measured it with extremely precise atomic clocks that were only about 33 centimeters, a foot, apart in height. The difference was tiny but real. It also matters in practice: GPS satellites need to correct for it, or they'd drift by kilometers each day.
The universe has been expanding from an extremely hot, dense state for about 13.8 billion years.

The evidence says the universe began as an incredibly hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, and has been expanding and cooling since. The Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître first proposed it in 1927. Three main things support it: galaxies are moving apart, the whole sky glows with leftover radiation, and the proportions of hydrogen and helium match the predictions. It describes what happened after the beginning, not what caused it.
Faint radiation from the early universe fills all of space.

In 1964 two radio astronomers at Bell Labs, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were bothered by a faint hiss in their big horn antenna. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings, thinking they might be the cause. The hiss turned out to be the afterglow of the Big Bang, light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old and had cooled enough to become transparent. They won the 1978 Nobel Prize.
Distant galaxies move away from us, and the farther they are, the faster.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that galaxies are moving away from us, and that the farther away they are, the faster they're receding. This built on the 1927 work of Georges Lemaître. It doesn't mean we're at the center. Space itself is stretching, so every galaxy sees the others moving away, like dots on the surface of an inflating balloon. It was the first key observation behind the Big Bang model.
Unseen matter holds galaxies together with its gravity.

In the 1970s the astronomer Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit at the edges of galaxies. They moved as fast as the stars near the center, which didn't match the visible matter. The best explanation is that there's an unseen halo of matter whose gravity holds everything together. It makes up about 27 percent of the universe. We don't know what it's made of, and experiments around the world are trying to find out.
Something is making the universe's expansion speed up.

In 1998 two teams studying distant exploding stars expected to find that the expansion of the universe was slowing down because of gravity. Instead, they found it was speeding up. Something is pushing space apart, and it's been named dark energy. It makes up about 68 percent of the universe, and nobody knows what it is. The leaders of the two teams shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Everything you can see, atoms and all, is about 5% of the universe.

Everything you can see, from the Earth to the stars to you, is made of ordinary atoms, and all of that is only about 5 percent of the universe. The other 95 percent is dark matter, about 27 percent, and dark energy, about 68 percent. The measurements come mainly from satellites studying the cosmic microwave background. We've learned that most of the universe is something we don't yet understand.
The part we can see is about 93 billion light-years across.

The part of the universe we can see is about 93 billion light-years across. That may sound odd, since the universe is only 13.8 billion years old. But space has been stretching all the while light was traveling to us, so the distance to the places that sent us the oldest light is much larger now. There may well be more beyond the edge, but its light hasn't had time to reach us.
Our galaxy has 100 to 400 billion stars and spans about 100,000 light-years.

Our galaxy is a spiral of somewhere between 100 and 400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. We live in one of its arms, about halfway out from the center. The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once around. In roughly four to five billion years the Milky Way will merge with its nearest large neighbor, the Andromeda galaxy, which is heading our way.
A middle-aged star, about 4.6 billion years old.

The Sun is a middle-aged star, about 4.6 billion years old. Every second, in its core, it turns about 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, and the small amount of mass that vanishes in the process becomes the energy that warms us. It has enough fuel for roughly another five billion years. After that it will swell into a red giant, and then shrink into a white dwarf.
A star's mass decides how it lives and dies.

A star's life is decided mainly by its mass. Small ones, called red dwarfs, burn their fuel slowly and can last trillions of years. Massive stars burn fast and bright, lasting only millions of years, and end in a supernova explosion that leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole. Our Sun, in the middle, will end more quietly as a white dwarf, a small, dense, cooling ember.
The carbon, oxygen and iron in your body were made in stars.

Just after the Big Bang, the universe was almost entirely hydrogen and helium. Every heavier element, including the carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe and the iron in your blood, was made later inside stars, and was scattered into space when stars died. Some heavy elements also come from the collisions of neutron stars. In a real sense, you're made of material that was cooked in stars.
The collapsed cores of massive stars, packing the Sun's mass into a city-size ball.

When a massive star explodes as a supernova, its core can collapse into a neutron star, a ball only about 20 kilometers across but with more mass than the Sun. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons. Some neutron stars spin hundreds of times a second. They're among the densest things in the universe, short of black holes.
Jocelyn Bell Burnell found a signal in 1967 that pulsed every 1.34 seconds.

In 1967 a graduate student at Cambridge, Jocelyn Bell, noticed a strange signal in her radio telescope data: a pulse repeating every 1.337 seconds, as regular as a clock. The team half-jokingly named it LGM-1, for "little green men." It turned out to be a rapidly spinning neutron star, sweeping a beam of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, shared the 1974 Nobel Prize for the discovery. She was not included.
The closest supernova in modern times, seen in 1987.

On February 23, 1987, astronomers saw a star explode in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy next to ours, about 168,000 light-years away. It was the closest supernova in about four centuries. A few hours before the light arrived, detectors deep underground in Japan and the US caught a burst of neutrinos, ghostly particles produced in the explosion, confirming how such stars die.
In 2017 astronomers saw two neutron stars collide and make heavy elements.

In August 2017, detectors picked up gravitational waves from two neutron stars spiraling into each other 130 million light-years away. Telescopes around the world watched the glow that followed. It showed signs of heavy elements being created, including gold and platinum. It helped answer a long-standing question about where the heaviest elements come from.
The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with a year of 88 days.

The closest planet to the Sun is also the smallest, a little bigger than our Moon. A year there lasts just 88 days. With almost no atmosphere to hold in heat, its temperature swings wildly, from about 430 degrees Celsius in the day to about minus 180 at night. Even so, scientists have found water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles.
A planet with a day longer than its year.

Venus is a strange world: it spins backward and so slowly that a day, 243 Earth days, is longer than its year of 225 days. Its thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect, making it the hottest planet at about 465 degrees Celsius, hotter than Mercury, even though it's farther from the Sun. The pressure at the surface is about 90 times Earth's.
You are moving about 30 kilometers per second around the Sun.

You're sitting still, but you're traveling. Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 kilometers per second, nearly 70,000 miles per hour. At the equator, the planet's spin carries you eastward at about 1,670 kilometers per hour. You don't feel any of it, because the speed is smooth and steady and everything around you is moving along with you. We notice only changes in motion.
The red planet owes its color to iron oxide, or rust.

Mars looks red because its surface is rich in iron oxide, which is rust. It has the biggest volcano known in the solar system, Olympus Mons, about 22 kilometers high, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest. Billions of years ago, it had rivers and lakes of liquid water, and rovers have found signs of old streambeds. Today it's cold and dry, with a thin atmosphere.
A giant that could hold more than 1,300 Earths.

Jupiter is by far the largest planet, with enough volume to hold more than 1,300 Earths. It's made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface to land on. Its Great Red Spot is a giant storm, wider than Earth, that has been observed for at least 150 years. Its strong gravity has probably shaped the solar system, and has pulled in comets and asteroids.
A planet less dense than water.

Saturn is the least dense planet in the solar system, with an average density lower than water. In theory, it would float if you could find a bathtub big enough. Its famous rings are made mostly of water ice, in pieces from dust to house-size boulders, and they spread out over hundreds of thousands of kilometers, yet in places they're only about ten meters thick.
A planet that spins on its side, tilted about 98 degrees.

Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it spins almost on its side, like a rolling ball. As a result, each pole gets 42 years of constant sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness. William Herschel found it in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope. A giant collision early in the planet's history may have knocked it over, though no one is sure.
Found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it.

Neptune was found with mathematics before anyone saw it. After Uranus was discovered, astronomers noticed its orbit wasn't quite as predicted, and in 1846 Urbain Le Verrier in France, and John Couch Adams in England, each calculated where an unseen planet must be. Johann Galle in Berlin pointed his telescope at the spot Le Verrier gave and found it that very night. Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 kilometers per hour.
Reclassified in 2006 as a dwarf planet.

Pluto was called the ninth planet from its discovery in 1930 until 2006, when the International Astronomical Union voted to define a planet as something that has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto hasn't, so it became a dwarf planet. In July 2015 NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew by it and showed a surprisingly active world, including a large heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen.
The Moon was probably made when a Mars-size body hit the young Earth.

The leading explanation, developed in the 1970s, is that about 4.5 billion years ago a planet-sized body, which has been called Theia, struck the young Earth. The debris from the collision orbited the planet and gradually came together as the Moon. Moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts have a chemistry very close to Earth's outer layers, which fits the idea. It's called the giant-impact hypothesis.
Two bulges of ocean follow the Moon around Earth.

The Moon's gravity pulls more strongly on the side of Earth nearest it and less on the far side. That stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side, and as Earth turns, coastlines pass through both, giving most places two high tides a day. The Sun adds its own pull. When Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon, the tides are higher, called spring tides.
It moves about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth each year.

The Moon is moving away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters a year, roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow. Scientists know this because Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the surface, and lasers fired from Earth bounce off them, letting us measure the distance to within a few millimeters. As it recedes, Earth's rotation slows slightly, so our days get gradually longer.
Why we only see one side of the Moon
The Moon turns exactly once for every orbit.

The Moon spins exactly once for every trip it makes around Earth, so the same face always points toward us. It's called tidal locking, and it happened because Earth's gravity slowly slowed the Moon's spin until the two matched. It's not a "dark side," though. The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. It was first photographed by a Soviet spacecraft in 1959.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away.

By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look nearly the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes exactly in front of the Sun, it can cover the disk completely and reveal the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona. Because the Moon is slowly drifting away, in about 600 million years it will be too small to cover the Sun fully.
The most volcanically active world in the solar system.

Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active place in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes. The reason is tidal heating: Jupiter and its other big moons tug on Io, squeezing and flexing it constantly, which heats the interior. Its volcanoes spray sulfurous material hundreds of kilometers into space. Voyager 1 spotted the first plumes in 1979, and an image analyst, Linda Morabito, noticed them.
A moon of Jupiter with an ocean of salty water under its icy shell.

Europa, a moon of Jupiter, has a surface of ice, and under it is an ocean of salty liquid water, kept warm by tidal flexing. It may contain twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans. Because liquid water is one ingredient of life as we know it, scientists are very interested. NASA launched the Europa Clipper spacecraft in 2024 to fly past it dozens of times and study whether it could be habitable.
Saturn's moon has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane.

Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and the only other place in the solar system where we've seen stable liquid on the surface. But it's not water: it's lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane, at about minus 180 degrees Celsius. In 2005 the Huygens probe landed there, and sent back pictures of a landscape that looks eerily like a shoreline.
A small moon of Saturn that sprays water into space.

Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn, only about 500 kilometers across. In 2005 the Cassini spacecraft discovered jets of water vapor and ice particles shooting from cracks near its south pole. Later flybys found salt, organic molecules and hydrogen in the spray, which suggests there's a liquid ocean beneath the ice and active chemistry. It's among the most promising places to look for life beyond Earth.
Between Mars and Jupiter orbit millions of rocky bodies, but they are far apart.

In movies, the belt between Mars and Jupiter is crowded with rocks, and ships weave between them. In reality it's mostly empty space. There are millions of asteroids, but they're spread so far apart that spacecraft have passed through without any close calls. The total mass of the belt is less than that of our Moon, and about a third of it is in the largest body, the dwarf planet Ceres.
An asteroid about 10 kilometers wide struck Mexico 66 million years ago.

About 66 million years ago, an asteroid roughly 10 kilometers wide struck what is now the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. In 1980 the father-and-son team of Luis and Walter Alvarez noticed a thin layer of clay around the world rich in iridium, a metal common in asteroids, and suggested that it came from an impact. In the 1990s, the buried Chicxulub crater was identified as the site. About three-quarters of species died.
It returns about every 76 years; last seen in 1986, next due in 2061.

Halley's comet comes back about every 76 years. It was last seen in 1986, and it's due again in 2061. In 1705 Edmond Halley noticed that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had similar orbits, and he used Newton's new laws to predict it would return in 1758. It did, after his death, and it was the first comet shown to travel in a regular orbit, a major triumph for Newtonian physics.
The most distant human-made object, launched in 1977.

Launched in 1977 to study the outer planets, Voyager 1 is now the most distant human-made object, and it entered interstellar space in 2012. It's still sending data from over 24 billion kilometers away, on only a couple of hundred watts of power. Attached to its side is a gold-plated record containing greetings in 55 languages, music and sounds from Earth, in case anyone ever finds it.
A 1990 photo from Voyager 1 shows Earth as a point of light.

In 1990, as Voyager 1 was leaving the solar system, Carl Sagan asked NASA to turn its camera back for one last look. In the resulting picture, from about 6 billion kilometers away, Earth is less than a single pixel, a tiny speck in a ray of sunlight. Sagan wrote of it that everyone you love, everyone you know, lived their lives on that dot. It's become a symbol of our place in the universe.
The first humans on the Moon
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on July 20, 1969.

On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle on the Moon, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit above in the command module. They spent about two and a half hours walking on the surface, collecting samples and setting up experiments, and brought back 21.5 kilograms of lunar rock and soil. About 600 million people watched on television.
The first satellite flew in 1957 and the first person in space in 1961.

On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a polished metal ball that beeped as it orbited Earth. It was the first artificial satellite and it started the Space Race. Less than four years later, on April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and completed one orbit in 108 minutes. Many people in the US were shocked, and it spurred major investment in science education.
Launched in 1990, it has changed our picture of the universe.

Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere, which blurs the view from the ground. Its first mirror was ground to the wrong shape, giving blurry images, until astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993. After that it transformed astronomy. It helped measure how fast the universe is expanding, and its "Deep Field" images revealed thousands of galaxies in a patch of sky the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length.
A giant infrared telescope that began its work in 2022.

The James Webb telescope launched on Christmas Day 2021 and began science work in 2022. It's an infrared telescope with a mirror 6.5 meters across, made of 18 gold-coated segments, and it sits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, shielded from the Sun by a tennis-court-sized sunshield. Because infrared passes through dust, it can see galaxies that formed in the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

Until 1995, we didn't know whether any other stars had planets. That year Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet orbiting the Sun-like star 51 Pegasi, a gas giant that circles its star in just four days. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Since then, astronomers have confirmed more than 5,000 exoplanets, and it appears that most stars have planets. Many are very unlike anything in our own solar system.
The range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface.

The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface, not too hot and not too cold, sometimes called the "Goldilocks zone." Being in it doesn't guarantee life or even water. Venus and Mars both lie close to the edges of the Sun's zone, and their very different atmospheres have made them hostile to life as we know it.
A way to organize the question of how many civilizations might be out there.

In 1961 the astronomer Frank Drake wrote a formula to organize the question of how many civilizations in our galaxy might be able to communicate with us. It multiplies factors like the rate of star formation, the fraction of stars with planets, the fraction of those where life arises, and how long civilizations last. We know a few of the numbers and have to guess the rest, so answers range from "we're alone" to "millions."
If life is common, where is everybody?

Around 1950 the physicist Enrico Fermi was having lunch with colleagues, discussing extraterrestrial life, when he asked, "Where is everybody?" If the galaxy is so old and so large, and life is common, why haven't we seen any sign of it? Suggested answers include that life is rare, that civilizations destroy themselves, or that we haven't looked in the right way. No one knows which, if any, is right.
Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.

In 1956 the geochemist Clair Patterson measured the ratios of lead isotopes in a meteorite and calculated that the Earth is about 4.55 billion years old. His reasoning was that meteorites formed at the same time as the planets. Later methods have refined the number slightly, to 4.54 billion, and it has held up. Patterson went on to discover that leaded gasoline was spreading lead around the planet, and he campaigned successfully to end its use.
Elements sorted by atomic number fall into repeating families.

Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, published his table in 1869. He arranged the known elements by weight and noticed that their properties repeated in a pattern. Where the pattern broke, he left a gap and boldly predicted that an element would be found to fill it, along with what it would be like. Gallium, scandium and germanium were discovered over the next seventeen years, and each matched his descriptions closely. That's what convinced chemists he was right.
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus decides which element it is.

What makes an element what it is? Not its weight, as early chemists thought, but the number of protons in its nucleus. In 1913 the young English physicist Henry Moseley measured the X-rays given off by different elements and found that their frequencies followed a neat series of whole numbers. That fixed the true order of the table, and showed exactly where the gaps were. Change the number of protons in an atom and you've changed the element.
Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon barely react with anything.

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon sit in the last column of the table, and they hardly react with anything. Their outer shells of electrons are full, so they have no reason to take part in chemistry. That's why airships and balloons now use helium instead of flammable hydrogen, and why the glowing gas in a neon sign doesn't burn or wear out. They were nicknamed "noble" because they keep to themselves.
The soft, shiny metals in the first column react violently with water.

The metals in the first column, lithium, sodium, potassium and the rest, are soft enough to cut with a knife and react strongly with water. Lithium fizzes, sodium skates around and burns, and potassium bursts into a lilac flame. Each atom has a single loose electron on the outside that it's eager to give away. The further you go down the column, the looser the electron and the more violent the reaction.
Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine, one electron short of a full shell.

Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine are one electron short of a full outer shell, so they're eager to grab one from another atom. That makes them very reactive, and they readily form salts. In fact "halogen" comes from Greek words meaning "salt-former." Fluorine is the most reactive of all the elements, and will even react with glass. Chlorine and iodine are used as disinfectants.
The 15 lanthanides are fairly common in Earth's crust but hard to separate.

The fifteen elements called the lanthanides, plus two relatives, are called rare earths, but the name is misleading. Cerium is about as common in Earth's crust as copper. What's rare is finding them concentrated in a spot where mining is worthwhile, and they're hard to separate from one another. They're in many things we use daily: magnets in headphones and electric motors, phone screens, lasers and lighting.
The lightest element and the most common in the universe.

Hydrogen has one proton and one electron, the simplest atom there is. It accounts for about three-quarters of all ordinary matter by mass, and it's what stars burn to make light. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave it its name in 1783, from the Greek words for "water-former," because when hydrogen burns, it makes water. It's also being developed as a clean fuel, since burning it produces only water.
A gas first found on the Sun before it was found on Earth.

In 1868, during a solar eclipse, astronomers saw a bright yellow line in the Sun's spectrum that didn't match any known element. They named the new element after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. Only in 1895 did the chemist William Ramsay find it on Earth, in a uranium mineral. On Earth it forms from radioactive decay deep underground and gets trapped in natural gas, from which we collect it. Once it escapes, it floats off to space.
The lightest metal; it is soft enough to cut with a knife and floats on water.

The lightest metal is so soft that you can cut it with a knife, and it floats on water. A Swedish chemist, Johan Arfwedson, found it in 1817. Today most people carry some in their pocket, in the lithium-ion battery that powers a phone. Lithium salts have also been used since the mid-twentieth century to treat bipolar disorder, as a mood stabilizer.
A light, stiff metal that is toxic as dust.

Beryllium is a light, stiff metal that is toxic as dust, so it's handled with care. Its qualities make it ideal for space: the 18 mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope are made of beryllium, coated with a thin layer of gold to reflect infrared light. In nature it also colors gems. Emerald and aquamarine are both forms of the mineral beryl.
An element that makes tough glass and plant cell walls.

Boron compounds are in more everyday things than you might guess. Borosilicate glass, the type used for lab glassware and some oven-safe dishes, can handle sudden changes in temperature without cracking. Borax, a boron mineral, has been mined for thousands of years and was used in ancient times for soldering gold. Plants also need a trace of boron to build healthy cell walls.
The backbone of all known life, in diamond, graphite and graphene.

Carbon atoms can link up in an astonishing variety of ways, which is why the chemistry of life is built on it. About 18 percent of your body's mass is carbon. Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, differently arranged. In 2004 Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov peeled single-atom-thick layers of graphite from a lump using sticky tape, making graphene, and they won the 2010 Nobel Prize for it.
Makes up 78% of the air we breathe, but plants cannot use it directly.

Nitrogen makes up 78 percent of the air, but plants can't use it in that form. For centuries farmers depended on manure and natural deposits. Between 1909 and 1913 the chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch worked out how to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia on a large scale, making artificial fertilizer possible. Roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body were fixed by the Haber-Bosch process.
The gas that makes up 21% of air and about 65% of your body's mass.

Oxygen is about 21 percent of the air, and about 65 percent of your body's mass, mostly as the oxygen in water. The Swedish chemist Carl Scheele and the English minister Joseph Priestley each found it independently in the 1770s, and Antoine Lavoisier worked out that it was what made things burn. Most of the oxygen in the air was produced by photosynthesis, by plants, algae and bacteria, over billions of years.
The most reactive of all the elements.

Fluorine is the most chemically reactive of all the elements, so it's hard to isolate. For decades, chemists were injured, and some were killed, by the poisonous fumes while trying. The French chemist Henri Moissan finally succeeded in 1886 and won a Nobel Prize for it. Fluoride, a compound of fluorine, is added to many toothpastes and water supplies because it strengthens tooth enamel and reduces cavities.
The gas that glows red-orange in a sign.

Neon was found in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers, who chilled air until it turned liquid and then let it boil off piece by piece. A noble gas, it glows a bright red-orange when electricity passes through it. It's not used in all signs called neon, though. Many use other gases, such as argon, or coatings inside the glass tubes, to produce other colors.
A soft metal that reacts violently with water and is half of table salt.

Sodium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts violently with water. In 1807 Humphry Davy was the first to isolate it, by passing an electric current through molten sodium hydroxide. Table salt is sodium combined with chlorine, a gas that's poisonous by itself. It's a striking example of how two dangerous substances can join to make something we eat every day. Your nerves also use sodium to carry signals.
A light metal that burns with a blinding white flame.

Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame, which is why it was used in the old camera flashes and in fireworks. It's also at the center of every chlorophyll molecule, the green pigment plants use to catch sunlight. In your body, it helps more than 300 enzymes work, and it's found in foods like nuts, seeds and leafy greens.
The most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8% of it.

Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, but it's always combined with other elements, and was very difficult to extract. For a time in the 1800s it was more valuable than gold. In 1886 two young inventors, Charles Hall in the US and Paul Héroult in France, independently found a way to extract it using electricity, and the price collapsed within a few years.
The second most abundant element in Earth's crust, and the basis of computer chips.

Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen. Sand and most rocks are silicon compounds. In its ultrapure crystal form it's a semiconductor, meaning it can be made to conduct electricity or not, which makes it the foundation of computer chips. California's "Silicon Valley" is named for it.
An element essential to DNA, cell membranes and the energy molecule ATP.

Phosphorus is essential to life: it's in DNA, in cell membranes and in ATP, the molecule that carries energy within cells. It was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, a German alchemist who was searching for the philosopher's stone and boiled down enormous quantities of urine. He ended up with a white substance that glowed in the dark. Today, much of it goes into fertilizer.
A yellow solid whose compounds smell like rotten eggs.

Sulfur is a yellow solid that has been known since ancient times. The "rotten egg" smell we associate with it comes from hydrogen sulfide gas, not from pure sulfur. In 1839 Charles Goodyear discovered that heating rubber with sulfur made it stronger and less sticky, a process called vulcanization. It made possible things like tires, shoe soles and rubber hoses.
A gas that disinfects water and was also used as a weapon.

Chlorine is a greenish, poisonous gas, and it's one of the most useful chemicals in public health. Adding small amounts to drinking water kills germs and has dramatically reduced diseases such as cholera and typhoid. But it also has a dark history. The German army first used it as a weapon on April 22, 1915, at the Second Battle of Ypres in the First World War.
About 1% of the air; its name means "lazy."

In 1894 Lord Rayleigh noticed that nitrogen taken from the air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made from chemicals. He and William Ramsay tracked down the difference to a previously unknown gas making up about 1 percent of the air. They named it argon, from the Greek for "lazy," because it won't react with anything. Light bulbs are often filled with it, to protect the filament.
A metal your nerves and heart need to work.

Potassium is a soft metal that reacts even more violently with water than sodium, and the hydrogen it releases ignites with a lilac flame. In your body it works with sodium to carry nerve signals and keep your heartbeat steady. A banana has about 420 milligrams, but many other foods, including potatoes, beans and avocados, have more, and most people don't get enough.
The most abundant metal in your body, with about 99% in bones and teeth.

Calcium is the most abundant metal in the human body, and about 99 percent of it is stored in bones and teeth. The other one percent plays an important role in making muscles contract, nerves send signals and blood clot. Chalk, limestone and marble are all forms of calcium carbonate, often formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures long ago.
A light metal found in 1879, which Mendeleev had predicted in 1871.

Scandium is a good example of Mendeleev's predictions. In 1871 he described a missing element beneath boron in his table, "eka-boron," and said what it should be like. In 1879 the Swedish chemist Lars Nilson found a new element in a Scandinavian mineral, named it after Scandinavia and it matched. Today it's used in small amounts to strengthen aluminum in bicycle frames and aircraft parts.
A strong, light metal that resists corrosion and is accepted by the body.

Titanium is as strong as many steels but about 40 percent lighter, and it doesn't corrode. In the 1950s the Swedish surgeon Per-Ingvar Brånemark found by accident that bone grows right into titanium and holds it firmly in place, a property he named osseointegration. That discovery led to dental implants and hip and knee replacements, and it's why those implants are made of titanium.
A metal that makes steel tougher.

Vanadium is a hard, silvery metal that makes steel much tougher. It's named for Vanadis, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds come in so many beautiful colors. Henry Ford used vanadium steel for the frame of the Model T because it was stronger and lighter than ordinary steel, which helped make the car affordable and durable.
The metal that makes steel stainless.

Chromium is what makes stainless steel stainless. Steel with at least about 10.5 percent chromium forms an invisible, self-repairing layer of oxide on its surface that prevents rust. The metal's name comes from the Greek word for color, because its compounds are so vivid, including the green in emeralds and the red in rubies. It's also the shiny coating on "chrome" car parts.
A metal that hardens steel and is a trace nutrient.

About 90 percent of the manganese mined goes into making steel, where it makes the metal harder and easier to work. In small amounts, it's an essential nutrient: it helps enzymes build bone and break down food. But too much, as workers in some industries have been exposed to, damages the brain, causing symptoms like those of Parkinson's disease.
The metal at the heart of Earth, of blood and of civilization.

Iron has shaped history. Earth's core is mostly iron and nickel, which generates the planet's magnetic field. In your blood, hemoglobin uses iron to carry oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body, and it's what makes blood red. In the Middle East, the Iron Age began around 1200 BCE, when people learned to make tools stronger than those of bronze.
A metal that makes blue pigment and is a part of vitamin B12.

For centuries, cobalt has given pottery and glass a brilliant deep blue, and "cobalt blue" is still a favorite pigment. Today, it's also an essential ingredient in the rechargeable batteries in phones and electric cars. About 70 percent of the world's supply comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its mining has been linked to child labor and unsafe conditions.
A metal used in coins, steel and batteries.

The name comes from German miners, who found an ore that looked like copper but yielded none. They blamed a mischievous spirit, "Old Nick," and called it Kupfernickel, "copper devil." The metal was isolated in 1751. Today it's used in stainless steel, batteries and coins. The American five-cent coin, called a nickel, is actually 75 percent copper and 25 percent nickel.
One of the first metals people used, around 10,000 years ago.

Copper was one of the first metals people used, about 10,000 years ago, because it can be found in a pure form and is easy to hammer. It conducts electricity almost as well as silver, so it's in nearly every wire in your house. It also kills many germs, and in 2008 the US Environmental Protection Agency approved copper alloys as the first solid surfaces that can claim to be antimicrobial.
A metal that protects steel from rust and helps your immune system.

Zinc is a bluish metal used to coat steel in a process called galvanizing, protecting it from rust even when scratched, since the zinc corrodes first. Mixed with copper, it makes brass. In your body, it's needed by hundreds of enzymes and plays a role in immunity and healing. Foods like oysters, beef and beans are good sources.
A metal that melts in your hand at 29.8 degrees Celsius.

Gallium is a soft metal that melts at 29.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, so a lump of it will melt in your hand. In 1871 Mendeleev predicted it as "eka-aluminum," and in 1875 Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered it, and measured properties that matched. Today, compounds of gallium are used in blue and white LED lights and in some of the most efficient solar cells.
The element of the first transistor.

In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain at Bell Labs built the first working transistor, and its crystal was germanium. The transistor replaced bulky vacuum tubes and launched the age of electronics, and it won a Nobel Prize for them and William Shockley. Silicon later took over as the main material because it's cheaper and works at higher temperatures, but germanium is still found in some fiber-optic and infrared devices.
A classic poison that was hard to detect until 1836.

For centuries, arsenic was the classic murder poison. It was odorless, tasteless and its symptoms resembled those of common illnesses, so it earned the nickname "inheritance powder." In 1836 the chemist James Marsh devised a sensitive test that could detect even tiny traces in a body. It was the first time that courts had reliable forensic proof of arsenic poisoning, and it made such murders much harder to get away with.
A trace element needed in tiny amounts and toxic in larger ones.

Selenium is a trace element that your body needs in tiny amounts to make antioxidant enzymes, but too much is toxic. Brazil nuts are unusually rich in it, and a single nut can contain more than a day's supply. Its name comes from Selene, the Greek goddess of the Moon, chosen because it was found along with tellurium, whose name comes from the Latin for Earth.
One of two elements that are liquid at room temperature.

Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature. Bromine is a dark reddish-brown liquid that gives off a harsh, irritating vapor, and its name comes from the Greek for "stench." Compounds of bromine have been used in photographic film, in fire retardants and in some medicines.
A gas that once defined the meter.

For 23 years, the meter was defined by this gas. From 1960 to 1983, one meter was officially 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red light given off by krypton-86 atoms. That was more precise and reproducible than the old metal bar kept in Paris. In 1983 it was replaced by a definition based on the speed of light. Its name comes from the Greek for "hidden."
A soft metal used in atomic clocks.

Atoms of rubidium can be made to flip between two energy states at an extremely precise frequency, so they make excellent timekeepers. Small rubidium atomic clocks are cheap and compact enough to be used in cell phone towers, in satellites and in telecommunications equipment, where accurate timing is vital. The name comes from the Latin for deep red, from the color of its spectral lines.
The element that makes fireworks red.

Strontium salts burn with a brilliant crimson color, and they're used in red fireworks and emergency flares. It also has a more worrying form. Strontium-90, a radioactive isotope released by nuclear weapons tests and accidents, is dangerous because the body mistakes it for calcium and deposits it in the bones, where it irradiates the marrow for years.
One of four elements named for the Swedish village of Ytterby.

Yttrium is one of four elements named for the village of Ytterby in Sweden, where a quarry yielded a black mineral that contained many new elements. The other three are ytterbium, terbium and erbium. Yttrium compounds are used in LED lights, in lasers and in superconductors, and they also helped create the red in old television screens.
A metal that lets neutrons pass, so it holds nuclear fuel.

Zirconium is remarkable because it barely absorbs neutrons, which makes it ideal for holding nuclear fuel. The fuel rods in most nuclear reactors are covered in a zirconium alloy. The mineral zircon is also the source of cubic zirconia, the sparkling diamond lookalike used in jewelry, which is made from zirconium dioxide.
A metal that is superconducting when cold, used in MRI magnets.

Alloys of niobium and titanium become superconductors when cooled below about 10 kelvin, meaning they carry electricity with no resistance at all. They're used to make the powerful magnets in MRI machines and in particle accelerators. The element was named for Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus in Greek mythology, since it's always found with tantalum and is chemically very similar.
A metal that strengthens steel and is vital to enzymes.

Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of all metals, about 2,620 degrees Celsius, and it makes steel stronger at high temperatures. It's also essential to life: plants need it for the enzyme that turns nitrogen into forms they can use, and many enzymes in your own body contain it. It's named from the Greek word for lead, because it was once confused with it.
The first element made by people, in 1937.

Technetium was the first element to be made artificially. In 1937 Emilio Segrè, an Italian physicist, got a strip of molybdenum that had been bombarded in a cyclotron at Berkeley, and with Carlo Perrier, found the new element in it. It has no stable isotopes, so it's nearly absent in nature. One form, technetium-99m, is widely used in medicine: it's involved in about 40 million diagnostic scans every year.
A hard metal used to harden platinum and in electronics.

Ruthenium is a rare, hard metal that's named for Ruthenia, the Latin name for Russia. The Russian-Baltic chemist Karl Claus identified it in 1844, from platinum ore from the Ural Mountains. It's used to harden platinum and palladium, and for tough electrical contacts. It's also used in electronics, for the layers in hard drives.
One of the rarest and most valuable metals, used in car exhaust cleaners.

Rhodium is one of the rarest and most valuable metals. About 80 percent of it goes to make catalytic converters, which turn the most harmful gases in car exhaust into less harmful ones. The name comes from the Greek for rose, because many of its salts are pink or red. Its price has at times been much higher than gold's.
A metal that can soak up hydrogen like a sponge.

Palladium has a remarkable ability to absorb hydrogen, in some cases hundreds of times its own volume. It's also an important metal for catalytic converters, and it's used in electronics and jewelry. William Wollaston discovered it in 1802 and named it for the asteroid Pallas, which had been found the same year, itself named after the Greek goddess Athena.
The best conductor of electricity and heat among all metals.

Silver is the best conductor of both electricity and heat among all the metals. It tarnishes because it reacts with tiny traces of sulfur in the air, forming black silver sulfide. Silver compounds were once the light-sensitive part of all photographic film and paper, because they darken when exposed to light. It's also a natural antibacterial, which is why silver was used in medicine.
A metal used in old rechargeable batteries and a hazard to health.

Cadmium was used in rechargeable batteries and in pigments, but it's a poison. In the early 1900s, people in parts of Japan along the Jinzu River developed itai-itai disease, which means "ouch-ouch," a painful bone disease caused by mine waste containing cadmium that got into rice and water. It led to stricter limits on cadmium, and today its use is much more limited.
A soft metal in the transparent coating on touchscreens.

Indium is a soft metal that, when combined with tin and oxygen, forms indium tin oxide, a coating that is both transparent and electrically conductive. That's the layer that senses your touch on the screen of almost every phone, tablet and flat-panel TV. The name comes from the bright indigo line in its spectrum, which is how it was identified in 1863.
The metal that, with copper, made the Bronze Age.

Tin was one of the keys to early civilization. About 3300 BCE people discovered that mixing tin with copper makes bronze, which is much harder than copper alone, and the Bronze Age began. When you bend a bar of pure tin, it makes a faint crackling noise called "tin cry," caused by the crystals inside it rubbing against each other.
A metalloid that ancient people used as eye makeup.

Antimony has been known since ancient times. In Egypt and elsewhere, a black powder from the mineral stibnite was ground up and used as kohl, an eye cosmetic. The chemical symbol Sb comes from "stibium," the Latin name for the mineral. Today, antimony is used to make flame retardants and to harden lead in batteries.
A rare element used in solar panels.

Tellurium is one of the rarest stable elements in Earth's crust, rarer than platinum. It's used in solar panels made with cadmium telluride, the second most common type of solar panel after silicon. It was first isolated in 1782 by a Hungarian-Austrian mineralogist, Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein, and named by Martin Klaproth for the Latin word for Earth, tellus.
A trace element your thyroid needs to make hormones.

Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make the hormones that regulate your metabolism. Without enough, it swells into a goiter. In 1924 Michigan began adding iodine to table salt, and the practice spread across the US, nearly eliminating goiter. Iodine deficiency is still a problem in parts of the world, and is a leading preventable cause of intellectual disability.
A heavy noble gas whose name means "stranger."

Xenon is a heavy noble gas, and the name comes from the Greek for "stranger." It was discovered in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers. It produces a bright, bluish-white light in car headlights and flash lamps. It's also used in ion engines for spacecraft, including NASA's Dawn mission to the asteroid belt, because its heavy atoms give more thrust.
The element that defines the second.

The length of a second is defined by cesium. Since 1967, one second has been 9,192,631,770 cycles of the microwave radiation given off by a cesium-133 atom. Atomic clocks based on it are accurate to within about a second over tens of millions of years. It's the reason your phone's time is right, and satellite navigation systems depend on that precision.
A heavy metal whose compounds block X-rays.

Barium compounds block X-rays, so patients are given a "barium meal," a chalky drink, to make the digestive tract show up clearly on an X-ray image. Barium salts also burn a bright green in fireworks. Although soluble barium compounds are poisonous, the one used for X-rays, barium sulfate, doesn't dissolve and passes through safely.
The first of the lanthanides, used in camera lenses and hybrid-car batteries.

Lanthanum is the first of the lanthanides, a row of 15 similar elements. Glass that contains lanthanum bends light strongly, which lets lens makers produce thinner and sharper camera and telescope lenses. It's also used in some batteries for hybrid cars. The name comes from the Greek for "to lie hidden," because it was hidden within other minerals when it was found in 1839.
The most abundant rare earth, as common as copper.

Cerium is the most abundant of the rare earths, about as common in the Earth's crust as copper. When cerium is mixed with iron, it makes ferrocerium, the material in lighter flints: scrape it, and tiny hot particles fly off as sparks. It's also in catalytic converters and in some self-cleaning oven walls, where it helps break down grease.
A rare earth that colors glass and ceramics yellow-green.

The name means "green twin," from the Greek for green and twin. For about forty years, scientists believed that "didymium," meaning "twin," was a single element. In 1885 the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach separated it into two, praseodymium and neodymium. Praseodymium gives glass and ceramics a yellow-green color, and is used in some strong magnets and welding goggles.
The metal in the strongest permanent magnets.

The neodymium-iron-boron magnet, developed in 1982, is the strongest type of permanent magnet commercially available. A small one can lift hundreds of times its own weight. You'll find them in headphones, computer hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbine generators. The name means "new twin," because it was split off from "didymium" in 1885.
A radioactive element with no stable form, found in only tiny amounts in nature.

Promethium has no stable isotopes, so it's extremely rare in nature, with only a tiny amount at any moment in Earth's crust. It was first identified in 1945 by scientists at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, from the fission products of uranium. It's named for Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire from the gods for humans. It was once used to make luminous paint for watch dials.
A rare earth used in strong magnets and in a cancer drug.

Samarium is a silvery metal named for the mineral samarskite, which was in turn named for a Russian mining official, Colonel Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets, making it the first element named, indirectly, for a person. Samarium-cobalt magnets stay strong at very high temperatures. A radioactive form, samarium-153, is used as a medicine to relieve pain from cancer that has spread to the bones.
A rare earth that glows red under ultraviolet, used to secure euro notes.

Europium glows brightly red under ultraviolet light, and euro banknotes use it as a security feature. Under UV, the genuine notes show glowing marks and fibers that counterfeit paper lacks. The element was named by the French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay in 1901 for the continent of Europe. It was also used to produce the red in older color televisions.
A metal whose compounds make MRI scans clearer.

Gadolinium is strongly magnetic near room temperature. Compounds containing it are injected into patients as "contrast agents" to make MRI images clearer, because they change the magnetic signal from nearby water molecules. The element is named in honor of Johan Gadolin, the Finnish chemist who discovered the first rare earth mineral in that quarry in Ytterby.
A rare earth that produces green light in phosphors.

Terbium is another of the elements named for Ytterby, the Swedish village where a quarry yielded a number of the rare earths. It glows a bright green when excited, which made it useful in the phosphors for fluorescent lamps and older color TVs. Today it's also used in some solid-state devices and in certain kinds of strong magnets.
A rare earth that keeps magnets strong at high heat.

Dysprosium is what keeps the strongest magnets working in hot conditions. A small amount added to neodymium magnets lets them keep their strength at high temperatures, which is important in electric car motors and wind turbines. The name comes from the Greek for "hard to get," because it took Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran more than 30 attempts to isolate it from holmium in 1886.
The element with the strongest magnetic moment.

Holmium has the strongest magnetic moment of any element, so it's used to concentrate magnetic fields in some of the world's most powerful laboratory magnets. It's also used in some medical lasers. The name comes from Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm, in honor of the Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve, who discovered it in 1878.
The element that boosts light signals in fiber-optic cables.

Erbium is the secret behind much of the internet. In fiber-optic cables, light signals fade as they travel. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, developed in 1986 and 1987, strengthen the light directly, without converting it to electricity and back. They sit along the undersea cables that carry internet traffic across oceans. It's another element named for Ytterby.
The least abundant of the stable rare earths.

Thulium is the least abundant of the stable rare earths, but it's still more common than gold or platinum. It's used in some medical lasers and in a few portable X-ray devices. Per Teodor Cleve named it in 1879 for Thule, the ancient Greek and Roman name for the most northerly region of the world, which came to mean Scandinavia.
A rare earth that keeps the most precise clocks.

Ytterbium atoms are used in the most precise clocks ever built. Optical lattice clocks that use them are stable to about one part in 10 to the 18th power, which means that if one had been started at the Big Bang, it would be off by less than a second today.
