These clocks are so sensitive that they can detect the effect of a height difference of a centimeter on the speed of time.
The densest and hardest lanthanide, used in medical scanners.

Lutetium is the heaviest and hardest of the lanthanides. Crystals that contain it are used in PET scanners, where they detect the gamma rays that come from a radioactive tracer injected into the patient. A radioactive form of it, lutetium-177, is also used in a newer treatment for certain prostate cancers and tumors, carrying radiation directly to cancer cells.
A metal used in computer chips and nuclear control rods.

Hafnium is excellent at absorbing neutrons, so it's used to make control rods that regulate nuclear reactors, including in some nuclear submarines. It also plays a role in computing. Starting in 2007, chipmakers like Intel began using hafnium oxide in place of silicon dioxide as the insulating layer in transistors, which let them keep making chips smaller without leaking current.
A tough metal that makes tiny capacitors for phones.

Tantalum is used to make tiny, reliable capacitors in phones and laptops, so there's probably some in your pocket. It's also extremely resistant to attack by body fluids, so it's used in surgical implants and in pacemakers. A lot of it comes from a mineral called coltan, and, as with cobalt, mining it in some regions has been linked to conflict and harm to workers.
The metal with the highest melting point, 3,422 degrees Celsius.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3,422 degrees Celsius, and the highest of all elements except carbon. That's why it was used for the glowing filaments in incandescent light bulbs for about a century. It's also very dense and hard. Tungsten carbide is used to make cutting tools and drill bits. Its chemical symbol, W, comes from its other name, wolfram.
One of the last stable elements discovered, in 1925.

Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered, in 1925 by Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg in Germany. It's among the rarest elements in the Earth's crust. It's used in superalloys for jet engine turbine blades, because it keeps its strength at extremely high temperatures, allowing engines to run hotter and more efficiently.
The densest natural element at about 22.6 grams per cubic centimeter.

Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element. A cubic centimeter weighs about 22.6 grams, roughly 22 times as much as the same volume of water. A volleyball-size lump would weigh over 200 pounds. Its name comes from the Greek word for smell, because one of its compounds, osmium tetroxide, gives off a strong, unpleasant odor, and it's also highly toxic.
A very dense metal, found in a layer that marks the dinosaurs' extinction.

Iridium is a very dense, corrosion-resistant metal that's rare in Earth's crust but much more common in asteroids and meteorites. In 1980 the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son Walter, a geologist, found a thin layer of clay rich in iridium in rocks around the world, exactly at the time the dinosaurs died out. It pointed them to the idea that an asteroid had struck the Earth.
A dense, rare metal used in catalytic converters and jewelry.

Platinum is a dense, rare metal that doesn't tarnish or corrode, and it's valued for jewelry and as a catalyst in car exhaust systems and chemical manufacturing. From 1889 until 2019, the international standard for the kilogram was a small cylinder made of an alloy of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, kept under three glass bells in a vault near Paris.
A metal that does not tarnish, which is why ancient gold still shines.

Gold is chemically inert, so it doesn't tarnish or rust, and ancient gold objects still look as bright as the day they were made. Most of its atoms were probably created in the collisions of neutron stars, and were scattered through space long before the Earth formed. It's incredibly malleable: a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about a square meter in size.
The only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

Mercury is the only metal that's liquid at room temperature, and its silvery blobs were fascinating to people for centuries. But it's a potent poison. In the 1950s, in the Japanese city of Minamata, a factory dumped mercury waste into the bay, which contaminated the fish that people ate and caused severe neurological damage and birth defects. Thermometers today use other liquids.
A soft metal that is a famously quiet poison.

Thallium is a soft metal whose salts have no taste or smell and cause a slow, mysterious illness that includes hair loss. That made it a favorite weapon of mystery writers. In Agatha Christie's 1961 novel The Pale Horse, a murderer uses it, and in 1977 a nurse in London who had read the book recognized the symptoms in a real patient, and the diagnosis saved a life.
A dense metal whose use in pipes and gasoline harmed millions.

Lead has been used for thousands of years. The Romans made water pipes out of it, and its Latin name, plumbum, gave us the word "plumbing" and the symbol Pb. But lead is a neurotoxin, especially harmful to children. After leaded gasoline was phased out in the US, average blood lead levels in Americans fell by about 78 percent between 1976 and 1991.
A metal that is nearly stable, forming bright rainbow crystals.

Bismuth was long thought to be the heaviest stable element, but in 2003 scientists found that it's very slightly radioactive. Its half-life is about 20 billion billion years, over a billion times the age of the universe, so for all practical purposes it's stable. It's the key ingredient in Pepto-Bismol, and when melted and cooled slowly, it forms beautiful rainbow-colored stair-step crystals.
An element found by Marie Curie in 1898 and named for her homeland, Poland.

Marie Curie discovered polonium in 1898, together with her husband Pierre, while searching a uranium ore for the source of its unusual radioactivity. She named it for her native Poland, then partitioned between other countries, as a political statement. It's intensely radioactive and highly toxic. In 2006, a former Russian intelligence officer, Alexander Litvinenko, died in London after being poisoned with it.
The rarest element in Earth's crust.

Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element on Earth. Scientists estimate that less than 30 grams exist in the entire crust at any moment, because its most stable isotopes decay within hours. The name comes from the Greek for "unstable." It was first made artificially in 1940, and is being studied as a way to deliver radiation to cancer cells.
A radioactive gas that seeps up from soil and rock.

Radon is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas that seeps up through the ground as uranium in rocks decays. It can collect in basements and houses, and after smoking it's the second leading cause of lung cancer in the US, according to the EPA. A home test kit costs only a few dollars, and if levels are high, a vent fan system installed under the house can reduce them.
An extremely rare and unstable element.

Francium is extremely rare and unstable, with its longest-lived isotope lasting only about 22 minutes. The French physicist Marguerite Perey discovered it in 1939 at the Curie Institute in Paris, and named it for her homeland. She was the first woman elected to the French Academy of Sciences. Only tiny amounts have ever been made, and it has never been seen as a visible sample.
A glowing radioactive element that harmed those who used it.

Marie and Pierre Curie discovered radium in 1898, and it glows faintly in the dark. After that, it was used in everything from luminous watch dials to supposed health tonics. In the 1920s, young women employed to paint watch dials with radium paint, who were told to point their brushes with their lips, developed severe illnesses. Their legal fight, as the "Radium Girls," led to workplace safety laws.
A radioactive metal that glows blue in the dark.

Actinium is a silvery radioactive metal that glows with a pale blue light in the dark, from the radiation it gives off. It's about 150 times as radioactive as radium. Its name comes from the Greek for "ray." One of its isotopes, actinium-225, is being tested in medicine, in drugs that deliver tiny particles of radiation directly to cancer cells.
A radioactive metal that is more abundant than uranium.

Thorium is a radioactive metal that's about three times more abundant than uranium in Earth's crust. It has been studied as a possible fuel for nuclear reactors, which some say could be safer. It was discovered in 1828 by the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, who named it for Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
A rare radioactive element between thorium and uranium.

Protactinium is a rare radioactive element found between thorium and uranium on the periodic table. It was identified in 1913 by Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring, and it wasn't isolated in a usable amount until 1934. Its name means "before actinium," because when it decays, it turns into actinium.
The heaviest element that occurs naturally in significant amounts, and the fuel of fission.

Uranium is the heaviest element found in nature in large amounts. In December 1938 the German chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann bombarded uranium with neutrons and found that it split into lighter elements, to their surprise. Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained the process, which they called fission, in early 1939. Today nuclear power plants supply about 10 percent of the world's electricity.
The first element beyond uranium, made in 1940.

Neptunium was the first element heavier than uranium to be made. In 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley, Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson bombarded uranium with neutrons, creating a new element. It was named for Neptune, the planet beyond Uranus, just as uranium was named for Uranus. Elements beyond uranium are called transuranic elements.
An element named for Pluto, used in nuclear weapons and spacecraft power.

Plutonium was first produced in 1940, by a team led by Glenn Seaborg at Berkeley, and named for Pluto, which was then considered a planet. It's the fuel in some nuclear weapons: the bomb dropped on Nagasaki in August 1945 was a plutonium device. Its isotope plutonium-238 produces heat as it decays, and that's used to power spacecraft, including Voyager and the Curiosity rover.
The radioactive element in most smoke detectors.

Americium is in more homes than you might guess. Most ionization smoke detectors contain a tiny amount of americium-241, which ionizes the air in a small chamber so that a small electric current flows. When smoke enters, it disrupts the current, and the alarm sounds. Seaborg's team made the element in 1944, and named it, like the element above it, europium, for a continent.
An element named for Marie and Pierre Curie.

Curium was made in 1944 by Glenn Seaborg's team at Berkeley and named for Marie and Pierre Curie, the pioneers of radioactivity research. One of its isotopes, curium-244, gives off alpha particles, which are used in instruments on several Mars rovers called alpha-particle X-ray spectrometers, to work out which elements are in rocks and soil.
An element named for Berkeley, California, where it was made in 1949.

Berkelium was first made in 1949 at the University of California, Berkeley, and named for the city, as was the next element, californium. It's highly radioactive and can only be made in tiny amounts, in specialized reactors. In 2010, a batch of berkelium that was made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory was used to make the first atoms of element 117, tennessine.
An element that is a strong source of neutrons.

Californium emits a lot of neutrons, which makes it useful. It's used to start up nuclear reactors, to detect explosives and to find gold and oil by seeing what's in rock. Just a microgram of californium-252 can give off about two million neutrons per second. It was first made at Berkeley in 1950, by bombarding curium with helium nuclei.
An element first found in the fallout of a hydrogen bomb test.

Einsteinium was discovered in an unusual place: the fallout from the first hydrogen bomb test, "Ivy Mike," in November 1952, in the Pacific. Scientists at Berkeley found it in the debris collected from the explosion. The discovery was kept secret for three years because of the Cold War. The element was named for Albert Einstein, who died in 1955.
Another element first found in the 1952 hydrogen bomb debris.

Fermium was found in the same fallout from the 1952 hydrogen bomb test as einsteinium. It's named for Enrico Fermi, who built the first nuclear reactor in 1942. It's the heaviest element that can be made by repeated capture of neutrons in a nuclear reactor. To make elements beyond it, scientists have to smash atoms together in particle accelerators.
The first element made one atom at a time.

Mendelevium was the first element to be made one atom at a time. In 1955 Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley bombarded a tiny speck of einsteinium and detected just 17 atoms in total, one by one, across several experiments. It's named for Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table, and who had predicted undiscovered elements, so it was fitting.
A heavy element, named for Alfred Nobel.

Nobelium is named for Alfred Nobel, who founded the Nobel Prizes. Its discovery was disputed for years. A group in Stockholm claimed it in 1957, but others couldn't repeat the work, and labs in the US and the Soviet Union each made competing claims. Eventually, the name Nobelium was kept by international agreement. It can only be made in tiny quantities.
An element named for Ernest Lawrence, who invented the cyclotron.

Lawrencium is named for Ernest Lawrence, the American physicist who invented the cyclotron, the type of particle accelerator that was used to discover so many new elements. It was first made in 1961 at the Lawrence Berkeley laboratory. It lasts only hours, and a few atoms at a time, so studying its chemistry is very difficult.
The first superheavy element, named for Ernest Rutherford.

Rutherfordium was the first of the superheavy elements, those beyond the actinide series. It's named for Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus. It has no stable isotopes, and the longest-lived known ones last about an hour. During the Cold War, teams in the US and the Soviet Union both claimed to have made it first, and they disagreed over the name.
An element named for Dubna, Russia, where a lab made it.

Dubnium is named for the town of Dubna in Russia, where the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research is located, and where a team created it. Its most stable known isotope lasts about 16 hours. For decades, the US and Soviet scientists disagreed about who found it first and what to call it. In 1997 the international chemistry body settled on dubnium.
The first element named after a living person.

Seaborgium honors Glenn Seaborg, who helped discover ten elements, including plutonium. It was controversial because he was still alive when the name was proposed in 1994, and the convention was not to name elements for living people. The rule was relaxed, and Seaborg said it was a greater honor than winning a Nobel Prize. He lived to see it officially named, and died in 1999.
An element named for Niels Bohr.

Bohrium is named for Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist who explained the structure of the atom. It was first made in 1981 by a German team at the GSI lab in Darmstadt, who fused atoms of bismuth and chromium together. Only a few atoms can be made at a time, and they last for only seconds before decaying.
An element named for the German state of Hesse.

Hassium is named for Hesse, the German state that includes Darmstadt, where it was first made in 1984. In 2001, chemists managed to study a few atoms of it, and showed that it forms a compound similar to that of osmium, as expected from its position in the periodic table. It's remarkable to do chemistry with only a handful of atoms that last seconds.
An element named for Lise Meitner.

Lise Meitner, an Austrian-Swedish physicist, helped to explain nuclear fission in 1938, but was left out when her colleague Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1944. Many consider this a serious injustice. Element 109 was first made in 1982 in Germany, and named for her in 1997. She's the only woman besides Marie Curie to have an element named for her.
An element named for Darmstadt, Germany.

Darmstadtium is named for the German city of Darmstadt, where the Society for Heavy Ion Research, the GSI, is located, and where it was first made in 1994. That lab also made bohrium, hassium, meitnerium and several other elements. The longest-lived known isotope of darmstadtium lasts about ten seconds, which is long for an atom this heavy.
An element named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays.

Roentgenium is named for Wilhelm Röntgen, the German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. It was first made in 1994 at the GSI lab in Darmstadt. Only a few atoms of it have ever existed, so nobody has seen a sample, and its properties are mostly predicted.
An element named for Nicolaus Copernicus.

Copernicium honors Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed that the Earth moves around the Sun. It was made in 1996 at the GSI lab, and officially named in 2010. Chemists have studied a few atoms of it and suggest that it behaves like a very volatile metal, and might be a liquid or even a gas at room temperature.
The first element named by a team in Asia.

Nihonium was the first element ever discovered in Asia. A team at Japan's RIKEN institute, led by Kosuke Morita, made three atoms of it, in 2004, 2005 and 2012, by firing zinc atoms at bismuth. "Nihon" is one of the Japanese names for Japan. The name was officially approved in 2016, and it was celebrated in Japan.
An element named for the Flerov Laboratory in Russia.

Flerovium is named for the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions in Dubna, Russia, which was named for the physicist Georgy Flerov. It was officially named in 2012. Scientists believe that it lies near an "island of stability," a predicted region where certain superheavy nuclei might live much longer than their neighbors, perhaps for minutes or even much longer.
An element named for the Moscow region.

Moscovium is named for the Moscow region, where Dubna is located. A team of Russian and American scientists first made it in 2003, by firing calcium-48 ions at americium. Its atoms are very short-lived, lasting a fraction of a second. It was officially named in 2016, along with nihonium, tennessine and oganesson, completing the seventh row of the periodic table.
An element named for the Lawrence Livermore laboratory in California.

Livermorium is named for the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, which collaborated with Russian scientists in Dubna to make it in 2000. It was officially named in 2012. Its atoms last mere milliseconds, so, as with the other superheavy elements, researchers can only make a few at a time and study how they decay.
The second-to-last element on the table, named for Tennessee.

Tennessine was first made in 2010 by a team of Russian and American scientists. They needed a rare target, berkelium, which was made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and that's why it's named after the state. It sits in the halogen column of the periodic table, though it's not known how closely it behaves like the others. It was named officially in 2016.
The heaviest known element, named for Yuri Oganessian.

Oganesson is the heaviest known element, and it completed the seventh row of the periodic table. It's named for the Russian nuclear physicist Yuri Oganessian, who led the team that made it. He was still alive when it was named in 2016, making him only the second person honored that way after Glenn Seaborg. Only a handful of its atoms have ever been made, and each one lasts for a fraction of a second.
All living things are made of cells, and all cells come from other cells.

In 1838 the botanist Matthias Schleiden suggested that all plants are made of cells, and in 1839 Theodor Schwann said the same of animals. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added the third part, that every cell comes from another cell. Before that, many people believed living things could arise from nonliving matter. A human body has around 30 trillion cells, and they all trace back to a single fertilized egg.
The parts of the cell that make most of its usable energy.

Mitochondria are the small structures in your cells that turn food into usable energy. They have their own little ring of DNA, and you inherit them from your mother. In 1967 the biologist Lynn Margulis argued that they began as free-living bacteria that were taken in by a larger cell, and the two ended up living together. Most biologists now accept this idea, called endosymbiosis, which also applies to plant chloroplasts.
Plants and algae use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen.

Plants, algae and some bacteria capture sunlight and use its energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, giving off oxygen as a byproduct. The pigment chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green. Tiny algae in the oceans produce roughly half of the oxygen we breathe, which means a lot of every breath comes from the sea.
Cells burn sugar with oxygen to make ATP, their energy currency.

Your cells burn sugar with oxygen to make ATP, a molecule that works as the cell's energy currency. One molecule of glucose can yield about 30 ATP. The body uses it so quickly that it recycles about its own weight in ATP each day, rebuilding it again and again. It's the reason you need to keep breathing and eating: the supply of ATP in your cells lasts only seconds.
DNA is two strands twisted around each other, joined by paired bases.

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick published their model of DNA's structure in a one-page paper in Nature: two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. It was built using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, and measurements by Maurice Wilkins. Watson, Crick and Wilkins won the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died in 1958, and the prize isn't given after death.
A always pairs with T, and G with C.

DNA is built from four letters, A, T, G and C. In 1950 Erwin Chargaff discovered that in any organism's DNA, the amount of A matches the amount of T, and the amount of G matches C. Watson and Crick used this to see that the letters pair up, A with T and G with C, across the two strands. That means each strand holds the information to rebuild the other, which is how DNA can copy itself.
Each new baby has about 60 new changes in their DNA that neither parent had.

Every baby is born with some brand-new changes in their DNA that neither parent had. A study in Iceland in 2012 counted about 60 new changes per person on average. Most land in parts of the DNA that don't matter. A few may be harmful, and a very few help. Over many generations, these random changes are the raw material that natural selection works on.
An Augustinian monk found the rules of inheritance by crossing garden peas.

Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk in what is now the Czech Republic. In the 1850s and 60s, he crossed thousands of pea plants and carefully counted the traits, such as tall versus short, in the offspring. He found consistent ratios, often about 3 to 1, and concluded that traits are passed on in distinct units, which we now call genes. His 1866 paper was ignored until 1900, years after he died.
Three-letter DNA words (codons) spell out the 20 amino acids that make proteins.

DNA is read in words of three letters, called codons. There are 64 possible codons, and they spell out the 20 amino acids that are strung together to make proteins, plus signals for start and stop. Since there are more codons than amino acids, several codons can mean the same thing. The code is almost the same in every living thing, from bacteria to humans, which is strong evidence that we share a common ancestor.
A tool that edits DNA at a chosen spot, adapted from a bacterial defense.

Bacteria have an immune system that cuts up the DNA of invading viruses, called CRISPR. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that this system could be reprogrammed to cut DNA at any chosen spot, making gene editing much easier and cheaper. They won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In late 2023, the UK and the US approved the first medicine based on CRISPR, for sickle cell disease.
Chemical tags on DNA change which genes are active without changing the letters.

Your cells all carry the same DNA, yet a liver cell is very different from a neuron. The difference lies in which genes are switched on, and chemical tags on the DNA and its packaging help control that. Diet, stress and age can alter them. Some people claim these changes can be inherited by grandchildren. Evidence for that in humans is limited and debated, though a few animal studies support it.
Unrelated species evolve similar solutions to similar problems.

Sometimes unrelated species end up with similar features because they face similar challenges. Eyes have evolved independently dozens of times. Dolphins, which are mammals, and sharks, which are fish, have similar streamlined bodies. Birds, bats and insects all developed wings separately. It's strong evidence that natural selection is a powerful force, and that certain solutions work again and again.
The same bones form a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper.

Look at the skeleton inside a human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper. The same bones, a single upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and fingers, appear in all three, though used for very different purposes. Charles Darwin saw this as strong evidence of common descent: different jobs, same blueprint, modified over time. It's a bit like the same recipe adapted for different meals.
Natural selection fits a species to its local conditions, not toward a goal.

It's common to imagine evolution as a ladder, with humans at the top. But natural selection only fits creatures to their local conditions. It has no goal. Cave fish living in total darkness have lost their eyes, and tapeworms have lost their guts, and both are perfectly suited to their lives. The biologist Stephen Jay Gould argued that life is better pictured as a bush with many branches.
Bacteria evolve to survive the drugs we use, in a few years.

Bacteria reproduce so fast that they can evolve resistance to drugs within years. Each time antibiotics are used, they kill the vulnerable bacteria and leave the resistant ones to multiply. A 2022 study estimated that drug-resistant bacterial infections directly caused 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019. Using antibiotics only when needed, and completing the course, slows the process.
Beak sizes of finches on Galápagos changed within a few years of a drought.

On the Galápagos Islands, Peter and Rosemary Grant spent four decades measuring finches. In 1977 a severe drought killed most of the small, soft seeds, leaving mainly big, hard ones. Birds with larger beaks could crack them and survived better. The next generation had measurably larger beaks. It showed natural selection at work within a single human lifetime, not just over millions of years.
Twelve E. coli populations have been evolving in a lab since 1988.

In 1988 the biologist Richard Lenski started twelve separate populations of E. coli bacteria in flasks in his lab. Every day since, a sample has been moved to fresh food. After more than 30,000 generations, one population suddenly evolved the ability to feed on citrate, which E. coli normally can't do. The experiment, still running, shows evolution as it happens, and can be replayed with frozen samples.
All living things on Earth descend from one population that lived 3.5 to 4 billion years ago.

All the life on Earth that we know of, from bacteria to blue whales, shares DNA, the same genetic code and similar basic cell machinery. That points to descent from a single ancestral population that lived somewhere between 3.5 and 4 billion years ago. A formal statistical test in 2010 found that this common-ancestry idea fits the data better than the alternatives. The differences between species are just branches of one tree.
We share about 98.8% of our DNA with chimpanzees in the parts that line up.

When scientists compared our genome with the chimpanzee's in 2005, they found that, where the sequences line up, about 98.8 percent of the letters are the same. That figure counts single-letter differences. When you include stretches that are inserted or missing, the difference is larger, about 4 to 5 percent. Either way, our closest living relatives are chimpanzees and bonobos.
Most people with ancestry from outside Africa carry 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA.

In 2010 the Swedish geneticist Svante Pääbo and his team published a draft of the Neanderthal genome, pieced together from tiny fragments of ancient bone. It showed that people whose ancestors lived outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. That means our ancestors met Neanderthals and had children with them. Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine for this work.
Modern humans emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago.

For a long time, we thought modern humans emerged about 200,000 years ago. In 2017 researchers reported fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, which they dated to roughly 300,000 years ago, with features of both modern humans and earlier forms. Our species spread through Africa and left in waves, and the main migration out was about 60,000 years ago.
Bacteria are living cells that antibiotics can kill; viruses are not cells and need a host to reproduce.

Bacteria are living single-celled organisms, and many are harmless or helpful, while a few cause disease. Viruses are much smaller and aren't cells at all. They're packets of genetic material that can only reproduce by hijacking a host's cells. Antibiotics target bacteria, so they do nothing against colds or the flu, which are caused by viruses. For viruses, we use vaccines and, in some cases, antiviral drugs.
A mold on a forgotten dish led to the first antibiotic.

In 1928 the Scottish doctor Alexander Fleming came back from vacation to find that a mold had contaminated one of his bacteria dishes, and the bacteria around it had died. He'd noticed the effect, but turning it into a drug took a decade of work by Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their team at Oxford, who made it in the early 1940s. The three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
One species that holds a whole community together.

In 1966 the ecologist Robert Paine experimented on the rocky coast of Washington state by removing all the starfish from a patch of shore. Without them, mussels took over and crowded out other species, and the variety of life dropped sharply. A single predator turned out to be holding the whole community in balance. He called such species keystone species, like the stone at the top of an arch.
Bringing back wolves in 1995 changed elk behavior and may have helped plants and rivers.

Wolves were removed from Yellowstone National Park by the 1920s and brought back in 1995. Some of the effects are well documented, such as fewer elk in some areas, and the elk behaving more warily. A popular story says that the wolves also changed the courses of the rivers, by letting trees grow back along the banks. That part is debated, since the effects on plants vary and other factors matter.
Only about a tenth of the energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next.

Energy is lost at each step up a food chain. A plant captures sunlight, a rabbit eats the plant, and a fox eats the rabbit. At each step only about a tenth of the energy gets passed on, since most is used for living and moving, and given off as heat. That's why there are far fewer lions than zebras, and why food chains rarely have more than four or five links. The real figure varies between about 5 and 20 percent.
The end-Permian extinction killed most species on Earth.

About 252 million years ago, the biggest mass extinction in Earth's history happened at the end of the Permian period. Massive volcanic eruptions in what's now Siberia pumped out huge amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases, and changed the climate and the chemistry of the oceans. An estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, and about 70 percent of land vertebrates, died. It took millions of years for life to recover.
A honey fungus in Oregon covers about 2,400 acres.

The largest known living organism by area is a honey fungus, Armillaria ostoyae, in the Malheur National Forest in Oregon. Most of it is underground, spreading through the soil and the roots of trees as thin threads. It covers about 2,400 acres, an area as big as well over a thousand football fields. It may be thousands of years old, and the part that you see is just a few mushrooms in the fall.
Do trees share food and warnings through underground fungi?

Popular books have described forests as having an underground "wood wide web" in which trees share food and send warnings through fungi connected to their roots. It's a beautiful idea. But in 2023 a team led by Justine Karst reviewed the research and found that the evidence for forest-wide sharing of nutrients and signals is far weaker than the stories suggest. Fungi do connect to roots, but what they do with the connection is less clear.

Have you noticed a houseplant bending toward a window? That's phototropism. In 1880 Charles Darwin and his son Francis experimented with grass seedlings, covering different parts of them, and found that the tip senses the light and sends a signal to the part below, which bends. The signal turned out to be a plant hormone, which was later named auxin. It was one of the first plant hormones to be identified.
A honeybee that finds food can tell the others its direction and distance.

When a honeybee finds a good source of flowers, it returns to the hive and dances on the honeycomb. The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance in the 1940s. The angle of the straight run shows the direction of the food compared with the sun, and how long it lasts shows the distance. He won the 1973 Nobel Prize for it, one of the few Nobels in the study of animal behavior.
An octopus has three hearts, blue blood and about two-thirds of its neurons in its arms.

An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one through the body. Its blood is blue, because it carries oxygen with copper instead of iron. About two-thirds of its neurons are in its arms, and each can taste, touch and even make simple decisions on its own. Octopuses have been seen solving puzzles, opening jars and escaping from tanks.
Microscopic "water bears" can survive extreme conditions.

Tardigrades are microscopic animals, less than a millimeter long, nicknamed water bears. They can survive being dried out for years, frozen near absolute zero, heated above boiling and exposed to high radiation. In 2007 a European Space Agency experiment exposed them to the vacuum and solar radiation of space for ten days. Some survived and even laid eggs after returning to Earth.
Small underground rodents that live about 30 years and rarely get cancer.

Naked mole rats are small, hairless rodents that live underground in colonies in East Africa. They live about 30 years, far longer than mice of similar size, which live about three. They also rarely get cancer. One reason may be that their cells make an unusually thick, sugary substance that stops cells from crowding together and forming tumors. Researchers study them for clues about aging and cancer.
The longest-lived vertebrate known, living for centuries.

The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate we know of. In 2016 a team in Denmark used radiocarbon dating on proteins in the lens of the eyes of 28 sharks and estimated that the biggest was about 392 years old, give or take 120 years. These sharks grow very slowly, only about a centimeter a year, and are thought to reach maturity at about 150 years of age.
Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to an earlier stage of life.

Turritopsis dohrnii is a tiny jellyfish that, when it's injured or stressed, can turn back into an earlier stage of life. The adult reverts to a polyp, a kind of larval form, and starts its life cycle again. In theory, it could do it indefinitely. In practice, most of them still get eaten or die of disease, but they are a subject of intense study in aging research.
Crows can recognize a person who threatened them, and tell others.

In a 2010 study, John Marzluff and colleagues at the University of Washington wore a rubber mask while they trapped and banded wild crows. For years afterward, crows scolded and swooped at anyone wearing the same mask, though not at people in other masks. Even young crows that had never seen the trapping joined in, which means that crows can pass on information about dangerous people.
Birds are the living descendants of feathered theropod dinosaurs.

Birds are not just related to dinosaurs, they are dinosaurs: the living descendants of a group of feathered, two-legged dinosaurs called theropods. Since the 1990s, spectacular fossils in China have shown many dinosaurs with feathers of various kinds. In that sense, a sparrow is a small dinosaur, in the same way that you are a mammal.
The largest animal that has ever lived, up to 30 meters long.

The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived, bigger than any dinosaur. It can grow up to 30 meters long, and weigh around 150 tons. It's astonishing that such an enormous animal feeds mainly on tiny shrimp-like creatures called krill, and it can eat up to about four tons of them a day during the feeding season.
Dogs were the first domesticated animal, at least 15,000 years ago.

Dogs were the first animal people domesticated, long before farming began. Genetic studies suggest that their ancestors split from wolves some time between 15,000 and 40,000 years ago, though experts debate exactly when. Dogs have evolved a talent that wolves, and even chimpanzees, lack: the ability to read human gestures such as pointing and to look to our faces for guidance.
A thin crust, a thick mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

Earth has four main layers. There's the thin outer crust that we live on, a thick, slowly flowing mantle, a liquid outer core of molten iron and nickel, and a solid inner core. The Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann discovered the inner core in 1936, by noticing that some earthquake waves bounced off something solid deep inside the planet. It's about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents move.

In 1912 the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined together and have slowly moved apart. He pointed to the way South America and Africa fit together, and to matching fossils and rocks on both sides of the ocean. Geologists mocked him because he couldn't explain what could move continents. In the 1950s and 60s, discoveries about the seafloor provided the answer, in the theory of plate tectonics.
A horseshoe around the Pacific where most earthquakes and volcanoes happen.

Around the edge of the Pacific Ocean lies a horseshoe-shaped zone of volcanoes and earthquake faults, 40,000 kilometers long, known as the Ring of Fire. About 90 percent of the world's earthquakes, and about 75 percent of its active volcanoes, occur there. The reason is that several tectonic plates meet along the Pacific's edge, where one plate slides under another.
Each whole step up in earthquake magnitude is about 32 times more energy.

The numbers used to describe earthquakes are logarithmic, so each whole step up means about 32 times more energy released. A magnitude 7 earthquake releases roughly 32 times as much energy as a magnitude 6, and about 1,000 times as much as a magnitude 5. The strongest earthquake ever recorded was a magnitude 9.5 in Chile in 1960.
The 1883 eruption was heard 4,800 kilometers away.

On August 27, 1883, the volcano Krakatoa in Indonesia exploded. The sound was heard on Rodrigues Island, 4,800 kilometers away, and is considered the loudest sound in recorded history. The giant tsunamis it generated killed more than 36,000 people. The ash and sulfur it pushed high into the atmosphere dimmed sunsets around the world and lowered global temperatures for several years.
A volcano in Indonesia changed the weather around the world in 1816.

In April 1815 Mount Tambora in Indonesia had the largest eruption in recorded history. It threw a huge cloud of ash and sulfur into the atmosphere, blocking some sunlight. In 1816, the following year, snow fell in New England in June and frosts came through the summer, and crops failed and food ran short across Europe. It was known as the "year without a summer."
Rocks are formed from magma, worn down into sediment and baked or squeezed into new rock.

Rocks are constantly being recycled. Magma that cools becomes igneous rock. Wind and water wear rocks down into sediment, which gets pressed into layers of sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure transform either type into metamorphic rock. Any of the three can be melted, buried, uplifted or worn down to become another, over millions of years, in a slow cycle with no beginning or end.
James Hutton found "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end" in 1788.

In 1788 the Scottish farmer and geologist James Hutton studied rock layers at a place called Siccar Point and realized that they showed the same processes we see today, slow erosion and deposition and uplift, repeating over and over. He wrote that he found "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end." It made people realize that the Earth is vastly older than the thousands of years that had been assumed.
If Earth's 4.5 billion years were 24 hours, humans arrived about six seconds before midnight.

Imagine all 4.5 billion years of Earth's history squeezed into 24 hours. The planet forms at midnight, and the first life appears around 4 a.m. Dinosaurs arrive around 10:40 p.m., and they die out at about 11:40 p.m. Modern humans show up only in the last six seconds before midnight. Written history would be a flicker in the last fraction of a second.
Mineral hardness from 1 to 10, from talc to diamond.

In 1812 the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs created a scale for the hardness of minerals, from 1 for talc, which you can scratch with a fingernail, to 10 for diamond. A harder mineral scratches a softer one. Your fingernail is about 2.5, a steel knife about 5.5 and quartz is 7. The scale shows order only, since the steps aren't equal: diamond is far harder than corundum, which is 9.
The oceans hold 97% of Earth's water, and only about 1% is fresh and easy to reach.

Oceans hold about 97 percent of Earth's water, and it's salty. Of the remaining 3 percent that's fresh, most is locked up in glaciers and ice sheets, so only about 1 percent of all the water is fresh water that's easy for us to reach. Of the liquid fresh water, most is underground, and rivers and lakes hold only a tiny fraction.
We have mapped the Moon in more detail than our own seafloor.

We know more about the surface of the Moon than about our own seafloor. In 2023, the Seabed 2030 project, which is working to map all of it, reported that about a quarter of the ocean floor had been mapped to high resolution. The deepest known point is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
The atmosphere has layers, and almost all weather is in the lowest one.

The atmosphere is made up of layers. The lowest, the troposphere, reaches about 12 kilometers up and holds most of the air and almost all weather. Above it is the stratosphere, which holds the ozone layer that absorbs harmful ultraviolet light. Space has no sharp edge, but by convention, it starts at the Kármán line, 100 kilometers above the surface.
A success story: the world agreed to stop the chemicals that were destroying it.

In the 1980s scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica, caused by chemicals called CFCs, used in aerosol sprays and refrigerators. In 1987 countries signed the Montreal Protocol, banning them. It worked: the UN reported in 2022 that the ozone layer is on track to recover to 1980 levels by about 2066 over Antarctica, much sooner elsewhere.
Gases like carbon dioxide trap heat, keeping Earth warmer than it would be otherwise.

Gases in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide, water vapor and methane, trap some of the heat that Earth radiates, keeping the planet warmer than it would otherwise be. Without any greenhouse effect, the average temperature would be about -18 degrees Celsius. John Tyndall measured it in the lab in 1859, and in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated how much extra carbon dioxide would warm the planet.
The level has risen from about 280 parts per million to over 420.

Before the Industrial Revolution, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air was about 280 parts per million. Today it's over 420. Ice cores, which trap ancient air in bubbles, show that for 800,000 years before industrialization, it stayed between about 180 and 300. Burning coal, oil and gas, and clearing forests, account for the recent rise.
Earth's average surface temperature has risen about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s.

Earth's average surface temperature has risen by about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the late 1800s. The 2021 report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change states that it's unequivocal that human influence has warmed the planet. Most of the increase has happened since about 1970, and the last decade has been the warmest on record.
Slow wobbles in Earth's orbit trigger cycles of ice and warmth.

For the last couple of million years, Earth has swung between long ice ages and warmer interglacial periods. The Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković worked out that slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt, in cycles of about 100,000, 41,000 and 23,000 years, alter how much sunlight reaches different latitudes and trigger the cycles. The last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago.
Hurricanes form over ocean water at least 26.5 degrees Celsius.

Hurricanes need warm ocean water, at least about 26.5 degrees Celsius, as fuel. The warm water gives them heat and moisture. When a hurricane moves over land or cooler water, it loses its fuel and weakens quickly. The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by their wind speed, with category 5 starting at 157 miles per hour.
Sunlight bends and reflects inside raindrops, and the colors always appear 42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun.

A rainbow forms when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, reflects off the back and bends again as it leaves, spreading into colors. The red light always exits at an angle of about 42 degrees from the direction directly opposite the Sun. Every raindrop sends colored light in many directions, but you see only the drops at the right angle. So no two people see exactly the same rainbow.
Each starts as a six-sided ice crystal because of the shape of water molecules.

A snowflake starts as a tiny ice crystal, and because of the shape of water molecules, it has six sides. As it falls, the shape it grows into depends on the temperature and humidity along the way, so each flake has its own history. Wilson Bentley, a farmer in Vermont, began photographing them with a microscope camera in 1885, and took more than 5,000 images.
Earth's spin bends the path of winds and ocean currents.

Because Earth spins, moving air and water curve to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. This is the Coriolis effect, and it's why storms rotate counterclockwise in the north. But it's far too weak to decide which way water swirls down a sink or toilet, which depends on the shape of the bowl and any currents in the water.
Every two to seven years the central Pacific warms and changes the weather worldwide.

Every two to seven years, the surface of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean warms, trade winds weaken, and weather patterns shift around the world. This is called El Niño. It can bring floods to Peru, droughts to Australia and Indonesia and milder winters in parts of North America. Its cooler opposite phase is called La Niña.
A scale from 0 to 14 for acidity; 7 is neutral.

The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is, from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral, like pure water. The Danish chemist Søren Sørensen introduced it in 1909. Each step is a tenfold change, so lemon juice, at about pH 2, is 100,000 times more acidic than water. Lye is at the other end, about 13.
Soap molecules have a water-loving end and a grease-loving end.

A soap molecule has two ends: one that's attracted to water and one that's attracted to grease. When you wash, the grease-loving ends stick into oil and dirt, and the water-loving ends face outward, so that water can carry the oil away. Soap can also break apart the fatty outer envelope of some viruses, including coronaviruses, which is why handwashing works so well.
Dissolved salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes.

Dissolving salt in water lowers the temperature at which it freezes. Seawater freezes at about -2 degrees Celsius, and a saturated salt solution won't freeze until about -21. That's why roads are salted in winter, so that ice melts and doesn't form. It stops working when it gets extremely cold, below about -10 degrees Celsius, when other chemicals are used.

Atoms are far too small to count one at a time, so chemists count them in huge groups called moles. A mole is 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd particles, known as Avogadro's number. It's set up so that a mole of carbon-12 atoms weighs 12 grams. That lets chemists, by weighing, count atoms. Since 2019, the number has been fixed as an exact value.
In a chemical reaction, nothing is lost or gained, only rearranged.

In a chemical reaction, nothing is created or destroyed. In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier carefully weighed everything before and after burning things in sealed vessels and showed that the total mass didn't change. When something burns, it gains the weight of the oxygen it combines with. His work ended the old theory that burning releases a substance called phlogiston.
Squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles.

If you squeeze a gas into half the space, its pressure doubles, as long as the temperature stays the same. Robert Boyle worked this out in 1662, with air trapped in a bent glass tube and mercury. It explains why a bicycle pump heats up when you use it and why your ears pop in an airplane when the pressure of the air around you changes.
Pollen in water jiggles because unseen molecules keep bumping it.

In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown noticed that tiny grains of pollen in water jiggle around constantly. He couldn't explain it. In 1905 Albert Einstein showed it happens because invisible water molecules are bumping into the grains from all sides. The French physicist Jean Perrin confirmed it with experiments in the following years, which also convinced skeptics that atoms and molecules really exist.
Bakelite, invented in 1907, was the first fully synthetic plastic.

In 1907 the Belgian-American chemist Leo Baekeland invented Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, from phenol and formaldehyde. Unlike earlier plastics, it didn't melt once it was set, so it could be used for things that got hot, like telephone housings, radios, and electrical parts. It was nicknamed "the material of a thousand uses."
PFAS are man-made chemicals that persist in the body and environment for decades or longer.

PFAS are a large family of man-made chemicals that were used for decades in non-stick pans, waterproof fabrics and firefighting foam. They're called "forever chemicals" because their carbon-fluorine bonds, among the strongest in chemistry, mean they don't break down, so they build up in the environment and our bodies. High levels have been linked to health problems including some cancers and reduced immune response.
A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. Enzymes are the catalysts of living things, making the reactions of life happen fast enough at body temperature. In a car's exhaust system, the catalytic converter uses platinum and related metals to turn harmful gases into less harmful ones. Without catalysts, many reactions in your cells would be too slow to keep you alive.
Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen; remove one and it goes out.

Fire needs three things: fuel, heat and oxygen. Take away any one, and it goes out. Water cools a fire, removing heat. A fire blanket or lid cuts off the oxygen. A firebreak removes the fuel. Fire safety experts now often use a fire tetrahedron, which adds a fourth element, the chemical chain reaction that keeps a flame going.
Iron slowly reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide.

Rust is what happens when iron slowly reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide, which is flaky and weak. Salt speeds up the process, which is why cars rust faster where roads are salted. Stainless steel resists rust because the chromium in it forms a thin, invisible protective layer. The damage from corrosion costs the world's economies trillions of dollars a year.
Zero as a number, not just a placeholder, came from India.

Many ancient peoples used a mark to hold an empty place in a number, but treating zero as a number you can add and multiply came from India. The Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark text carbon-dated to somewhere between the 3rd and 4th centuries, uses a dot for zero. In 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta wrote down rules for arithmetic with zero, including what happens when you add it to or subtract it from other numbers.
They were used in China 2,000 years ago and resisted in Europe until the 1600s.

Chinese mathematicians were working with negative numbers around 2,000 years ago. The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art used red counting rods for positive numbers and black ones for negative. European mathematicians were much slower to accept them, and for centuries many called negative answers "absurd" or "fictitious," since you can't have less than nothing of something. They only became standard in the 1600s and later.
The ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159, never ending and never repeating.

Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159, and the digits go on forever with no repeating pattern. In 1761 Johann Lambert proved that it can't be written as a fraction. In 1882 Ferdinand von Lindemann proved the stronger result that it's transcendental, not the solution of any ordinary algebraic equation. That showed that the ancient puzzle of "squaring the circle" with a compass and straightedge is impossible.
How many digits of pi do we need?

You might think space navigation would need thousands of digits, but NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory says that it uses 15 for its most exacting calculations. They've calculated that even for a circle with a radius of about 15 billion miles, farther than Voyager 1 has traveled, 15 digits would put the circumference off by only about an inch. Computers have calculated 100 trillion digits, for the sheer fun of it.
About 2.71828, the base of natural growth.

The number e, about 2.71828, appears wherever things grow or decay continuously. Jacob Bernoulli found it in 1683 while asking a question about money: if a bank pays 100 percent interest, what happens if it's compounded more and more often, every month, every day, every second? The amount doesn't grow forever, it approaches e. The number turns up in population growth, radioactive decay and the bell curve.
e to the power i times pi, plus 1, equals 0.

Euler's identity is e raised to the power of i times pi, plus one, equals zero. It joins five of the most fundamental numbers in mathematics, e, i, pi, 1 and 0, in a single short equation using addition, multiplication and exponents. It comes from a formula discovered by Leonhard Euler in 1748. Many mathematicians consider it the most beautiful equation, and in a survey of readers it was voted that.
The square root of minus one, written i, turns out to be useful.

The square root of minus one can't be an ordinary number, since any number times itself is positive. Yet in 1545 the Italian Girolamo Cardano found that using such "impossible" numbers in the middle of a calculation could give correct, real answers, though he thought they were useless. Today, mathematicians write the square root of minus one as i, and use such numbers for alternating current, signal processing and quantum mechanics.
Euclid proved around 300 BCE that the primes never run out.

A prime number is divisible only by one and itself. Around 300 BCE the Greek mathematician Euclid proved that there are infinitely many. His argument is short: suppose you had a complete list of all the primes. Multiply them together and add one. The result isn't divisible by any prime on your list, so there must be another prime, and the list wasn't complete after all. It's still a model of an elegant proof.
A number with more than 41 million digits.

The largest known prime number has more than 41 million digits. In October 2024 a former NVIDIA engineer, Luke Durant, found it by running software on graphics processors in cloud computers across many countries. It's two raised to the power 136,279,841, minus one, which is the kind of number called a Mersenne prime. The record is usually broken every few years, with the help of volunteer computing.
Every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes.

In 1742 the mathematician Christian Goldbach wrote to Leonhard Euler suggesting that every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes. For example, 10 is 3 plus 7, and 28 is 5 plus 23. Computers have checked it for every even number up to about four quintillion, and it's never failed. But nobody has found a proof, and it remains one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics.
1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13: each is the sum of the two before.

In 1202 Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published a book that included a puzzle about how many pairs of rabbits there would be after a year, if each pair has a new pair every month. The answer gave the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Indian mathematicians had noticed the sequence earlier. Pine cones, sunflower heads and pineapples often show spirals that count in Fibonacci numbers.
About 1.618, the number where the whole is to the larger part as the larger part is to the smaller.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is the number you get when a line is cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter. It's the limit of the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Many people say it's the secret behind the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and beauty itself, but those claims are mostly myth and wishful measuring. It's a lovely number without needing the legend.
In a right triangle, the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the longest.

In any right-angled triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two. A Babylonian clay tablet from about 1800 BCE, known as Plimpton 322, lists number sets that fit the rule, so people knew it a thousand years before Pythagoras. Pythagoras's name is attached to it because the first proofs known to us came from the Greek tradition. It's the basis of how we measure distance.
It cannot be written as a fraction.

The diagonal of a square with sides of length one is the square root of two, and it can't be written as a fraction. The ancient proof is a clever argument by contradiction. Suppose it were a fraction p over q, in lowest terms. Then you can show that both p and q would have to be even, which contradicts "lowest terms." A legend says the Pythagoreans, who believed all numbers were ratios, were deeply disturbed by the discovery.
There are more real numbers than whole numbers.

It sounds absurd, but there are different sizes of infinity. In 1874 and again in 1891, the German mathematician Georg Cantor showed that you can't make a complete list of all the real numbers, the decimals, even an infinite one. Whatever list you offer, you can build a new number by changing one digit in each entry, and it can't be on the list. So the real numbers are a bigger infinity than the whole numbers. Some contemporaries thought he was mad.
A hotel with infinitely many rooms can fit new guests even when full.

The German mathematician David Hilbert used a thought experiment in 1924 to illustrate infinity. Imagine a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all full. A new guest arrives. No problem: ask each guest to move to the room with double their number, which leaves all the odd-numbered rooms empty. It shows that with infinite sets, a part can be as big as the whole, which is bizarre.
In a race, the fast Achilles can never catch the tortoise, said Zeno.

Around 450 BCE the Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea argued that the fast runner Achilles could never catch a tortoise with a head start. By the time Achilles reaches where the tortoise was, it's moved on a bit, and so on forever. The puzzle bothered thinkers for two thousand years, until mathematicians showed that an infinite series of ever smaller steps can add up to a finite total, so that Achilles does catch up.
The mathematics of change, built from two ideas: slopes and areas.

Calculus is the mathematics of change. It rests on two ideas: finding the slope of a curve at a point, which tells you the rate of change, and finding the area under a curve, which adds up many small pieces. Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz developed it independently, between the 1660s and 1680s, and their followers carried on a bitter dispute over who deserved the credit. It underlies physics, engineering and economics.
Is there a walk that crosses each of the city's seven bridges exactly once?

The city of Königsberg, now Kaliningrad, had seven bridges that connected two islands and the banks of a river. Residents wondered whether you could walk through the city and cross each bridge exactly once. In 1736 Leonhard Euler showed that you could not. He simplified the map to dots and lines, which created graph theory. It now helps describe networks of all kinds, from roads to the internet to friendships.
A loop with a half twist has only one side and one edge.

Take a long strip of paper, give it a half twist and tape the ends together. You get a Möbius strip, a loop with only one side and one edge. August Möbius and Johann Listing described it independently in 1858. If you draw a line along the middle until you return to the start, you'll find you've covered what looked like both sides. It's a classic example of a surface with surprising properties.
In topology a coffee cup and a doughnut are the same shape.

Topology is a branch of mathematics that studies shapes in terms of what stays the same when you stretch, bend or squash them, without tearing. To a topologist, a coffee cup and a doughnut are the same shape, because each has exactly one hole, and one can be smoothly deformed into the other. It might sound like a game, but topology has real uses in physics, biology and data analysis.
Any map can be colored with four colors so no neighbors match.

In 1852 a mapmaker's observation raised a question: can any map be colored with just four colors, so that no neighboring regions share a color? For over a century, nobody could prove it. In 1976 Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did, with the help of a computer that checked nearly 2,000 cases, using over 1,200 hours of computer time. It was the first major theorem proved with a computer, and some mathematicians were uneasy about that.
No whole numbers satisfy a^n + b^n = c^n for n above 2.

Around 1637 the French lawyer and mathematician Pierre de Fermat scribbled in a book margin that no whole numbers satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for n above two. He added that he had a marvelous proof, but the margin was too small. Nobody found a proof for 357 years. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in 1994, after seven years of working in secret in his attic, using mathematics that didn't exist in Fermat's day.
In any consistent system of arithmetic, some true statements cannot be proved inside it.

In 1931 the young logician Kurt Gödel proved something startling. In any consistent system of rules rich enough to include arithmetic, there are true statements that can't be proved within the system. It ended the dream of David Hilbert and others of finding a complete and consistent set of rules for all of mathematics. It showed that there are built-in limits to what proof can do.
No program can decide, for every program, whether it will finish or run forever.

In 1936 Alan Turing asked whether it's possible to write a program that can look at any other program and tell, in advance, whether it will eventually stop or run forever. He proved it can't be done, using a clever self-referring argument. It's a real limit on what computers can do, not just a limit of today's technology, and it was one of the first such results in computer science.
Can every problem whose answer is quickly checkable also be quickly solved?

Some problems, like solving a big Sudoku or finding the best route through many cities, are hard to solve but easy to check once someone shows you an answer. The question of whether every problem whose answer can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is called P versus NP. It's one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a million-dollar prize. Most experts believe the answer is no, but nobody has proved it.
Seven great problems, with $1 million each; only one is solved.

In 2000 the Clay Mathematics Institute named seven of the deepest unsolved problems in mathematics and offered $1 million for the solution of each. Only one has been solved so far: the Poincaré conjecture, by the Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman, in 2002 and 2003. He declined the prize and the other honors. The rest, including the Riemann hypothesis and P versus NP, remain open.
In many real data sets, about 30% of numbers start with the digit 1.

In many real collections of numbers, like river lengths, populations and stock prices, about 30 percent of them begin with the digit 1, and fewer than 5 percent begin with 9. Simon Newcomb noticed in 1881 that the early pages of logarithm tables were more worn than the later ones, and Frank Benford rediscovered it in 1938. Auditors use it to catch fraud, since invented numbers tend not to follow the pattern.
The second most common word appears half as often as the first, the third a third as often.

In nearly any large body of text, the most common word appears about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on. The linguist George Zipf described it in 1935. In English, "the" makes up about 7 percent of words. Strikingly similar patterns appear in the sizes of cities and the traffic to websites, though no one fully understands why.
Many measurements cluster around an average with symmetric tails.

Many measurements, such as heights, test scores and measurement errors, cluster around an average and thin out symmetrically on either side, in what's called the normal distribution. About 68 percent of values fall within one standard deviation of the average, 95 percent within two, and 99.7 percent within three. Carl Friedrich Gauss used it in the early 1800s to handle errors in astronomical measurements.
Averages of many independent things tend to form a bell curve, whatever the shape of the originals.

Here's a remarkable fact: if you take the average of many independent random things, the result tends to form a bell curve, whatever the shape of the original distribution. It explains why so many things in nature look bell-shaped. A general version of the theorem was proved by Pierre-Simon Laplace in 1810. It's one of the main reasons that statistics works.
With enough trials, averages settle close to the true value.

If you flip a fair coin only a few times, you might get seven heads in ten. But as the number of flips grows, the share of heads gets closer and closer to a half. This is the law of large numbers, proved by Jacob Bernoulli, published in 1713. It's why casinos always win in the long run, and it's also a warning that small samples can easily mislead.
Two letters in 1654 started the mathematics of chance.

In 1654 the French mathematicians Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters about a gambling problem: how should the stakes be divided fairly if a game of chance is interrupted before it's finished? Their solutions laid the foundations of probability theory. Before then, people had played games of chance for thousands of years but had no mathematics to describe them.
There are about 8 times 10 to the 67th ways to order 52 cards.

The number of ways to arrange a deck of 52 cards is 52 factorial, which is about 8 followed by 67 zeros. That's so large that every time you properly shuffle a deck, you almost certainly create an order that has never occurred before in the history of the world. If every person on Earth shuffled a deck every second since the start of the universe, they'd barely scratch the surface.
A monkey typing at random would eventually produce Shakespeare.

The idea that a monkey hitting keys at random on a typewriter would eventually type the complete works of Shakespeare goes back to Émile Borel in 1913. It's true in theory, if given infinite time. But it would take far longer than the age of the universe for any realistic number of monkeys. The theorem is really about the nature of large numbers and chance, not about literature.
A way to turn multiplying into adding.

A logarithm turns multiplication into addition. In 1614 the Scottish mathematician John Napier published tables of them, which saved astronomers and navigators years of tedious arithmetic. Slide rules, used by engineers for 350 years, were based on them. Many quantities are measured on logarithmic scales, including earthquakes on the Richter scale, sound in decibels and acidity in pH.
Doubling grains on each square gives more than 18 quintillion on the last.

A legend says the inventor of chess asked a king for a reward of one grain of rice on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, doubling each time. The king agreed, thinking it modest. By the 64th square, the amount would be about 18 quintillion grains, more rice than has ever been grown. It's a classic illustration of exponential growth.
Take any number; if it's even halve it, if odd triple it and add 1. You always reach 1.

Pick any positive whole number. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add one. Keep going. The conjecture is that you'll always eventually reach 1. Lothar Collatz posed it in 1937, and computers have tested it for every number up to nearly 300 quintillion, but there's no proof. The mathematician Paul Erdős said that mathematics may not be ready for such problems.
Computers count in base 2, with just 0 and 1.

Computers use the binary system, where there are only two digits, 0 and 1, instead of our ten. In 1703 the German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz wrote about it, and was fascinated that all numbers could be made from just those two symbols. Each digit is a bit, and eight bits make a byte. Any number, letter, picture or sound can be written in binary, which suits machines that have switches that are either on or off.

We divide hours into 60 minutes and minutes into 60 seconds because the ancient Babylonians counted in base 60. It's a handy number: 60 can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, so fractions are easy. We still use it for time, and the 360 degrees of a circle also come from the Babylonians, from base 60 and the length of the year.
A 300 BCE textbook that taught rigorous proof for over 2,000 years.

Around 300 BCE the Greek mathematician Euclid wrote the Elements, a textbook that built all of geometry from a handful of simple assumptions, called axioms, by logical proof. It was used for over 2,000 years and became one of the most influential books ever written. Abraham Lincoln is said to have studied it as a young lawyer, to learn how to argue and prove a point.
On a curved surface the angles of a triangle add up to more or less than 180 degrees.

Euclid assumed that, given a line and a point not on it, there's exactly one line through the point that never meets the first. For centuries, mathematicians tried to prove this, until in the 1820s and 30s, Gauss, János Bolyai and Nikolai Lobachevsky showed that you can build consistent geometries without it. On a curved surface, the angles of a triangle add up to more or less than 180 degrees. A century later Einstein used it to describe curved spacetime.
Shapes that look similar at every scale, like a coastline or a fern.

A fractal is a shape that looks similar at every scale, like a coastline, a fern, or a snowflake edge. The mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot named them in 1975. He asked a famous question in 1967, "How long is the coast of Britain?" and showed that there's no single answer: the more finely you measure, the longer it gets. Fractals help describe many natural shapes.
Tiny changes in the starting conditions can lead to huge differences later.

In 1961 the meteorologist Edward Lorenz was running a weather simulation on a computer. To save time, he restarted a run in the middle, typing in 0.506 instead of the full figure, 0.506127. The tiny difference grew until the forecast was completely different. It showed that small changes can lead to large differences later, and it's one reason that weather can only be forecast about ten days ahead.
Assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show it leads to nonsense.

In this method, you assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show that it leads to an absurdity, so the assumption must be false. It's used to prove that the square root of 2 is irrational, and that there are infinitely many primes. The English mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote that it "is one of a mathematician's finest weapons." It's like checking a door by assuming it's open and finding you'd walk through a wall.
Prove it for the first case, then prove that each case leads to the next, and it holds for all.

Induction is a way of proving that something is true for all whole numbers. First show that it's true for the first case. Then show that, if it's true for any case, it must be true for the next one. It's like a line of dominoes: if the first falls, and each one knocks over the next, then they all fall. It can prove, for example, that the sum of the first n numbers is n times n plus one, divided by two.
A teacher asked a young Gauss to add the numbers 1 to 100 to keep him busy.

According to a well-known story, when Carl Friedrich Gauss was about ten, his teacher asked the class to add up the numbers from 1 to 100, hoping to keep them busy. Gauss gave the answer in moments. He saw that 1 plus 100 is 101, 2 plus 99 is 101, and so on, making 50 pairs of 101, which is 5,050. The tale may have been embellished in the retelling, but the method is real and useful.
A 1999 NASA probe was lost because of a units mix-up.

In September 1999 NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter, which had traveled nine months to reach Mars, approached the planet too low and was lost. The cause was a mix-up in units. Software built by one team gave the thrust in pound-force seconds, which is the English system, and the navigation team expected newton-seconds, which is metric. The $125 million spacecraft probably burned up in the atmosphere.
Bees build hexagons because they use the least wax to cover a flat area.

Honeybees build their wax cells as hexagons, and a mathematician explains why: it's the most efficient shape. The honeycomb conjecture, which goes back to the ancient Greeks, says that dividing a flat surface into equal-area cells with the least total boundary is best done with a hexagonal grid. Thomas Hales proved it in 1999. Bees use the least wax to store the most honey.
Every symmetry in nature corresponds to a conservation law.

In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved a result that physicists consider one of the most beautiful and important. Every symmetry in nature leads to a conservation law. If the laws of physics are the same at all times, energy is conserved. If they're the same everywhere in space, momentum is conserved. When she died, Einstein wrote that she was the most significant creative mathematical genius since women were admitted to higher education.
Some cicadas emerge every 13 or 17 years, both prime numbers.

In the eastern United States, some cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground and then emerge together in huge numbers. Both numbers are primes. One hypothesis is that prime-numbered cycles make it hard for predators or other cicada broods with shorter cycles to line up with them. It's an elegant idea, but it's a hypothesis, and not all biologists are persuaded.
For 350 years engineers did calculations by sliding two scales.

Before pocket calculators, engineers used slide rules, two sliding scales marked with logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition by sliding. The English minister William Oughtred invented it around 1622. For about 350 years, it was a standard tool. Apollo astronauts carried slide rules as a backup. Pocket calculators replaced them in the early 1970s.
March 14, because 3.14 is the start of pi.

Pi Day is celebrated on March 14, because 3.14 are the first digits of pi. The physicist Larry Shaw organized the first celebration at the Exploratorium museum in San Francisco in 1988, with a march around a circular space, followed by fruit pie. March 14 is also Albert Einstein's birthday. In 2019 UNESCO proclaimed it the International Day of Mathematics.
Three different "averages", and the right one depends on the data.

These are three ways of saying "typical," and they can give very different answers. The mean is the usual average, found by adding everything up and dividing. The median is the middle value when you line them all up, and the mode is the most common one. If Bill Gates walks into a bar, the average wealth of the people in it shoots up, but the median hardly moves. For things like income or house prices, where a few huge values pull the mean, the median is usually the more honest summary.
How spread out the numbers are around the average.

The average on its own doesn't tell you how spread out the numbers are. The standard deviation does. Karl Pearson gave it its name in 1893. Imagine two classes that both average 70 on a test. In one, the standard deviation is 5, so almost everyone scored between 60 and 80. In the other it's 20, so you have students at 30 and others at 100. The averages match, but the classes are very different places.
A 95% interval comes from a method that captures the true value 95% of the time.

Studies often report a "95% confidence interval." It sounds like there's a 95 percent chance the true value is inside the range, but that's not quite what it means.
