It means that the method used would capture the true value in 95 percent of repeated studies. The difference is subtle, and surveys have found that many researchers get it wrong. A practical reading is that the interval shows the range of values the data can't rule out.
A poll of about 1,000 people has a margin of about 3 percentage points.

News stories about polls often mention a margin of error, usually about plus or minus 3 percentage points for a poll of around 1,000 people. It reflects only random chance in picking the sample. It doesn't cover badly worded questions, or people who didn't respond, which can matter more. If a poll shows 52 percent to 48 percent with that margin, the two sides are statistically tied, even if the headline says someone's ahead.
In 1936 a poll of 2.4 million people got the election wrong.

In 1936 the magazine Literary Digest mailed out ten million ballots and got back more than 2.4 million, and predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt in a landslide. Roosevelt won in one of the biggest landslides in history. The magazine had drawn its sample from its own readers and from telephone and car-owner lists, which in the Depression skewed richer. George Gallup, polling a much smaller but representative sample, got it right.
How big a difference is, not just whether it exists.

A study can find that something "works" and still tell you nothing about how much. Effect size measures how large the difference is. Jacob Cohen suggested rough benchmarks for a standardized difference: 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium and 0.8 is large. A "statistically significant" result with a tiny effect may be of no practical use, particularly in large studies where even trivial differences can be detected.
Small studies often miss real effects.

A study with too few participants may fail to detect a real effect. That's low statistical power. A 2013 review of neuroscience studies estimated that the typical study had a power of only about 21 percent, which means it would miss most real effects. Worse, low power also means the results that do cross the threshold of significance tend to exaggerate the true effect.
How to make music make you younger
A 2011 paper "showed" listening to "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people 18 months younger.

In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn published a paper claiming that listening to the Beatles song "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people nearly a year and a half younger. It was a deliberate demonstration of how researchers, by making flexible choices about which data to include and which tests to run, can find "significant" results in nonsense. They then proposed rules to stop that kind of p-hacking.
A dead fish in a brain scanner appeared to react to photos of people.

In 2009 the neuroscientist Craig Bennett put a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI brain scanner, showed it photographs of people in social situations, and asked it to determine their emotions. Without correcting for the thousands of statistical tests involved, the analysis found brain activity in the dead fish. It was a joke with a serious point: you have to correct for multiple comparisons. It won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012.
Writing down your plan before you collect data.

In pre-registration, researchers publicly record their hypotheses and methods before collecting data. That stops them from quietly changing the question after they see which results turn out well. A 2021 comparison of studies found that 44 percent of those published in a "registered report" format found a positive result, compared with 96 percent of standard published papers, which suggests the usual literature is skewed toward positive findings.
A study of studies, combining results to see the overall picture.

A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies on a question to give a clearer overall picture. The psychologist Gene Glass coined the term in 1976, when he combined hundreds of studies of psychotherapy. A larger body of evidence gives more precise answers than any single study. But it can only be as good as the studies it includes, and if negative results were never published, even the pooled answer can be biased.
"Doubles your risk" can mean almost nothing if the risk was tiny.

A headline says a drug "doubles your risk," which sounds alarming. But if the risk was tiny to begin with, doubling it may mean very little. In 1995 the UK government warned that a new type of contraceptive pill doubled the risk of blood clots. The actual risk went from about 1 in 7,000 women to about 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and there was a rise in unwanted pregnancies and abortions.
How many people must take a treatment for one to benefit.

One helpful way to express how well a treatment works is the number of people who need to take it for one person to benefit. If a drug cuts a risk from 2 percent to 1 percent, you could call that a 50 percent reduction. But 100 people have to take it for one to be helped, and the others get the costs and side effects. The number makes the trade-offs clearer.
A test's power to find the sick, and to clear the healthy.

Any medical test can make two kinds of error. Sensitivity is how good it is at finding people who do have the condition, and specificity is how good it is at correctly clearing people who don't. A test can do very well on one and badly on the other. A very sensitive test catches nearly everyone who's sick but may also flag many healthy people, which is why a positive result often needs a follow-up.
Earlier detection can make survival look longer without extending life.

Screening tests find diseases earlier, and the apparent survival time after diagnosis gets longer. But that can be an illusion. Suppose a cancer is found at age 63 without screening and the patient dies at 70, which is 7 years of survival. With screening, it's found at 60, and the patient still dies at 70, so survival after diagnosis is 10 years, but the person didn't live any longer. The fairer test of screening is whether fewer people die of the disease.
Four data sets can have the same averages and correlation but look completely different.

In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made up four small sets of numbers that have almost identical averages, spreads and correlations. Yet when you plot them, they look completely different: one is a neat line, one is a curve, one has a single outlier pulling the line, and one is a vertical stack of points. His point was that you should always graph your data, because summary numbers can hide what's really going on.
A scatter of dots shaped like a dinosaur has the same statistics as a cloud of random dots.

In 2016 the data visualizer Alberto Cairo made up a data set that, when plotted, looks like a dinosaur, yet has the same averages, spread and correlation as a random scatter of dots. In 2017 researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice built on it, showing a dozen other shapes, including a star and a bullseye, that all share the same summary statistics. It's a modern version of Anscombe's lesson: always look at the picture.
Cutting the bottom off an axis makes small differences look huge.

A bar chart is supposed to show quantities in proportion to the height of the bars. If the vertical axis starts at 95 percent instead of zero, a difference between 97 and 99 can look like the second bar is several times as tall. It's a common way to make small differences look dramatic, sometimes by accident. Always check where the axis starts. Edward Tufte called misleading graphs a violation of graphical integrity.
The law of truly large numbers
With enough chances, even very unlikely things will happen.

When there are enough chances, even extremely unlikely things are bound to happen. The statisticians Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller pointed out that if an event has a one-in-a-million chance on a given day, then with hundreds of millions of people in America, it should happen to hundreds of people every day. So coincidences aren't strange. They're expected, when you consider how many opportunities there are.
Deaths from horse kicks in Prussian army corps fit a simple chance pattern.

In 1898 the Russian-Polish statistician Ladislaus Bortkiewicz looked at records of how many Prussian cavalry soldiers were killed by horse kicks each year, in 14 army corps over 20 years. He showed that the numbers fit a mathematical pattern known as the Poisson distribution, which describes rare events that occur independently at a steady average rate. It's a classic example of how even odd accidents follow statistical laws.
Ronald Fisher's famous experiment on whether a woman could tell the milk was added first.

In the 1920s, at an English country research station, a woman claimed that she could tell whether the tea or the milk had been poured into a cup first. The statistician Ronald Fisher turned this into a famous experiment: eight cups, four of each kind, presented in random order. If she's just guessing, the chance of getting all eight right is 1 in 70. The example became a model for randomization and significance testing.
Show two versions to different random users and see which does better.

When a website wants to know which version of a page works better, it can show version A to some visitors and version B to others, chosen at random, and compare the results. It's the same logic as a medical trial. In 2009 Google reportedly tested 41 shades of blue for a link bar, and a designer left the company partly because he felt that such testing was replacing design judgment.
The Powerball jackpot has odds of about 1 in 292 million.

The chance of winning the Powerball jackpot is about 1 in 292 million. If you bought a ticket for every weekly drawing, you'd have to keep going for about 5.6 million years to expect to win once. On average, a ticket is worth less than what you pay for it. People still play, and most of the pleasure is in the daydream.
A formula for how much to bet when you have an edge.

If you're offered a bet that's in your favor, how much of your money should you put on it? John Kelly, a physicist at Bell Labs, published a formula in 1956 for the answer. Bet too much, and a bad run can wipe you out, even though you have an edge. Bet too little, and you waste the edge. Many professional gamblers and investors use half the Kelly amount, to be safer.
Prices rise when something is scarce and fall when it is plentiful.

When something is scarce, its price tends to rise. When it's plentiful, it falls. The English economist Alfred Marshall drew the now-famous crossing curves of supply and demand in his 1890 textbook. The point where they cross is the price at which the amount that sellers want to sell equals the amount that buyers want to buy. It's a simple picture, but it explains a lot about how markets work.
Decisions depend on the next unit, not the average.

Water is essential for life but cheap, and diamonds are useless for survival but expensive. Economists puzzled over this paradox until the 1870s, when Carl Menger, William Stanley Jevons and Léon Walras each realized that value depends on the next unit, not the total. Because you already have plenty of water, one more glass is worth little, while one more diamond is scarce. Decisions are made at the margin.
Countries and people gain from trading even if one is better at everything.

In 1817 the economist David Ricardo showed something surprising: two parties can both gain from trade even if one is better at everything. Imagine a lawyer who also types faster than her assistant. She still comes out ahead by letting the assistant type, because her time is worth more spent on legal work. The same logic applies to countries, and it's the main reason that economists generally favor trade.
Dividing work makes everyone far more productive.

In The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, Adam Smith described a pin factory where the work was divided into about eighteen distinct steps. He said ten workers, each specializing in a few tasks, could produce about 48,000 pins a day, while a single worker doing everything might make one pin a day, or at most twenty. The division of labor makes everyone far more productive.
Individuals pursuing their own interests may unintentionally help society.

The phrase "invisible hand" is one of the best-known in economics, and Adam Smith used it only once in The Wealth of Nations, in 1776. He argued that people pursuing their own interests may, without intending it, end up helping society. Yet he was no simple cheerleader for business: in the same book, he warned that merchants rarely meet together without it ending in a conspiracy against the public.
A general rise in prices, which means your money buys less.

Inflation means that prices in general are rising, so each dollar buys less. Many central banks aim for about 2 percent a year, which they consider a healthy level. Even that adds up. At 2 percent, prices double in about 36 years. At 7 percent, they double in about 10. That's why money sitting in a drawer slowly loses what it can buy.
When prices spiral out of control, money becomes worthless.

When a government prints too much money, prices can spiral out of control. In Germany in 1923, prices at one point doubled every few days, and people were paid twice a day and rushed to spend the money before it lost value. In Zimbabwe, in November 2008, monthly inflation reached an estimated 80 billion percent. When money stops working, people turn to barter or foreign currencies.
Institutions that set interest rates to steer the economy.

A central bank sets short-term interest rates to influence the economy: lowering them to encourage borrowing and spending, and raising them to cool down inflation. The US Federal Reserve was created in 1913, after a series of bank panics, especially one in 1907. It has what's called a dual mandate from Congress: to keep prices stable and to promote maximum employment.
Money that has value because governments say so and people accept it.

The dollar bill in your wallet has no gold behind it, and it isn't worth much as paper. It's money because the government says it is and because everyone accepts it. That's called fiat money, from the Latin for "let it be done." Until 1971, the US dollar could be exchanged for gold at a fixed rate, and when President Nixon ended that, the world moved fully to fiat currencies. Most money today is just numbers in bank accounts.
Spreading your money lowers risk without lowering the average return.

"Don't put all your eggs in one basket" has a mathematical backing. In 1952 Harry Markowitz showed that if you combine investments that don't all move in the same direction at the same time, you can reduce your overall risk without lowering your expected return. He won a Nobel Prize for it in 1990. It's often called the only free lunch in finance.
A fund that owns the whole market instead of trying to pick winners.

An index fund simply buys all the stocks in a market, rather than trying to pick winners. John Bogle founded the first one available to ordinary investors in 1976, at Vanguard, and he was ridiculed for it at the time. Reports that compare funds, such as the S&P SPIVA scorecards, regularly find that over a 15-year period, around nine in ten professional stock funds do worse than the index they're trying to beat.
Prices already reflect what is publicly known, so beating the market is very hard.

Eugene Fama proposed in 1970 that stock prices already reflect all publicly available information, so it's very hard to consistently beat the market. Other economists, like Robert Shiller, argued that markets can be driven by emotion and bubbles. In 2013 Fama and Shiller, with another economist, shared the Nobel Prize in economics, an indication of how both views have supporters. It's still debated.
The 1637 Dutch craze for tulip bulbs is a famous bubble.

In the 1630s tulip bulbs in the Netherlands sold at extraordinary prices, and the craze is retold as the classic example of a speculative bubble that ruined thousands. Modern historians, like Anne Goldgar, who looked through the records, say it was much smaller than the legend: few people seem to have been ruined, and the evidence is thin. The story has been told so many times that the myth became the lesson.
Investing all your money at once beat spreading it out about two-thirds of the time.

If you have a pile of money to invest, is it better to invest it all at once, or to spread it out over several months? A 2012 Vanguard study found that investing all at once did better about two-thirds of the time, simply because markets tend to rise more often than they fall. Spreading it out makes you less likely to regret putting everything in just before a drop, so it's a trade-off.
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year.

Would you rather have $100 today or $100 in a year? Most people say today, and they're right. You could invest the money and have more later, and prices will likely have risen. Economists "discount" future money to reflect this. It's the principle behind interest on loans and savings, and it's how the value of any investment or business is worked out.
Benjamin Franklin left money to Boston and Philadelphia, to be used after 200 years.

When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left 1,000 pounds each to the cities of Boston and Philadelphia, to be loaned out at interest and not fully used for 200 years. By 1990 the funds had grown to millions of dollars: about $5 million in Boston's fund and $2 million in Philadelphia's. It's a vivid example of the power of compound interest over a long time.
Shared resources get overused when each user gains and the cost is spread.

In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin described a pasture open to all herders. Each herder gains by adding another cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture gets destroyed. It's an image for many shared resources, such as fisheries and the atmosphere. Elinor Ostrom, who won the 2009 Nobel Prize in economics, showed that many communities have managed shared resources well by creating their own rules.
Two people each do better by betraying, yet both do worse than if they cooperated.

Two suspects are held separately. Each is offered a deal to betray the other. Whatever the other does, betraying seems best for you. But if both betray, they do worse than if both had stayed quiet. Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game in 1950, and Albert Tucker told the prison story. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments around 1980, the winning strategy was "tit for tat": cooperate first, then copy the other player's last move.
A situation where nobody gains by changing their choice alone.

A Nash equilibrium is a situation in which no player can do better by changing only their own choice, given what the others are doing. John Nash proved in 1950 that every game with a finite number of players and choices has at least one. It describes stable outcomes, not necessarily good ones, as the prisoner's dilemma shows, where both players betraying is a stable result that's bad for both. Nash won the Nobel Prize in 1994.
Some things become more valuable as more people use them.

Some things become more valuable as more people use them. A telephone is useless if you're the only one who has one, and valuable if everyone you know does. That's a network effect. Metcalfe's law says that the value of a network grows with the square of the number of users, but studies of real networks suggest it grows more slowly. It helps explain why one social network or payment system can come to dominate.
When buyers cannot tell good from bad, bad goods can drive out good ones.

In 1970 the economist George Akerlof wrote a paper about the used-car market. Sellers know whether their car is good or a "lemon," but buyers can't tell, so buyers are only willing to pay an average price. At that price, owners of good cars won't sell, and the market fills up with lemons. The paper showed how a lack of information can make markets fail. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for it.
People take more risks when someone else bears the cost.

When someone else bears the cost of a risk, people tend to take more of it. A driver with full insurance may be a little less careful. A bank that expects the government to bail it out if it fails may place bigger bets. Insurers try to limit it with deductibles and co-payments, so that the person still has something to lose.
A cost or benefit that falls on people who did not choose it.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on someone who didn't choose to take part. A factory's pollution harms people downwind, a negative externality. A neighbor's beautiful garden pleases passers-by, a positive one. In 1920 the economist Arthur Pigou argued that a tax on the polluter can make the price of a product reflect its true cost to society. Many modern carbon taxes follow the idea.
Things everyone can use, like street lights or defense, are hard to fund voluntarily.

Some things, like street lighting, clean air or national defense, benefit everyone, whether or not they pay. That creates a free-rider problem: if you can use it either way, why pay? Voluntary contributions tend to fall short. That's the reason economists give for why governments usually pay for such goods with taxes, to make sure that everyone chips in.
If people can bargain cheaply, they will settle on an efficient outcome whoever holds the rights.

Ronald Coase argued in a 1960 paper that if people can bargain easily with each other, they'll reach an efficient arrangement no matter who starts out holding the legal rights. For example, a factory and its neighbors could settle the problem of smoke by negotiation, without a government rule. In real life, the costs of getting everyone together and agreeing are often too high, so the theorem works best for small groups.
How much demand changes when the price changes.

Price elasticity is how much demand changes when the price changes. For things people need and can't easily replace, like gasoline in the short run, demand barely drops when the price goes up. That's low elasticity. For things with lots of substitutes, like one brand of soda, a small price rise sends buyers elsewhere. That's high elasticity. Businesses and governments use it to predict how changes in price will play out.
Gross domestic product counts output, not well-being.

Gross domestic product measures the total value of goods and services a country produces. Simon Kuznets, who developed the measure in the 1930s, warned in a 1934 report to Congress that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income. GDP counts cleaning up after a disaster as growth, but it doesn't count unpaid housework, leisure or the health of the environment.
A single number for inequality, from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has everything).

The Gini coefficient is a single number that measures how unequal an income distribution is, from 0, where everyone has the same, to 1, where one person has everything. The Italian statistician Corrado Gini introduced it in 1912. It's handy for comparing countries: Scandinavian countries are around 0.25 to 0.28, and some other countries are above 0.6. It doesn't show where in the distribution the inequality lies.

Does raising the minimum wage cost jobs? In 1994 the economists David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had raised its minimum wage, with neighboring Pennsylvania, which hadn't. They found no loss of jobs in New Jersey. Other studies have found different results, so the debate continues. David Card shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on such "natural experiments."
Using chance events to study cause and effect.

Economists can't usually run controlled experiments on whole economies. But sometimes events create something close: a lottery for the military draft, a state border where laws differ or a sudden change in a rule. These are called natural experiments. In 2021 David Card, Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens shared the Nobel Prize in economics for developing ways to learn about cause and effect from them.
Small changes in how choices are presented can steer behavior.

A nudge is a small change in how choices are presented that steers people toward a better decision, without forbidding anything, such as making organ donation or saving for retirement the default. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularized the idea in their 2008 book. A 2022 review found that, once publication bias is accounted for, the average effect shrinks to nearly zero, though some well-designed nudges clearly work.
Things people want more as the price goes up.

Normally, when a price goes up, people buy less. But for some luxury goods, demand can rise as the price rises, because the high price is part of the appeal. In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen wrote about "conspicuous consumption," buying things to show status. Designer handbags, luxury watches and certain sports cars fit. Ordinary goods don't work that way.
A company can be profitable and still run out of cash.

A company can show a profit on paper and still run out of cash. Profit counts sales when they're made, even if customers haven't paid yet. Cash flow is the money that's actually in the bank. Many businesses that look healthy fail because customers pay slowly while suppliers and employees need to be paid right away. It's why experienced owners say "cash is king."
Margin is profit as a share of price, markup is profit as a share of cost.

Margin and markup are easy to mix up. Markup is profit as a percentage of what the item cost you. Margin is profit as a percentage of the price you charge. If you buy something for $60 and sell it for $100, the profit is $40, so the markup is about 67 percent and the margin is 40 percent. Confusing the two is a common cause of pricing too low.
Does each sale make money after what it costs to make and win it?

Unit economics asks whether you make money on each individual sale, after counting everything it costs to make the product and to win the customer. Suppose it costs $50 in advertising to get a customer who brings in $30 of profit. Every sale loses $20, and growing faster just loses money faster. It's worth working out before you try to scale a business.
The sales you need to cover all your costs.

The break-even point is how much you need to sell to cover all your costs. You work it out by dividing your fixed costs, such as rent and salaries, by the profit you make on each unit. Below that number, you lose money, and above it, every additional sale adds to your profit. It's one of the first numbers to know before starting a business or launching a product.
Cheaper, simpler products can start at the bottom and overtake leaders.

In 1997 the Harvard professor Clayton Christensen argued that successful companies can be overtaken by cheaper, simpler products that start at the bottom of the market, and improve until they threaten the leaders. It became enormously influential. Critics, including the historian Jill Lepore in a 2014 article, said that his examples were chosen after the fact, so it's better as a way of describing the past than predicting the future.
The simplest version of something that tests whether people want it.

A minimum viable product is the simplest version of a product that you can put in front of real customers to learn whether they want it. Eric Ries made the term popular in his 2011 book The Lean Startup. The idea is to learn early, with little cost, before spending months building something nobody wants. It's about testing assumptions, not about shipping something poor.
An hour spent on one thing is an hour not spent on another.

Money can be saved for later, but time can't. Every hour is spent on something, and spending it on one thing means not spending it on another. That's why the question "Is this worth doing?" is a weak test, because nearly anything has some value. A better question is "What else could I do with this hour?" That brings the real cost into view.
The first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

Marie Sklodowska was born in Warsaw and moved to Paris to study, and she went on to a career that nobody has matched. In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel for their work on radioactivity, a word she coined. In 1911 she won the Chemistry prize for discovering polonium and radium. In the First World War she helped equip vehicles with X-ray machines, which soldiers called "little Curies."
He pointed a telescope at the sky and found that the heavens were not perfect.

In 1609 Galileo heard of a Dutch invention and built a better telescope himself, then turned it to the sky. He saw mountains and craters on the Moon, four small moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus, all evidence that not everything in the heavens circled the Earth. In 1633 the Inquisition forced him to renounce the Sun-centered view, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest.
He proposed in 1543 that the Earth moves around the Sun.

For more than a thousand years most people believed that the Sun and planets circled the Earth. Copernicus, a Polish astronomer and church official, worked out in detail a system with the Sun at the center. His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was printed in 1543, and according to tradition he was handed a copy on his deathbed. The idea wasn't entirely new, but he supplied the mathematics.
He found that planets move in ellipses, not circles.

Kepler, a German astronomer, had access to the careful naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, and spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle. It wouldn't fit. Eventually he realized the orbit was an ellipse. He published three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, which Isaac Newton later used to arrive at his theory of gravity. Kepler also wrote an early work of science fiction about a trip to the Moon.
He spent 20 years gathering evidence before publishing his theory.

Darwin returned from his five-year voyage on HMS Beagle in 1836 with the beginnings of an idea. For more than twenty years, he gathered evidence and told only a few friends. In 1858 he received a letter from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who had independently come to the same idea. A joint paper was read to the Linnean Society, and Darwin's book On the Origin of Species came out in 1859.
He came up with natural selection independently, while ill with fever on an island.

Wallace was a self-taught naturalist who made a living collecting specimens in the Amazon and in Southeast Asia. In 1858, lying sick with a fever on an island in Indonesia, he thought of natural selection, wrote it up in a few days and sent it to Darwin. Darwin was alarmed to see his own theory, and the two agreed to publish together. Wallace also found that animals on either side of a line through Indonesia are strikingly different, now called Wallace's Line.
He proved that germs cause disease and fermentation.

In the 1860s the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that microbes, not "spontaneous generation," were responsible for fermentation and spoilage. He boiled broth in flasks with long swan-shaped necks, which let in air but trapped dust and germs, and the broth stayed clear. That supported germ theory, the idea that germs cause disease. In 1885 he gave a boy named Joseph Meister, who'd been bitten by a rabid dog, the first rabies vaccine, and the boy lived.
He made surgery much safer by cleaning wounds and tools with carbolic acid.

In the 1860s surgeons in hospitals operated in street clothes and wiped their instruments on their aprons, and many patients died of infection afterward. The British surgeon Joseph Lister read about Pasteur's work on germs and began to clean wounds and tools with carbolic acid. In 1867 he reported that deaths among his amputation patients fell from about 45 percent to about 15 percent. The mouthwash Listerine was named after him.
He found that doctors' unwashed hands were killing new mothers.

In 1847 the Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in the hospital ward where doctors worked were dying of fever at a much higher rate than in the ward staffed by midwives. He realized that doctors were coming straight from autopsies, and he told them to wash their hands in chlorine solution. Deaths fell from about 18 percent to about 2 percent. His colleagues rejected the idea, and he ended his life in an asylum.
He tested the first smallpox vaccine using cowpox in 1796.

In the 1790s the English country doctor Edward Jenner heard that milkmaids who'd caught cowpox seemed not to get smallpox. In 1796 he took matter from a cowpox sore and scratched it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. Later he exposed the boy to smallpox, and the boy didn't catch it. The word "vaccine" comes from the Latin word for cow, vacca.
The nurse who was also a pioneering statistician.

Florence Nightingale is remembered as the "Lady with the Lamp," a nurse in the Crimean War, but she was also a brilliant statistician. She gathered data and drew striking charts, including a polar-area diagram, to show that far more soldiers died of disease than of battle wounds. After sanitary reforms at the hospital at Scutari, the death rate dropped from over 40 percent to about 2 percent. In 1858 she became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society.
She wrote what is considered the first computer program, in 1843.

Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, and she studied mathematics. She translated an article about Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was never completed, and added her own notes in 1843. They included a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, which is regarded as the first computer program. She also saw that such a machine could work with symbols and even music, not just numbers.
He defined what a computer can do, helped break Enigma and asked whether machines can think.

In 1936 the young British mathematician Alan Turing described an imaginary machine that could carry out any calculation, a model of what we now call a computer. In the Second World War, he worked at Bletchley Park and helped break the German naval Enigma code, work that is thought to have shortened the war. In 1950 he asked whether machines can think, and proposed a test. He was convicted in 1952 for being gay, and the British government pardoned him in 2013.
A rear admiral who wrote one of the first compilers, which turns human-readable code into machine code.

Grace Hopper was a mathematician who became a rear admiral in the US Navy. In 1952 she created one of the first compilers, a program that translates instructions into machine code, and she argued that programming should be done in words close to English, which led to the language COBOL. In 1947, when a moth was found stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer, she taped it into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found."
A NASA mathematician whose calculations took Americans to space.

Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at NASA who worked as a human "computer" at a time when Black women were segregated at the agency. She calculated the flight path for Alan Shepard's 1961 mission. In 1962, before John Glenn's orbital flight, the astronaut asked for "the girl" to check the computer's numbers by hand, and he wouldn't fly until she had. President Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015.
Her X-ray image of DNA, Photo 51, revealed its helical structure.

The British chemist Rosalind Franklin was an expert in X-ray crystallography. In 1952 she and her student Raymond Gosling produced "Photo 51," a sharp X-ray image of DNA that showed a helical pattern. Without her knowledge, a colleague showed it to James Watson, and it gave him and Francis Crick crucial information for their 1953 model. She died of ovarian cancer in 1958, at 37, and the Nobel Prize isn't awarded posthumously.
She discovered that genes can move around in a chromosome, decades before others believed her.

Barbara McClintock studied corn, and from the 1940s she noticed that certain genes could move from one place on a chromosome to another, changing the color patterns of the kernels. Most scientists didn't believe her, and she stopped publishing about it for years. Decades later, other researchers found similar "jumping genes" in many organisms. She won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Medicine, alone, at the age of 81.
A "computer" at Harvard who found a way to measure the distance to stars.

In the early 1900s, Henrietta Leavitt worked at Harvard College Observatory as one of the women hired to measure photographs of stars, for low pay. Studying pulsing stars in the Magellanic Clouds, she noticed that the brighter ones took longer to pulse. That gave astronomers a way of measuring distances to faraway stars and galaxies. Edwin Hubble later used it to show that the Andromeda nebula is a separate galaxy.
She showed in 1925 that stars are made mostly of hydrogen.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne, then a graduate student at Harvard, concluded in her PhD thesis that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, not of the same mix as the Earth, as scientists had assumed. A prominent astronomer, Henry Norris Russell, persuaded her to describe the result as probably not real. Four years later, he reached the same conclusion by other means and published it, giving her credit. The astronomer Otto Struve called her thesis the most brilliant ever in astronomy.
She proved that nature can tell left from right, and was left out of the Nobel Prize.

Physicists believed that nature doesn't distinguish left from right. In 1956 Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang suggested that it might not hold for the weak nuclear force and needed someone to test it. Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American experimentalist at Columbia, ran a delicate experiment on cobalt-60 at very low temperatures and found that it did break the symmetry. Lee and Yang won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics, but she did not.
In 1905, at 26, he published four papers that changed physics.

In 1905, while working as a patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland, the 26-year-old Albert Einstein published four papers in a single year, now called his miracle year. They explained the photoelectric effect, which showed that light comes in packets, proved the existence of atoms by explaining Brownian motion, presented the special theory of relativity, and gave the equation E equals mc squared.
He started quantum theory in 1900 as a reluctant fix.

In 1900 Max Planck was trying to explain the glow of hot objects, and found that the numbers worked only if energy came in tiny packets, which he called quanta. He thought of it as a mathematical trick and was uneasy about it. It took years for physicists, including Einstein, to realize it described something real, and Planck's constant became a foundation of quantum theory. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics.
He proposed in 1913 that electrons in atoms occupy fixed energy levels.

In 1913 the Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in atoms can only occupy certain fixed energy levels and give off light when they jump between them. It explained why hydrogen glows in specific colors. He later led the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. During the Second World War, he helped Jewish scientists escape from Nazi-occupied Europe, and he escaped to Sweden himself in 1943.
He predicted antimatter from an equation, before anyone had seen it.

In 1928 the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote down an equation that combined quantum mechanics and special relativity to describe the electron. To his surprise, it had solutions that implied a particle with the electron's mass but opposite charge, which he first thought was the proton. In 1932 Carl Anderson found just such a particle, the positron, in cosmic rays. It was the first evidence of antimatter, and Dirac shared the 1933 Nobel Prize.
He showed that electricity, magnetism and light are one thing.

In the 1860s the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a set of equations that described how electric and magnetic fields behave. He found that they predicted waves that travel at the speed of light, and he concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic wave. Later, Heinrich Hertz generated such waves, which led to radio. Einstein said that Maxwell's work was the most profound change in physics since Newton.
A bookbinder's apprentice who discovered electromagnetic induction.

Michael Faraday left school at 13 to work as a bookbinder's apprentice, and he read the books he bound. He became assistant to the chemist Humphry Davy, and in 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field creates an electric current. That's how generators work. He also began the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825, which are still held every year.
His alternating-current system made power networks possible.

Nikola Tesla was a Serbian-American inventor who worked briefly for Thomas Edison. He designed a practical alternating-current induction motor, which he patented in 1888, and the American industrialist George Westinghouse bought his patents. In the "war of the currents," Westinghouse and Tesla's alternating current beat Edison's direct current, because AC can be sent over long distances at high voltage. It's how electricity is still distributed today.
He showed the Challenger disaster's cause with a glass of ice water.

Richard Feynman was a physicist who won the 1965 Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics. He was also a gifted teacher. After the Challenger disaster in 1986, he served on the investigating commission. At a televised hearing, he dropped a piece of a rubber O-ring into a glass of ice water and showed that it lost its springiness in the cold, which explained why the seals had failed on the cold launch morning.
He founded information theory and gave us the bit.

In 1937, as a master's student, Claude Shannon realized that electrical circuits could carry out logic, laying the foundations for digital computers. In 1948 he published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," which founded information theory. It showed that any information can be measured in bits and sent through a noisy channel without error, if coded properly. It's behind everything from phone calls to the internet.
A mathematician who helped shape computers, game theory and quantum mechanics.

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-American mathematician who made major contributions to quantum mechanics, game theory and the design of computers. The stored-program architecture used by most computers today, in which instructions and data live in the same memory, is still called the von Neumann architecture. His colleagues, many of them brilliant themselves, often said that he was the fastest mind they ever met.
The British scientist who invented the World Wide Web.

In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist at CERN in Switzerland, proposed a system for sharing documents through links over the internet. His boss wrote "vague but exciting" on the proposal. In 1990 he built the first web browser and server. In 1993 CERN announced that the technology would be free for everyone to use, with no royalties, which is a big reason the web took off.
He gave every species a two-part Latin name.

The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus created the system that scientists still use to name living things. In his Systema Naturae of 1735 and in Species Plantarum of 1753, he organized plants and animals into groups, and gave each species a two-part Latin name, a genus and a species. Our own species name, Homo sapiens, means "wise human." Before this, names were long, descriptive phrases.
He saw nature as a connected web, long before the word ecology.

The German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt traveled through Latin America from 1799 to 1804, measuring and collecting at every opportunity. He saw nature as an interconnected web, in which climate, altitude and plants were all linked, long before the word ecology existed. He influenced Charles Darwin, who carried his books on the Beagle, and many others, including the writer Henry David Thoreau.
A fossil hunter who found some of the first complete ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons.

Mary Anning grew up poor in the English seaside town of Lyme Regis, where she and her family collected fossils from the cliffs and sold them. Around 1811, when she was about twelve, she and her brother found the skeleton of a giant marine reptile, an ichthyosaur. Later she found the first complete plesiosaur. She was largely uncredited by the scientific community, and as a woman she couldn't join the Geological Society.
She watched wild chimpanzees use tools and changed our idea of what makes us human.

In 1960 Jane Goodall, then 26, went to Gombe in Tanzania to study wild chimpanzees. She watched one, whom she called David Greybeard, strip leaves from a twig and use it to fish termites out of a mound. It was the first observation of tool-making in animals other than humans. Her mentor Louis Leakey wrote that we must now redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human.
Her 1962 book "Silent Spring" showed how pesticides harm wildlife and people.

The American marine biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring in 1962, a book that described how pesticides such as DDT were poisoning birds and the food chain. It was attacked by the chemical industry, but it changed public opinion. It helped lead to the US ban on DDT for agricultural use in 1972 and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. She wrote it while being treated for breast cancer, and died in 1964.
The plant scientist whose wheat helped feed hundreds of millions.

The American agronomist Norman Borlaug spent years in Mexico breeding wheat that was high-yielding and resistant to rust disease. In the 1960s his varieties were introduced in India and Pakistan, and yields nearly doubled in a few years, helping to prevent widespread famine. This was a key part of what became known as the Green Revolution. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
He made fertilizer from air, and also poison gas.

The German chemist Fritz Haber invented a way to make ammonia from nitrogen in the air, which made artificial fertilizer possible and now feeds billions. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. But he also led the German chemical weapons program in the First World War, and personally oversaw the first major chlorine gas attack in 1915. His wife Clara, a chemist who opposed his work, took her own life that year.
He made the first widely used polio vaccine, and did not patent it.

In 1955 the American physician Jonas Salk announced that his polio vaccine was safe and effective, following a huge trial with 1.8 million children. At the time polio paralyzed and killed thousands every year, and people were jubilant. When the journalist Edward R. Murrow asked who owned the patent, Salk reportedly replied, "Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?"
The film star who co-invented frequency hopping.

Hedy Lamarr was a famous film actress in the 1930s and 40s who was also an inventor. In 1941 she and the composer George Antheil filed a patent for a system of "frequency hopping," in which a radio signal rapidly changes frequencies in a pattern known to sender and receiver, to prevent enemy jamming of torpedo guidance. It was granted in 1942. The principle is related to technologies later used in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS.
She started a movement that planted tens of millions of trees.

In 1977 the Kenyan environmentalist Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement, which paid poor rural women a small amount to plant trees, to restore forests, prevent erosion and provide firewood. Over the decades, the movement planted tens of millions of trees. She was jailed and beaten for her activism. In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize, the first African woman to receive it.
She found a malaria medicine in an ancient Chinese herbal text.

In the late 1960s the Chinese government set up a secret project to find a malaria cure, and Tu Youyou led a team that searched ancient Chinese medical texts. A recipe for sweet wormwood gave her an idea: the instructions said to soak the plant in cold water, not boil it, and she realized that heat might destroy the active ingredient. The compound she extracted, artemisinin, has saved millions of lives. She won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
A self-taught clerk in India who wrote to Cambridge and astonished G. H. Hardy.

Ramanujan was a clerk in Madras, India, who taught himself advanced mathematics from a single textbook. In 1913 he sent a letter with pages of formulas to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, who recognized his genius and brought him to England. Once when Hardy visited him in the hospital, he mentioned that his taxi had a boring number, 1729. Ramanujan replied that it's the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
The Greek who worked out the lever, buoyancy and the area of the circle.

Archimedes of Syracuse was the greatest scientist of the ancient world. He worked out the principle of the lever, found the rule for floating bodies and calculated the area of a circle. In the famous story, he stepped into a bath, realized how to measure the volume of a king's crown by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting "Eureka." He was killed in 212 BCE when the Romans captured his city.
A Greek librarian who measured Earth's size around 240 BCE.

Eratosthenes was the head of the great Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE. He'd heard that at noon on midsummer day, the Sun shone straight down a well at Syene in southern Egypt, while in Alexandria, a stick cast a shadow. From the angle of that shadow and the distance between the two cities, he calculated Earth's circumference. His result was within a few percent of the true value, depending on which unit of length he used.
A mathematician and astronomer who taught in Alexandria.

Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher in Alexandria, Egypt, in the late 4th and early 5th centuries. She taught students from various religions and was widely respected. In 415 she was killed by a mob during a period of political and religious conflict in the city, and her death has been remembered as a symbol of the loss of ancient learning.
A scholar in Cairo who tested theories by experiment in the 11th century.

Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, worked in Cairo around the year 1000. In his Book of Optics, he proved that we see because light enters the eye, and not because rays leave the eye, as many ancient thinkers believed. He tested ideas with experiments, used the camera obscura to study light and insisted that claims should be tested. Some historians call him a founder of the scientific method.
A Baghdad scholar whose name gave us "algorithm" and whose book gave us "algebra."

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad in the early 9th century. His book on solving equations, whose title included the word al-jabr, gave us the word algebra. Another of his books introduced the Hindu-Arabic numerals to the Arab world and, through Latin translations, to Europe. His name, in Latin form, gave us the word algorithm.
A Persian physician whose Canon of Medicine was used in Europe for 600 years.

Ibn Sina, known as Avicenna in Europe, was a Persian physician and philosopher. His Canon of Medicine, completed around 1025, was a huge encyclopedia that described how infectious diseases can spread, recommended quarantine and set out rules for testing drugs. It was translated into Latin and used as a textbook in European universities for about six centuries, into the 1600s.
An Indian astronomer who said the Earth spins.

The Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata wrote a short, dense book in the year 499. In it he stated that the Earth rotates on its axis, and that this causes the apparent daily motion of the stars, a thousand years before Copernicus. He also gave a value for pi, 3.1416, which is very accurate. India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after him.
A painter whose notebooks show he was also an engineer and anatomist.

Leonardo is famous as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, but he filled thousands of pages of notebooks with studies of anatomy, water, flight and machines. About 7,000 pages survive. He drew the valves of the heart and flying machines centuries before others. But he never published his notes, which were scattered after his death, so they had little influence on science at the time.
He corrected 1,400 years of anatomy by dissecting bodies himself.

For about 1,400 years, doctors relied on the writings of the Roman physician Galen, who'd mostly dissected animals. In 1543 the young Flemish anatomist Andreas Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica, based on his own dissections of human bodies, and showed that Galen was wrong in many details. The book had magnificent illustrations, and it transformed the teaching of medicine.
He proved that blood circulates around the body.

In 1628 the English physician William Harvey published a book arguing that blood circulates around the body, pumped by the heart. He had made a simple calculation: the heart pumps out far more blood in an hour than the body could possibly manufacture, so it must be going around in a circle. It contradicted ancient teaching, and many doctors rejected it for years, but he was right.
He coined the word "cell" after looking at cork under a microscope.

In 1665 the English scientist Robert Hooke published Micrographia, a book with spectacular drawings of what he'd seen under his microscope, including a flea and a louse. Looking at a slice of cork, he saw little box-like compartments, which reminded him of monks' cells, and he called them "cells." He was also involved in famous disputes with Isaac Newton over credit for discoveries in optics and gravity.
A cloth merchant who first saw microbes.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant in Delft in the Netherlands who ground his own tiny lenses, some magnifying nearly 270 times, better than any microscope of his time. In the 1670s he looked at pond water, and the plaque on his own teeth, and saw swarms of tiny living things, which he called "animalcules." The Royal Society in London doubted him until Robert Hooke confirmed the observations.
A printer who invented the lightning rod and studied electricity.

Benjamin Franklin was a printer, writer and diplomat, and a serious scientist. He proposed in 1749 that a pointed iron rod could protect buildings from lightning, and the lightning rod was in use by 1752. He also invented bifocal glasses, made one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream and introduced the terms positive and negative for electric charge.

This Greek prefix means "against" or "opposite," and it turns up all over science and daily life. An antibody is a protein your body makes to fight an invader. An antidote works against a poison. Antisocial behavior goes against society, and an antonym is a word whose meaning runs opposite to another's. So when you meet a word that starts with anti-, ask what it's set against.

From the Greek word for "self," auto- shows up whenever something acts by itself or on itself. An automatic machine works on its own. An autobiography is a life written by the person who lived it. Autonomy means governing yourself. An autograph is your own writing of your own name. The word "automobile" is a car, a vehicle that moves by itself, without a horse.

The Latin prefix bi- means "two," and you'll find it in a lot of everyday words. A bicycle has two wheels. A bilingual person speaks two languages. Binary describes something built from two parts, like the zeros and ones in a computer. A biennial event happens every two years. If you spot bi- at the start of a word, there's probably a pair involved.

Tri- means "three," and it comes from both Latin and Greek. A triangle has three angles, and a tricycle has three wheels. A trilogy is a set of three connected stories, like a film series told in three parts. A triplet is one of three babies born together. It's an easy prefix to spot, and the idea of three is nearly always there somewhere.

The Latin prefix uni- means "one." A unicorn is a creature with one horn. A uniform is made of one form, so everyone looks the same. Unity is the state of being one. Even "universe" comes from words meaning "turned into one," and the root of "unique" is the same, meaning there's only one of something.

Mono- is Greek for "one" or "alone." A monologue is a speech by one person. A monotone is a voice that stays on one note. A monopoly is a market with just one seller. A monarchy is rule by one person. When you see mono- at the start of a word, think of something single or solitary, as in a monorail running on a single track.

The Greek prefix poly- means "many." A polygon is a shape with many angles. A polyglot is someone who speaks many languages, from the Greek for "many tongues." Polytheism is belief in many gods. A polymath is a person who has learned many things, like Leonardo da Vinci. It's the opposite of mono-, and it's often a good clue to what a word means.

This Latin prefix also means "many," and it's more common in modern words. To multiply is to make many. A multitude is a great number of people. Multimedia mixes many forms of media, like text, sound and video. Someone who is multilingual speaks several languages. Think of it as the Latin partner of poly-, used in the same way.

Semi- comes from Latin and means "half." A semicircle is half a circle. A semifinal is the round before the final. A semiconductor is a material that conducts electricity partly, somewhere between a conductor and an insulator, and it's the basis of computer chips. A semi, the truck, is short for semitrailer, a trailer that has wheels only at the back and rests its front on the tractor.

Omni- is Latin for "all." An omnivore eats all kinds of food, both plants and animals. Omnipotent means all-powerful, and omnipresent means present everywhere at once. An omnibus, from the same root, means "for all," and it's where we get the word "bus." The root appears whenever a word is about everything or everyone.

The Greek prefix pan- means "all." A panorama is a view of everything, from the Greek for "all" and "sight." A pandemic is a disease that affects all the people, over a wide area. A panacea is a supposed cure for everything. The Pantheon in Rome was a temple to all the gods. So if you see pan- in a word, it probably means "everything" or "everywhere."

Macro- comes from a Greek word meaning "large" or "long," and it's used when you look at the big picture. Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, like national employment and prices. Something macroscopic is big enough to see with the naked eye. A macrocosm is the large world, as opposed to the small one inside it. It pairs naturally with micro-.

The Greek prefix micro- means "small." A microscope lets you see small things. A microbe is a small living thing. A microchip is a tiny piece of electronics, and microeconomics looks at small-scale choices made by individual people and firms. The prefix is also used in measurement, for a millionth. It's the opposite of macro-.

Mega- is from the Greek for "great," and it gets used a lot. A megaphone makes your voice great, or loud. A megabyte is a million bytes of computer memory. A megalith is a great stone, like the ones at Stonehenge. Megalomania is a mania, an obsession, for greatness and power. It's an eye-catching prefix that has become popular in modern names for big things.

The Greek prefix hyper- means "over" or "too much." Someone hyperactive is too active. Hyperbole, meaning exaggeration, comes from a Greek word for "throwing beyond." Hypertension is high blood pressure, and something hypersensitive reacts too strongly. It's a good clue that a word is about going past the usual limit, in speed, size or amount.

Hypo- comes from Greek and means "under" or "below." Hypothermia is when the body temperature drops below normal. A hypodermic needle goes under the skin. The word "hypothesis" means something placed under, a foundation on which an argument is built. A hypocrite is one who plays a part, from the Greek for "an actor," a word that has the same prefix. It's the opposite of hyper-.

The Latin prefix inter- means "between" or "among." To interact is to act between each other. International means between nations. To interrupt is to break in between. An intermission is a break between two parts of a performance. Even the word "internet" is a network between networks. Whenever you see inter-, something is happening in the space between things.

Intra- is Latin for "within" or "inside." An intravenous drip goes into a vein. An intranet is an internal network, available only within an organization, as opposed to the internet. Intramural sports are played within the walls of a school, between its own teams. Intrapersonal means within a single person. It's the opposite of inter-, and the two are easy to mix up.

The Latin prefix extra- means "outside" or "beyond." Something extraordinary goes beyond the ordinary. An extraterrestrial comes from beyond Earth. An extrovert is someone turned outward, who gets energy from other people. Extravagant means wandering beyond the limits, which is how it came to describe spending too much. The prefix often signals going past a boundary.

Ultra- is Latin for "beyond." Ultraviolet light lies beyond violet in the spectrum, at wavelengths too short for our eyes to see. Ultrasound is sound beyond the range of human hearing, and doctors use it for pictures of babies in the womb. Ultramarine means "beyond the sea," because the blue pigment was imported from far across the Mediterranean. It's now used to mean "extremely."

Trans- is Latin for "across" or "through." To transport is to carry across. To translate is to carry a meaning across from one language to another. To transform is to change shape. Something transparent lets light shine through. A transatlantic flight goes across the Atlantic. The prefix is all about crossing from one side to the other, or from one state to another.

The Latin prefix circum- means "around." The circumference is the distance around a circle. To circumnavigate is to sail around something, such as the whole world, as Magellan's expedition did. A circumstance is something that stands around you, the conditions of a situation. To be circumspect is to look around carefully before acting. A circus is a ring, from the same root.

Peri- is Greek for "around." A perimeter is a measure around an area. A periscope lets you look around, or over, obstacles, as on a submarine. A period was originally a path around, a circuit, which is why it can mean a stretch of time. Something peripheral is at the outer edge, around the center. It's the Greek partner of circum-.

The Latin prefix sub- means "under." A submarine travels under the sea, and a subway runs under the street. To subtract is to draw something away from underneath. To submit is to send yourself under another's authority. Sub- often appears as suc-, sup- or sur- before certain letters, as in "suppose" and "suffer." It's one of the most common prefixes in English.

Super- is Latin for "above" or "over." To supervise is to look over someone's work. Something superior is higher in rank or quality. Superhuman goes beyond what a human can do, and the supernatural is above nature. It's the Latin source of "superb" and "supreme," and in everyday speech it's become a general word for "very," as in "super tired."

The Latin prefix pre- means "before." To predict is to say something before it happens. To prevent is to come before an event and stop it. A preview is a look beforehand, and prehistoric describes the time before written records. It's one of the most useful prefixes to know, because it can turn up in front of any word that has a time dimension, like "pre-teen" or "pre-order."

Post- is Latin for "after." To postpone is to put something off until later. A postscript, or P.S., is something written after the main letter. A postmortem is an examination after death, and it's also used for any review done after an event. Postwar means after the war. If pre- tells you something comes earlier, post- tells you it comes later.
Latin for "before," often in time or place.

The Latin prefix ante- means "before," in time or place. An antecedent is something that went before, such as the noun a pronoun refers to. An anteroom is a small room before the main room. Antebellum means "before the war," and in the US, it usually refers to the time before the Civil War. Antediluvian means before the Flood, and is used humorously for anything extremely old. Don't confuse it with anti-.

The Latin prefix re- means "again" or "back." To return is to turn back. To review is to see again. To rebuild is to build again, and to recall is to call back to mind. It's one of the most productive prefixes in English: you can stick it onto almost any verb to say that something is done a second time, from "retry" to "rewrite."

Retro- is Latin for "backward." To think about the past is retrospect, looking back. A retroactive law applies to things that happened before it was passed. Retrograde describes backward motion, like the apparent backward movement of a planet in the sky. To retrofit is to add new equipment to something old. These days "retro" by itself means in the style of the past.

Pro- comes from Latin and Greek, and has several meanings: "forward," "in front of," and "in favor of." Progress is a step forward. To promote is to move something forward. To be proactive is to act ahead of events, instead of waiting. A proponent is someone who speaks in favor of something. Its opposite in the "in favor of" sense is con, as in the old phrase "pros and cons."

This Latin prefix means "with" or "together," and it changes its spelling depending on the next letter. To connect is to join together. A community is a group of people together. To compose is to put things together, and a conference is a gathering that brings people together. When you see con- or com- at the start of a word, it's usually about joining, sharing or doing something collectively.

The Latin prefix contra- means "against." To contradict is to speak against what someone says. Something contrary is opposite. To contrast is to stand things against each other and show their differences. Contraband is goods brought in against the ban, in other words smuggled. It's a cousin of anti-, but it often suggests opposition from the other side rather than a flat rejection.

Dis- is a Latin prefix meaning "apart," "away" or "not." To disagree is to not agree. To disconnect is to unjoin. To disperse is to scatter apart, and to dismiss is to send someone away. It can reverse the meaning of a word, as in "dislike" or "disappear," which makes it easy to coin new words. Its meaning is nearly always some form of separation or negation.

The Latin prefix ex- means "out" or "from." To exit is to go out. To extract is to draw out, like a tooth or a lesson from a story. To exclude is to shut out. To expel is to drive out. The prefix also means "former" when used with a hyphen, as in "ex-president." The core meaning is movement away from the inside.

The Latin prefix de- means "down," "away" or "reversal." To descend is to climb down. To decline is to lean away, and to deform is to undo the form. To depart is to go away. It can also reverse an action, as in "defrost" and "decode." So de- often means that something is being taken off, taken down or undone.

Ab- is Latin for "away from." Something abnormal is away from the norm. To be absent is to be away from a place. To abduct is to lead someone away by force. To abstract is to draw an idea away from the particulars. It becomes "abs-" or "a-" before some letters, as in "abstain" and "avert." The idea is separation, getting away from something.

The Latin prefix ad- means "to" or "toward." To adhere is to stick to something. To advance is to move forward, toward. Adjacent means lying next to. To admire, from the Latin for "to wonder at," is to look at something with wonder. Ad- changes to match the next letter, as in "attract," "assist" and "arrive." It's the opposite of ab-.

Ambi- is Latin for "both." An ambidextrous person is equally skilled with both hands, though the word literally means "right-handed on both sides." To be ambivalent is to have both feelings at once. Something ambiguous leads in both directions, so it has more than one meaning. Ambient means going around, which is how we describe the surrounding light or sound.

The Greek prefix a-, or an- before a vowel, means "without" or "not." An atheist is without belief in a god. Something amoral is without moral sense. Anonymous means without a name. Asymmetry means not symmetrical. It's a handy way of making an opposite, and in medicine, "anemia" literally means "without blood."

Mal- is Latin for "bad" or "badly." A malfunction is a bad function, a failure to work. Malicious means full of ill will. Malnutrition is bad nutrition. Malaria comes from Italian words meaning "bad air," from the old belief that the disease came from foul air in swamps, before it was found to be spread by mosquitoes. It's the opposite of bene-.

Dys- comes from Greek and means "bad," "difficult" or "disordered." Dyslexia is difficulty with reading words. Dysfunction is bad function. A dystopia is a bad place, the opposite of a utopia, a word invented by Thomas More. Dysentery is a painful disease of the intestines. In medicine, many disorders begin with dys-, and it generally signals that something isn't working properly.

This Greek prefix means "together" or "with." Synonyms are words that have the same meaning, literally "same name." To synchronize is to make things happen at the same time. A symphony is a sounding together, an orchestra's piece. Sympathy is feeling together with another person. Before certain letters, syn- turns into sym-, as in "symmetry" and "symbol."

The Greek prefix para- means "beside" or "beyond." Parallel lines run alongside each other. A paragraph was originally a mark written beside the text to show a break. A paramedic works beside, or alongside, the doctor. A parable is a story placed beside a lesson, to illustrate it. It also appears in "paranormal," meaning beyond the normal.

Neo- comes from the Greek for "new." Neonatal means relating to newborn babies. A neologism is a new word, like many that were invented by the internet. Neoclassical describes a revival of the style of ancient Greece and Rome. Even the gas neon takes its name from the same root, since its discoverers called it "the new one" in 1898.

The Latin prefix bene- means "well" or "good," and it appears in a family of positive words. A benefit is a good result, from "well done." Someone benevolent wishes others well. Benign means kind or harmless, and a benediction is a good word, a blessing. It's the opposite of mal-. If you ever feel unsure about the meaning of a word starting with bene-, assume that it's good.

The Latin word aqua means "water." An aquarium is a place for water animals. Something aquatic lives in or near water. An aqueduct is a channel for carrying water, such as the great stone ones the Romans built. An aquifer is a layer of rock that holds underground water. The same root gives us "aquamarine," the color of seawater, which is also the name of a blue gem.

Aud comes from the Latin verb audire, "to hear." An audience is a group who listen. Audio is sound, the thing heard. An auditorium is a place for hearing, a hall. Audible means able to be heard, and an audition is a hearing of a performer. Even "audit" comes from it, since early auditors listened to people read out accounts.

Bio comes from the Greek word for "life." Biology is the study of life. A biography is the writing of a life. An antibiotic is a medicine against bacteria, literally "against life," although it's against only the harmful kind. A biome is a large community of living things, like a desert or rainforest. It's one of the most productive roots in science.

This root comes from the Latin verb capere, "to take" or "seize." To capture is to take hold of. To accept is to take something to yourself. A concept is a thing taken together in the mind, an idea. To intercept is to take something between its sender and receiver. The spellings vary with the word, but the idea of grasping is always in there.

This Latin root means "to go" or "to yield." To proceed is to go forward. To recede is to go back, like a hairline or a tide. Access is a way of going to a place. To concede is to yield, or give way, in an argument. And "ceed" is the spelling in only three common English words: exceed, proceed and succeed.

Chron comes from the Greek word for "time." Chronology is the order of events in time. To synchronize is to make things happen at the same time. A chronic illness is one that lasts a long time. An anachronism is something that doesn't belong in its time, like a clock in a play set in ancient Rome. Chronos was also the Greek personification of time.

This Latin root means "to kill" or "to cut." Homicide is killing a person, and suicide is killing oneself. A pesticide kills pests. An incision is a cut into something, like the one a surgeon makes. Scissors, precise, and decide, which means to cut off other options, are relatives. So is "concise," cut down to the essentials.

Clud comes from the Latin word for "to close" or "to shut." To include is to shut something in. To exclude is to shut it out. A conclusion is a closing, the end of an argument. Claustrophobia, the fear of closed spaces, comes from the same root. A cloister is a closed courtyard, and a clause was originally a closing part of a sentence.

Cogn comes from the Latin cognoscere, "to know." To recognize is to know again. Cognitive means relating to knowing and thinking, as in cognitive science. Incognito means unknown, hiding who you are. To be cognizant is to be aware of something. It's related to the English word "know" itself, through a common ancestor older than Latin.

From the Latin corpus, "body," this root shows up in more words than you might expect. A corporation is a legal body made of many people. A corpse is a dead body. A corps, pronounced "core," is a body of people, like the Peace Corps. To incorporate is to put something into a body. Even "corpulent" comes from it, meaning having a large body.

Cred comes from the Latin credere, "to believe" or "to trust." Credit is trust that you'll pay later. Something credible is believable, and incredible is not believable, though we now use it to mean amazing. A creed is a statement of belief, from the Latin word for "I believe." A credential is something that makes people trust you.

This Greek root means "circle" or "wheel." A cycle is a circle of events that repeats. A bicycle has two wheels. A cyclone is a circling storm. An encyclopedia was originally a "circle of learning," a complete course of education. Even "cycle" in a washing machine follows the idea: a series of steps that returns to the start.

Dem comes from the Greek demos, meaning "the people." Democracy is rule by the people. Demographics are statistics about a population. An epidemic is a disease that comes upon the people, spreading through a community. A demagogue is a leader who appeals to the people's emotions. The ancient Greek city of Athens gave us both the idea and the word.

From the Latin dicere, "to say" or "speak," this root fills our vocabulary of speech. To dictate is to say aloud for someone else to write. To predict is to say before. A verdict is a true saying, the decision of a jury. To contradict is to speak against. A dictionary is a book of sayings, or words. Diction is the way you speak.

This Latin root, from ducere, means "to lead." To produce is to lead forth, to bring something out. To reduce is to lead back, to make smaller. To conduct is to lead with, as in guiding an orchestra or electricity. Education comes from "leading out," drawing out what's in a person. A duke was originally a leader, and a duct is a channel that leads air or water.

Equi comes from the Latin aequus, "equal" or "even." Something equal is the same in measure. An equation says that two things are equal. Equilibrium means equal balance, when forces cancel out. An equinox, in spring and fall, is the time when day and night are equal in length, from "equal night." Equity, meaning fairness, is also related.

From the Latin facere, "to make" or "to do," this root gives us many words about making. A factory is a place of making. To manufacture was originally to make by hand. An effect is something made by a cause. Something perfect is completely made, or finished. A fact was originally a thing done, and facile means easy to do.

This Latin root from ferre means "to carry" or "to bring." To transfer is to carry across. To refer is to carry back, as in referring to a book. A ferry carries people across water. A conifer is a tree that bears cones. Fertile means able to bear fruit, and a "conference" is a bringing together. It's one of those roots that appear in many short words.

Fid comes from the Latin fides, "faith" or "trust." Fidelity is faithfulness, which is why the motto of the US Marine Corps is "Semper Fidelis." To confide is to trust someone with a secret. Being confident is having trust, especially in yourself. A fiancé is a person who has pledged to marry. The common dog name "Fido" is the Latin for "I trust."

This Latin root means "to bend." To reflect is to bend back, as a mirror does with light, or as your mind does with a memory. Something flexible can bend without breaking. An inflection is a bend in the voice, or in a word's ending. To deflect is to bend something away from its course. A flexible schedule is one that can bend as needed.

From the Latin forma, "shape," this root gives us many words. To transform is to change shape. A uniform has one shape, so everyone looks alike. To reform is to give something a new shape, or improve it. A formula was originally a little form, a small pattern or rule. Information is what gives a shape to your thoughts.

Fort comes from the Latin fortis, "strong." To fortify is to make strong, as with a castle wall. Effort is strength put out, the force you apply. Fortitude is inner strength, the courage to endure. To comfort someone is to strengthen them with your presence. A fort is a strong place. Even "force" is closely related.

This Latin root, from frangere, means "to break." Something fragile is easily broken. A fracture is a break, especially in a bone. A fraction is a broken piece of a whole number. To refract is to break back, which is what happens to light when it bends as it moves from air into water. Fragments are broken pieces.

Gen is an old root from Latin and Greek that means "birth," "kind" or "origin." To generate is to give birth to something, to produce it. Genesis is origin, the first book of the Bible, a word that means "beginning." A genre is a kind of art or writing. A gene is a unit of heredity, passed from parent to child.
