It's a very productive root.

Geo comes from the Greek word for "earth." Geography is earth writing, the description of the planet. Geology is the study of the earth, its rocks and history. Geometry was originally earth measure, because it began with measuring land in ancient Egypt. Geothermal energy comes from the earth's heat. It's a good clue that a word concerns the planet.

This Greek root means "to write" or "to draw." An autograph is your own writing of your name. A telegram is writing that goes far, a message sent by wire. A graph is a drawn diagram. A photograph is light writing, and grammar is the art of letters and writing. It's why we use "graphic" for images that are drawn or written.

Grat comes from the Latin gratus, "pleasing" or "thankful." To be grateful is to be full of thanks. Gratitude is thankfulness. Gratis means free of charge, given as a favor. To congratulate is to rejoice together with someone. A gratuity is a tip, a pleasing extra. The Spanish "gracias" and French "grâce" come from the same root.

This Latin root means "step" or "go," from gradus, a step. To progress is to step forward. To graduate is to step up a grade, a level. Something gradual happens step by step, bit by bit. To regress is to step back. A "grade" in school is a step in the ladder, and a "gradient" is a slope you can step up or down.

Hydr comes from the Greek word for "water." To hydrate is to add water to the body. A hydrant is an outlet where water comes out. Hydroelectric power makes electricity from moving water. To dehydrate is to remove water. The element hydrogen is named for it too, because when it burns, it produces water.

This Latin root means "law" or "right." A judge is a person who speaks the law. Justice is rightness, fairness. Injustice is its opposite. Prejudice is a judgment made before knowing the facts. A jury is a group sworn to give a lawful verdict. Words related to law and courts often share this root.

Junct is Latin for "join," from jungere. A junction is a place where things join, like a road meeting another. A conjunction is a word that joins others, such as "and" or "but." An adjunct is something joined to a main thing as an extra. An injunction is, originally, a command that joins someone to an obligation, a court order.

Lab comes from the Latin labor, "work." A laboratory is a place of work, where experiments are done. To elaborate is to work something out in detail. To collaborate is to work together with others. Labor is work itself, especially hard work. A related word, "laborious," means taking much effort, and "belabor" means to work at something too long.

From the Latin liber, "free," this root has to do with freedom. Liberty is the state of being free. To liberate is to set free. Someone liberal was originally generous, free-giving, before the word took on its political meanings. To deliver is to set free, as in delivering someone from danger. The Statue of Liberty is named from it.

This Greek root, from logos, means "word," "reason" or "study." A dialogue is words exchanged between two people. Biology is the study of life. Logic is the art of reason. A prologue is words that come before the main part of a story. "Logos" had deep meanings for the Greeks, including the idea of an order behind things, which is why it appears at the start of the Gospel of John.

This Latin root means "light." Lucid describes something clear and bright, such as a lucid explanation. To illuminate is to throw light on something. Something luminous gives off light. Translucent means letting light through, but not clearly. The name Lucy and the word "Lucifer," meaning light-bringer, come from the same root, as does "lunar," relating to the moon.

Magn comes from the Latin magnus, "great." To magnify is to make something appear greater. Something magnificent is great in deed or appearance. Magnitude is size or greatness, as in the magnitude of an earthquake. Someone magnanimous has a great soul, and is generous. The word "magnum" for a large bottle of wine comes from it, too.

This root comes from the Latin manus, "hand." A manual is done by hand, or a book that you hold in your hand. A manuscript is handwritten. To manufacture was to make by hand. To manipulate is to handle something skillfully, or to handle people. A manicure is hand care, and to "emancipate" is to release from the hand, to set free.

Mar comes from the Latin mare, "sea." Something marine belongs to the sea. A submarine travels under the sea. Maritime means relating to the sea, as in maritime law. A mariner is a sailor. The Spanish word for sea is "mar," and the name of the planet Mars comes from a different root, as does the month March.

From Latin memor, meaning "mindful," this root is about remembering. Memory is the power to remember. A memorial is something that helps people remember, like a statue. A memento is a reminder, a keepsake. To remember is, literally, to bring back to mind. A memorandum is "something to be remembered," a note, and a memoir is a written memory.

This Greek root, from metron, means "measure." A thermometer measures heat. Geometry measures the earth. Symmetry means measured together, with matching parts. A diameter measures across a circle. A kilometer is a thousand measures, a meter. The word "meter" for a unit of length was set up in France in the 1790s.

From the Latin migrare, "to move," this root is about changing places. To migrate is to move from one place or region to another, as birds do. An immigrant moves into a country, and an emigrant moves out of it. Migration is the movement of a group. Both words describe the same journey seen from opposite ends.

This Latin root means "to send." To transmit is to send across, like a radio signal. A mission is a sending, a task someone is sent to do. To dismiss is to send away. To permit is to send through, to allow. A missile is something sent, and an emissary is someone sent out. It's one of the most common roots in English.

Mort comes from the Latin mors, "death." Something mortal is subject to death, and immortal is not. A mortgage is a "dead pledge": the pledge ends, or dies, when the loan is paid off or when the debt is lost. A mortuary is a place for the dead. Even "mortified" means feeling as if you could die of shame.

This Latin root means "to move." To remove is to move away. Motion is moving. Emotion is a moving out, since feelings stir us from calm. To promote is to move forward. A motor is something that moves, and a "motive" is what moves you to act. A movie is a moving picture.

From the Latin nasci, "to be born," this root connects birth and nature. Something native is born in a place. Nature is the way things are born and grow. A nation is people born together in the same land. Prenatal means before birth. Natal means relating to birth, and "innate" means born in you, as in an innate talent.

Nov is the Latin root for "new." A novel was once simply something new, which is why the book form got that name when it was a new kind of story. To innovate is to make something new. To renovate is to make it new again. A novice is a new learner, a beginner. The month November has a different origin, as "ninth month."

This Latin root means "father." Paternal means fatherly. A patriot loves the fatherland, from the Latin for "country of one's fathers." A patron was a protector, like a father, who looked after his dependents. Paternity is fatherhood. Even "pattern" may come from the same root, since a father was a model to copy, though that origin is debated.

Mater is the Latin word for "mother." Maternal means motherly. Matrimony is the state of marriage, from a Latin word that meant the condition of being a mother. A matriarch is a woman who rules a family or tribe. The word "matter" is closely related to it, and so is "material," the stuff things are made from.

This Greek root, from pathos, means "feeling" or "suffering." Sympathy is feeling with someone. Empathy is feeling into someone else's situation. Apathy is a lack of feeling. Pathology is the study of disease. A psychopath is someone with a diseased mind. "Pathetic" originally meant arousing pity, and "pathos" is the quality in a story that makes us feel for the people in it.

Ped comes from the Latin pes, "foot." A pedal is a lever that you push with your foot. A pedestrian is someone who goes on foot. A centipede has, or seems to have, a hundred feet. To expedite is to free the feet, from a Latin word for getting something out of a snare, so that it can be quick. A pedicure is foot care.

Pod comes from the Greek word for "foot," a cousin of the Latin ped. A podium is a place to stand. A tripod is a stand with three feet. An octopus has eight feet, or arms. A podiatrist is a foot doctor. Even "antipodes," the opposite side of the world, means those whose feet are opposite ours.

This Latin root means "to hang" or "to weigh." To suspend is to hang something under. A pendulum is a hanging weight that swings. Expensive means weighed out, because money used to be weighed, and so is "expend." A pension was a payment weighed out regularly. To "depend" is to hang from something else.

Phil comes from the Greek philein, "to love." Philosophy is the love of wisdom. Philanthropy is love of humankind, giving to help others. The city of Philadelphia was named for the Greek for "brotherly love." A bibliophile is a lover of books. A "philharmonic" orchestra is one that loves harmony.

From the Greek phone, "sound" or "voice," this root is about sound. A telephone carries sound far. A symphony is sounds together. Phonics teaches reading by the sounds of letters. A microphone makes small sounds bigger. The word "phonetic" describes spelling that follows pronunciation, and "saxophone" is named for its inventor and its sound.

Photo comes from the Greek phos, "light." A photograph is a drawing or writing with light. Photosynthesis is how plants put together sugar using light. A photon is a particle of light, the smallest unit. A photocopy is a copy made with light. In the 1830s the astronomer John Herschel is credited with first using the word "photography."

This Latin root, from plicare, means "to fold." To apply is to fold something onto something else, to bring it to bear. Something complicated is folded together, tangled. To reply is to fold back an answer. Implicit means folded in, not stated openly. The word "simple" comes from the same root, meaning "one fold," and "duplicate," from "two folds."

Port comes from the Latin portare, "to carry." To transport is to carry across. To import is to carry in, and to export is to carry out. Something portable can be carried easily. A porter carries your bags. The word "support" means to carry from below, and "report" means to carry back news.

From the Greek psyche, "mind," "soul" or "breath," this root is about the mind. Psychology is the study of the mind. A psychiatrist is a healer of the mind, a medical doctor. The psyche is the soul or inner self. Something psychosomatic involves both mind and body. In Greek myth, Psyche was a mortal woman who became the goddess of the soul.

This Latin root means "to ask" or "to seek." A query is a question. A question is a thing asked. To inquire is to ask into something. To request is to ask again and again, or just to ask. A quest is a search, and an inquisition is an investigation. Even "exquisite" comes from it, meaning sought out, and so, choice.

Rupt is Latin for "break," from rumpere. To erupt is to break out, like a volcano. To interrupt is to break between. To be bankrupt is to be broken financially, from Italian words meaning "broken bench." To corrupt is to break together, or ruin. A "rupture" is a break, and "abrupt" means broken off, sudden.

This Latin root means "to write." To describe is to write down what something is like. Scripture is a writing, especially a sacred one. To prescribe is to write before, as a doctor does with medicine. To subscribe is to write under, to sign your name, as to a magazine. A script is writing for actors, and a manuscript is handwritten.

Sect comes from the Latin secare, "to cut." A section is a cut part of something. To dissect is to cut apart, as a biology student does with a frog. An insect is a cut-up creature, named for its body, which looks as if it's cut into segments. To intersect is to cut between, as two roads cross. A "sector" is a cut piece of a circle, too.

This Latin root means "to feel" or "to sense." A sense is a way of feeling the world. A sentiment is a feeling. To consent is to feel together, to agree. To resent is to feel again, a lasting bitterness. Something sensible is full of sense. "Sensation" and "sensitive" belong to the same family.

Spect comes from the Latin specere, "to look." To inspect is to look into. A spectator is someone who looks on. Perspective is looking through, a way of seeing things. To respect is to look back at someone, to regard them with honor. A spectacle is something worth looking at, and "suspect" means to look at from below, with doubt.

From the Latin spirare, "to breathe," this root links breath with spirit. To inspire is to breathe into, to fill with an idea or feeling. Respiration is breathing again and again. To expire is to breathe out, or to breathe one's last. To conspire is to breathe together, to whisper a plot. The word "spirit" itself is "the breath of life."

This Latin root from struere means "to build." A structure is a built thing. To construct is to build together. To instruct is to build up knowledge in someone's mind. To destroy is to unbuild, to take down. An "instrument" is a tool for building, and "industry" is related, as organized work.

Tact comes from the Latin tangere, "to touch." Contact is touching together. Something tactile is related to touch. Something tangible can be touched, so it's real and solid. Something intact has not been touched, and so is whole. And "tact," the skill of handling delicate situations, means a delicate touch.

Techn is from the Greek techne, "art" or "skill." Technique is the way of doing a skill. Technology is the study of skills and craft, and now of machines. A technician is a skilled worker. A polytechnic teaches many skills. For the Greeks, techne covered both craft and art, and that's why the root can sound artistic as well as technical.

Tele is the Greek word for "far" or "at a distance." The telephone carries sound far away. The telescope looks far, and television sees far. Telepathy would be feeling far, a communication of minds. The prefix is useful in new words as technology advances, such as "teleconference" and "telecommute."

This Latin root means "to stretch." To extend is to stretch out. Tension is a stretching, a pulling tight. Something intense is stretched tight, to a high degree. To pretend is to stretch something forward, like a cover. A tent is stretched cloth, and a "tendon" is a cord that stretches from a muscle.

Terr comes from the Latin terra, "earth" or "land." Terrain is the ground, its shape and features. A territory is a piece of land. A terrace is a raised, flat platform of earth. Something terrestrial is of the earth. A terrier is a dog that goes into the earth after burrowing animals, and a "terrarium" is a little land habitat.

This Greek root, from theos, means "god." Theology is the study of god or the divine. An atheist is someone without belief in god. Enthusiasm originally meant to have the god within you, as with a prophet in a trance. Monotheism is belief in one god. A theocracy is a state ruled in the name of god.

Therm is from the Greek therme, "heat." A thermometer measures heat. A thermostat is a device that keeps heat steady. Thermal means relating to heat. Hypothermia is low body heat, a dangerous cold. A thermos bottle keeps drinks hot or cold. The root appears whenever something concerns temperature.

This Latin root, from trahere, means "to pull" or "to drag." To attract is to pull toward. A tractor is a machine that pulls. To subtract is to pull away from underneath. To distract is to pull apart your attention. A "contract" pulls people together, and "traction" is the pulling grip of a tire.

Urb comes from the Latin urbs, "city." Something urban is of the city. A suburb is under, or near, the city. Urbane means polished and refined, as city people were once thought to be. A conurbation is a group of cities that have grown together. "Urban" and "rural" are opposites.

This Latin root, from vacare, means "empty." Something vacant is empty. A vacuum is an empty space, with no air. To evacuate is to empty out a place, such as a building in an emergency. A vacation is a time emptied of work, or school. "Vacate" means to leave a place empty.

Ven comes from the Latin venire, "to come." An event is a coming out, something that happens. To prevent is to come before. An adventure is a thing that is about to come, a chance event. A convention is a coming together of people. "Revenue" is what comes back, and "avenue" is a way of coming to a place.

Ver is Latin for "true," from verus. To verify is to make true, by checking. A verdict is a true saying, the jury's decision. Veracity is truthfulness. To aver is to declare something to be true. Even the word "very," as in "the very truth," comes from it, from an Old French word for true.

This Latin root means "to turn," from vertere. To convert is to turn around, to change. To reverse is to turn back. An introvert is someone turned inward. Something versatile turns easily, from task to task. A "version" is a turning, a different telling, and "adverse" means turned against.

This Latin root means "to see," from videre. Video means "I see." Vision is a seeing, the power of sight. Evident means clearly seen, obvious. To supervise is to see over, to oversee. "Visit" is to go to see someone. The word "television" is a hybrid, Greek tele for far and Latin visio for sight.

Vit and viv come from the Latin vita, "life." Something vital is of life, essential to it. Something vivid is full of life, bright. To survive is to live beyond, to outlive danger. A vitamin was named "vitamine" in 1912, a life amine, because these nutrients are necessary to life. The word "vivacious" describes a lively person.

Voc comes from the Latin vocare, "to call," and vox, "voice." Vocal means of the voice. To invoke is to call upon, as in a prayer or a law. An advocate is one called to help, to speak for someone. A vocation is a calling, the job you feel meant to do. A "vocabulary" is a collection of words you can call on.

This Latin root, from volvere, means "to roll" or "to turn." To revolve is to roll around and back. To evolve is to roll out, to unfold gradually. A revolution is a turning around, a complete change. To involve is to roll into, to wrap up in something. A "volume" was originally a scroll, rolled up.

Zoo comes from the Greek zoon, "animal." Zoology is the study of animals. A zoo is short for "zoological garden," where animals are kept. The zodiac is a circle of animals, the constellations in the sky that have animal names. Protozoa are the first animals, tiny single-celled creatures. It's a handy root for anything about living creatures.

From the Greek anthropos, "human," this root is about people. Anthropology is the study of humans, their cultures and history. Philanthropy, from the Greek for "love of humankind," is giving to help others. A misanthrope is a hater of humankind. Anthropoid means humanlike, as in apes. It's a root that scientists use for the study of our species.

Arch comes from the Greek archos, "ruler," and arche, "first." A monarchy is rule by one. Anarchy is without rule, a lack of government. Archaic means from the first, very old. An architect is a chief builder. An "archbishop" is a chief bishop, and an "archenemy" is the chief enemy.

This Greek root means "star." Astronomy is the law, or study, of the stars. An asterisk is a little star, the symbol *. An astronaut is a star sailor, one who travels in space. A disaster was originally an "ill star," a bad omen, since people thought that a calamity came from an unfavorable position of the stars.

Carn comes from the Latin caro, "flesh." A carnivore is a flesh eater, an animal that eats meat. Carnival is usually traced to words meaning "farewell to meat," the feast before Lent. To incarnate is to make flesh, to give a body to a spirit. Carnage is the slaughter of many people. "Carnation," the flower, may come from a related word for the flesh color.

Cardi is from the Greek kardia, "heart." Cardiac means of the heart. Cardiology is the study of the heart. A cardiogram is a record of the heart's beats, an electrocardiogram. The pericardium is the sac around the heart. In English, "cordial" and "courage" are related words from the Latin cor, which also means heart.

Dent is from the Latin dens, "tooth." A dentist is a doctor for the teeth. A trident is a three-toothed spear, like the one that Poseidon carries. To indent is to cut a notch, like a tooth, into the edge of something, as with a paragraph. Dental means relating to teeth. A "dandelion" is named from French for "lion's tooth," from its jagged leaves.

Derm comes from the Greek derma, "skin." Dermatology is the study of the skin. The epidermis is the upper skin, the outer layer. Hypodermic means under the skin, as with a needle. A pachyderm is a thick-skinned animal, like an elephant or rhinoceros. "Taxidermy" is arranging the skin, preserving animals.

This Greek root, from gaster, means "stomach." Gastric means of the stomach, as in gastric juice. Gastronomy is the art of eating well, literally, "stomach law." Gastritis is stomach inflammation. A gastropod is a stomach-foot, such as a snail, which seems to crawl on its stomach. It's a root for food and digestion.

Hem comes from the Greek haima, "blood." Hemoglobin is the protein in blood that carries oxygen. A hemorrhage is a bursting of blood, heavy bleeding. Hematology is the study of blood. Anemia means without blood, a shortage of red blood cells. It also appears in "hemophilia," the disease in which blood clots poorly.

Neuro is from the Greek neuron, "nerve." A neuron is a nerve cell. Neurology is the study of the nervous system. A neurosis was once thought to be a nerve disorder. A neurotransmitter is a chemical that carries messages between nerve cells. The Greeks used the word for "sinew" and "cord," before it came to mean nerve.

This Greek root, from ops, means "eye" or "sight." Optic means of the eye or sight. An optician makes eyeglasses. Myopia is short sight, or nearsightedness. An optometrist is an eye measurer, who tests your sight. The word "optics" is the science of light and vision, and "synopsis" is a seeing together, a summary.

Oste is from the Greek osteon, "bone." Osteoporosis is a condition of porous, weakened bones. An osteopath is a bone healer, a kind of doctor. Osteology is the study of bones. The periosteum is the membrane that surrounds a bone. "Ostracize" is a different root, from the Greek for "shell," though it sounds alike.

Somn comes from the Latin somnus, "sleep." Insomnia is no sleep, difficulty in sleeping. A somnambulist is a sleepwalker. Somnolent means sleepy, drowsy. Somniloquy is talking in your sleep. The Roman god of sleep was Somnus, and his Greek counterpart was Hypnos, who gave us "hypnosis."

Vor is Latin for "to eat" or "to devour," from vorare. A carnivore eats flesh. A herbivore eats plants. Voracious means eating greedily, with great appetite. To devour is to eat up, to consume quickly. A "locavore" is a recent coinage for someone who eats local food.

This Greek ending means "fear." Claustrophobia is the fear of closed spaces. Xenophobia is the fear of strangers or foreigners. Acrophobia is the fear of heights. Phobos was the Greek god of fear, and a phobia is an intense, irrational fear. There are hundreds of named phobias, and new ones are often invented for fun.

This Greek ending, from kratos, means "rule" or "power." Democracy is rule by the people. Aristocracy is rule by the best, the nobles. Bureaucracy is rule by desks, or offices, from the French word for a desk. A theocracy is rule by god, or by religious leaders. It's a handy ending that you can recognize in the names of governments.

This Greek ending, from ektome, means "cutting out." An appendectomy is the surgical removal of the appendix. A tonsillectomy removes the tonsils. A mastectomy removes the breast, often because of cancer. A vasectomy cuts part of the tube that carries sperm. It always signals an operation to take something out, and so it's a useful clue in medical terms.

This Greek ending means "inflammation." Arthritis is inflammation of the joints. Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils. Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways, the bronchial tubes. Dermatitis is inflammation of the skin. It's become a joke ending as well, as in "senioritis," a student's lack of motivation near graduation.

This Greek ending, from skopein, means "to look at" or "to see." A microscope is for seeing small things. A telescope is for seeing far. A periscope looks around. A stethoscope is for looking at the chest, from the Greek for "chest." Many instruments for viewing end in -scope, from the kaleidoscope to the horoscope, which is literally "a look at the hour."

This Greek ending means "the study of," from logos, "word" or "reason." Biology is the study of life. Geology is the study of the earth. Psychology is the study of the mind, and anthropology of humankind. It's the most common ending for names of sciences, and it often appears joined to a Greek root that tells you the subject.

The English ending -less means "without." To be careless is to be without care. A homeless person is without a home. Something endless goes on without end. To be fearless is to be without fear. Unlike many suffixes, this one is not from Latin or Greek. It comes from Old English, and is related to the word "loose," meaning free of something.

This ending, from Latin, means "full of" or "having." Something famous is full of fame. Dangerous means full of danger. Joyous is full of joy. Glorious is full of glory. It turns nouns into adjectives, and it's a very common ending in English, often with a slight spelling change, as in "adventurous" or "ambitious."

This Latin ending, from facere, means "to make." To purify is to make pure. To simplify is to make simple. To magnify is to make great, or larger. To clarify is to make clear. It's a helpful ending for turning an adjective or a noun into a verb, as in "beautify," "solidify" and "justify."

This Greek ending, from -izein, means "to make" or "to become." To modernize is to make modern. To realize is to make real, to understand. To criticize is to act as a critic. To apologize is to give an apology. In the US it's the standard ending, while some other countries spell it -ise.

The word means "ill star." It comes from Italian disastro, built from dis- meaning bad, and astro meaning star. It's from astrology: people used to believe that a calamity was caused by an unfavorable position of the stars and planets. Today we use the word for any sudden catastrophe, with no thought of the sky.
It once meant being possessed by a god.

Today it just means eagerness, but the word began as something religious. It comes from the Greek en theos, "having the god within." In ancient Greece, it described a prophet or priestess who was possessed by a god and speaking his words. By the 1700s the word had broadened to mean any passionate fervor, and then, gradually, a cheerful interest.

The word means "dead pledge." It comes from Old French mort, meaning dead, and gage, meaning pledge. The idea is that the pledge of property "dies" in one of two ways: either when the loan is paid off, so the pledge is no longer needed, or when the borrower fails to pay and the property is lost.

The word means "forty days." It comes from the Italian quaranta giorni. In the era of the Black Death, port cities like Venice and Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, made ships wait offshore for a period, first 30 days and then 40, to see whether plague appeared among the crew before they were allowed to land.

The word means "little mouse." It comes from the Latin musculus, a diminutive of mus, "mouse." The Romans thought that a flexed muscle, like a bicep, moving under the skin, looked like a mouse running under a cloth. So the name stuck, and has been passed down into English through French.

It means "wind eye." The word comes from Old Norse vindauga, from vindr, "wind," and auga, "eye." Before glass was common, a window was just a hole in the wall that let in air and light, and that you could look through. English took the word from the Vikings, replacing the older "eyethirl," or "eye-hole."

When it first entered English, in the 1300s, "nice" meant "foolish" or "ignorant." It comes from the Latin nescius, "not knowing," through Old French. Over the next 600 years, the meaning drifted: to "fussy," then "precise" or "delicate," as in "a nice distinction," and finally, in the 1700s, to "agreeable" and "kind."
It once meant to kill one in ten.

In ancient Rome, if an army unit had mutinied, its commander could order that every tenth soldier, chosen by lot, be killed as punishment. That's decimation, from the Latin decem, ten. The modern sense, to destroy a large part of something, came later, and some people still insist that the word should be used only for one in ten.
It means "one with whom you share bread."

The word means "one with whom you share bread." It comes from the Latin com, "with," and panis, "bread." The same root gives us "pantry," the room where bread is kept, and the French word "copain," for pal. A companion, in the old sense, was someone you ate with, which says a lot about friendship.

The word comes from the Latin trivialis, "of the crossroads," from tri, "three," and via, "road." The idea is of a place where three roads meet, where people exchanged common talk and gossip. What was said there was ordinary, so the word came to mean unimportant. The same root gave medieval schools their "trivium," the three basic subjects.
It comes from the Greek for "to tear flesh."

The word comes from the Greek sarkazein, which means "to tear flesh," as dogs do, and later "to speak bitterly." It entered English in the 1500s. The image is of a remark meant to cut, to wound with biting irony. It's a fitting name for a type of humor that says the opposite of what it means, in order to sting.

This word was made up in 1688 by a Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer. He put together the Greek nostos, "return home," and algos, "pain," to describe the severe homesickness that he saw among Swiss soldiers fighting abroad. For about 200 years, doctors treated nostalgia as a real disease, with symptoms like fever and loss of appetite, before it became a gentle word for wistfulness.
From the Czech word for forced labor.

The word comes from the Czech robota, which means forced labor or drudgery. It was first used in the 1920 play R.U.R., "Rossum's Universal Robots," by the Czech writer Karel Čapek, in which artificial workers rebel against humans. Čapek said that he got the word from his brother, the painter Josef, who suggested it when Karel was stuck for a name.

The writer Horace Walpole made up this word in a letter in 1754. He took it from a Persian fairy tale, "The Three Princes of Serendip," whose heroes were always making happy discoveries of things they weren't looking for. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka. The word has become useful to scientists, since many discoveries, like penicillin, were happy accidents.
It comes from a man's name.

Unlike most words, this one comes from a real man's name. Charles Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo, Ireland, in 1880, who refused tenants' demands for lower rents. In response, tenants, shopkeepers and even the postman refused to deal with him. The newspapers described it as "boycotting," and within a year the word was used across Europe and America.

The word means "clothed in white." It comes from the Latin candidatus, from candidus, "bright white." In ancient Rome, people who ran for public office wore specially whitened togas, to look pure and honest, and to stand out in a crowd. So anyone seeking office became known as a candidatus, and we still call them candidates.
It comes from a pottery shard.

The word comes from a piece of pottery. In ancient Athens, citizens could vote to send away a person who was seen as a threat to the city, for ten years, by scratching his name on an ostrakon, a broken piece of pottery, used like a ballot. Archaeologists have found thousands of these shards. To ostracize is now to exclude someone from a group.
It comes from the god Pan.

The word comes from the Greek god Pan, the goat-legged god of shepherds and wild places. The Greeks believed that sudden, unexplained terror, especially when alone in the hills, was caused by Pan, who could cry out and frighten flocks. So the fear was called panikon, "of Pan," and it became our word for sudden fright.

The word means "to count with pebbles." It comes from the Latin calculus, which means a small stone, used for counting on an abacus-like board. The same word gives us "calculus," the branch of mathematics. In the medical world, a calculus is also a small stone, such as a kidney stone. All come from pebbles.

The word means "day's eye." It comes from the Old English dægesege, which is "day" plus "eye." The name fits the flower, which opens its petals in the morning, when the Sun comes up, and closes them at night, like an eye opening and closing. It's a rare word that has changed little in a thousand years.

The word means "broken bench." It comes from the Italian banca rotta. In Renaissance Italy, money changers did business at benches in the marketplace, and, according to the traditional story, if a banker failed and couldn't pay what he owed, his bench was broken, publicly, so that everyone would know. That's the origin of the word "bank," too.
It comes from a ball of thread.

The word began as a ball of thread. The old spelling was "clew," and it meant a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, the hero Theseus used one to find his way out of the Minotaur's labyrinth: he unrolled it behind him on the way in and followed it back. Following a clew gradually became following a clue, a trail that leads you to the answer.
It comes from the French for "cover the fire."

The word comes from the French couvre-feu, which means "cover the fire." In medieval towns, most buildings were wooden and had open fires, so a bell was rung each evening to tell people to cover their fires and go to bed, to prevent fires from burning down the whole town. The word later came to mean any rule about when you have to be home.

The word comes from Arabic. It's from al-kuḥl, which originally meant a very fine powder of antimony, used as eye makeup. Later the Arabic term was applied to anything refined to its essence by a process like distillation, and when it passed into Latin and European languages, it came to mean the spirit that is distilled from wine.
Two English words from one Arabic word.

Two English words come from the same Arabic one. Arabic sifr means "empty," and it was a translation of the Sanskrit shunya, the Indian word for the zero. "Cipher" came into English first, in the 1300s, and it came to mean both zero and, later, secret code. "Zero" arrived through Italian in the 1600s.
It was invented by the poet John Milton.

The poet John Milton made up this word for his epic Paradise Lost, published in 1667. In it, Pandæmonium is the capital of Hell, a great palace built by the fallen angels. He formed it from the Greek pan, "all," and daimon, "demon." It later came to mean any wild, noisy confusion, a place where all the demons are loose.
It comes from a Greek myth.

In Greek myth, King Tantalus offended the gods, and as his punishment, he stood in the underworld in water up to his chin, beneath branches of fruit. Whenever he bent to drink, the water drained away, and whenever he reached for the fruit, the wind blew it out of reach. To tantalize is to tease someone with something that they can see but not have.
It was the name of a person in the Odyssey.

In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor was an old friend of Odysseus, who was left in charge of Odysseus's household and who advised his young son, Telemachus, when the king was away. The goddess Athena sometimes took Mentor's form to guide the boy. His name has become a word for any wise and trusted adviser.

The word comes from the Greek myth of Narcissus, a beautiful young man who fell in love with his own reflection in a pool. In the Roman poet Ovid's version, he couldn't tear himself away, and wasted away, and was turned into a flower. Sigmund Freud and later psychologists used the name for an excessive love of oneself.
Writing began in Sumer, in what is now Iraq, around 3400 to 3200 BCE.

Writing began in Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq, around 3400 to 3200 BCE. It seems to have started out as a bookkeeping tool, with little clay tokens and marks pressed into clay to keep track of grain, sheep and beer. Over the centuries, the marks became wedge-shaped signs, called cuneiform, that could stand for sounds. Then people could write names, laws, letters and stories, and the oldest known literature was born.
The earliest known wheels turned pots, then carts, about 5,500 years ago.

The first wheels weren't for carts. They turned the potter's wheel, and wheeled vehicles appear a little later, around 3500 BCE. A wheel and axle found in the Ljubljana marshes in Slovenia has been dated to about 3150 BCE, among the oldest known. It seems odd that the wheel came well after boats and plows, but it's actually hard: the axle and the hole have to fit very closely, and that takes skilled work.
People began planting crops about 11,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent.

About 11,000 years ago, in a region of the Middle East called the Fertile Crescent, people began to plant seeds on purpose. Wheat, barley, lentils and peas were among the first crops. Farming let people stay in one place, store food and support larger numbers, and that led to villages, then cities, kings, and writing. It also brought new problems, such as crowded living and disease.
A temple of carved stone pillars, built about 11,500 years ago, before farming.

In 1994 the German archaeologist Klaus Schmidt began to dig on a hilltop in southeastern Turkey, and found huge T-shaped stone pillars carved with animals, arranged in circles. It was built about 11,500 years ago, before farming, and before pottery. It overturned the idea that people first settled down in towns and only then built monuments. Perhaps the need to gather for such a place helped to start settled life.
Built around 2560 BCE for King Khufu, it was the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years.

The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE as the tomb of the Egyptian king Khufu. It stood about 146 meters high, and it was the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England surpassed it in the 1300s. The workers weren't slaves, as people used to think. Archaeologists found their town nearby, with bakeries and graves, which shows they were paid and fed.
A Babylonian king set out 282 laws on a stone pillar around 1754 BCE.

Around 1754 BCE the king of Babylon, Hammurabi, had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar, so that everyone could see them. It covered trade, property, family and crime. Punishments depended on the social rank of the victim and the offender, and many were based on "an eye for an eye." It's one of the oldest long written law codes, and it reflects the idea that the king's role is to ensure justice.
Most of the world's alphabets descend from one invented about 3,800 years ago.

Most of the world's alphabets descend from a single invention. Around 1800 BCE, workers from Canaan in Egypt's Sinai turquoise mines adapted a few Egyptian hieroglyphs into a simple script, with a sign for each sound. The Phoenicians spread it around the Mediterranean, the Greeks added vowels, and the Romans passed their version on to us. A system of about two dozen signs was far easier to learn than hundreds.
A slab with the same decree in three scripts unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs.

For 1,400 years, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. In 1799 French soldiers digging near the town of Rashid, or Rosetta, found a stone slab carved with the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script and ancient Greek. It dates from 196 BCE. Using the Greek as a key, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he could read hieroglyphs.
The ancient Games began in 776 BCE, by tradition, in Olympia, Greece.

By tradition, the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE at Olympia in Greece, in honor of Zeus. They took place every four years, and included foot races, wrestling, boxing and chariot races. A sacred truce was declared so that athletes could travel safely, even when cities were at war. Only free Greek men were allowed to compete, and the Games continued for more than a thousand years.
In 508 BCE Cleisthenes gave Athenian citizens a vote in an assembly.

In 508 BCE the Athenian leader Cleisthenes reformed the government, giving citizens a vote in an assembly that made the laws. Any citizen could speak and vote. But citizens were only free adult men born in Athens, perhaps a fifth of the population. Women, slaves and foreigners were left out. It was a limited democracy, but it introduced the idea that ordinary people should decide.
The Athenians beat a larger Persian army at Marathon in 490 BCE.

In 490 BCE the Athenians defeated a much larger Persian army at the plain of Marathon, one of the most famous battles in history. The popular story that a runner raced 26 miles to Athens with the news, shouting "Victory!" and then dropped dead, is a much later legend. What's better documented is that a runner named Pheidippides ran about 150 miles to Sparta to ask for help. The modern marathon race comes from the legend.
He built an empire from Greece to India by age 32.

Alexander became king of Macedon at the age of 20, in 336 BCE, after his father was murdered. In just over a decade he conquered the Persian Empire, defeating King Darius, and led his army as far as the Indus River in India by 326 BCE. His soldiers refused to go further. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, at 32, and his generals divided up the empire. It spread Greek culture across much of Asia.
Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BCE.

In 221 BCE King Zheng of Qin finished conquering the other states of China and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor. He standardized writing, weights and measures, and even the width of cart axles. His tomb is guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers, the Terracotta Army, which was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well.
The Great Wall of China cannot be seen from the Moon.

One of the most popular facts is that the Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon, and it's not true. Astronauts say it's barely visible, if at all, even from low Earth orbit, because it's narrow and is similar in color to the land around it. The claim appeared in print in the 1930s, decades before anyone went into space.
Rome threw out its last king in 509 BCE and was governed by elected officials.

According to tradition, the Romans overthrew their last king in 509 BCE and set up a republic, in which leaders were elected. Two consuls shared power for a year, and the Senate advised them. The Republic lasted nearly 500 years, as Rome grew from a city into the ruler of the Mediterranean. Then a series of civil wars gave power to one man, Augustus, in 27 BCE.
Julius Caesar was killed by senators on March 15, 44 BCE.

On March 15, 44 BCE, the Ides of March in the Roman calendar, Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in the Senate by a group of about 60 senators. They hoped to save the Republic from a man who'd had himself made dictator for life. But the killing led to another civil war, and within 17 years to the rule of Caesar's adopted heir, Augustus, as the first emperor.
About 200 years of relative peace within the Roman Empire.

The "Roman Peace" was a period of about 200 years, from Augustus in 27 BCE to the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, when the Roman Empire was relatively stable. Trade and travel flourished, with good roads and shipping across the Mediterranean. The peace was kept by large armies on the borders, and the people conquered by Rome didn't always feel peaceful. But it was a time of prosperity.
A network of trade routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome.

The Silk Road wasn't one road but a network of trade routes linking China, India, Persia and Rome. The Han emperor sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, west around 138 BCE to find allies, and that opened up the routes. Silk, paper, spices and ideas traveled along them, as did religions. So did diseases. Most traders only carried goods part of the way, passing them to others.
It did not burn down in one fire.

The popular story is that the great Library of Alexandria in Egypt was destroyed in a single great fire. In fact, it declined over centuries. Funding was cut, scholars were driven out in political purges, and a number of fires damaged parts of it, including one set by Julius Caesar's troops in 48 BCE that burned some storage warehouses. Historians reject the idea of one dramatic loss.
China had paper by the 2nd century CE, and it took 1,000 years to reach Europe.

The Chinese had paper by the 2nd century CE, and it was a thousand years before Europe took it up. The court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with inventing it around 105 CE, but archaeologists have found older fragments. Arab papermakers learned the craft after 751, at the Battle of Talas, according to tradition, and it reached Europe in the 1100s, through Spain. Paper made printing and widespread literacy affordable.
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE and buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.

In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. A young man named Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and described the towering cloud in two letters to the historian Tacitus. The ash preserved homes, shops, loaves of bread, paintings and graffiti so well that we can read about daily life in a Roman town.
In 325 CE, bishops gathered in Nicaea to settle a dispute about the nature of Christ.

In 325 CE the Roman emperor Constantine called bishops from across the empire to Nicaea, in what's now Turkey, to settle a dispute over the nature of Christ: whether the Son was created or eternal. The council produced an early form of the Nicene Creed, which affirms that the Son is of one substance with the Father. A revised version is still recited in many churches today.
The last Western Roman emperor was deposed in 476.

In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer removed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus, and didn't bother to replace him. That date is traditionally given as the end of the Western Roman Empire. Historians now see it as a slow change over about a century, not a sudden collapse, as barbarian kingdoms took over provinces. The Eastern Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople, continued until 1453.
The great church in Constantinople was built in only five years.

The great church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, now Istanbul, was built in only five years, from 532 to 537, for the emperor Justinian. Its enormous dome, about 55 meters high, seems to float on a ring of windows. For almost a thousand years it was one of the largest enclosed spaces in the world. It was later a mosque, then a museum, and in 2020 became a mosque again.
The year 622 is year 1 of the Islamic calendar.

The Islamic calendar counts years from 622 CE, the year of the Hijra, when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina after persecution. The calendar is lunar, with twelve months of 29 or 30 days, so the year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year. This means the Islamic months, like Ramadan, move through the seasons.
A center of scholarship in Baghdad in the 800s and 900s.

In ninth-century Baghdad, the caliphs supported a center of scholarship known as the House of Wisdom. Scholars there translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and added their own discoveries in mathematics, astronomy and medicine. Al-Khwarizmi, who gave us the word algebra, worked there. Many ancient texts, including some by Aristotle and Galen, survived because they were translated.
The Frankish king was crowned Emperor in Rome on Christmas Day, 800.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as Emperor in Rome. He ruled much of western Europe, and promoted education, setting up schools in monasteries. His scribes also developed a clear and legible handwriting style, Carolingian minuscule, which later became the model for our lowercase letters.
Norse explorers reached Newfoundland around the year 1000.

About 500 years before Columbus, Norse explorers reached North America. At L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, archaeologists found the remains of buildings, and wood that had been cut with metal tools, which the locals didn't have. In 2021 scientists used a solar storm recorded in tree rings to date the cutting precisely, to the year 1021. It's the earliest known European presence in the Americas.
William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings on October 14, 1066.

On October 14, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English King Harold at the Battle of Hastings. Harold was killed, perhaps by an arrow in the eye, as the Bayeux Tapestry seems to show, though that's debated. French became the language of England's rulers for around 300 years, and English absorbed thousands of French words, which is why we have both "cow" and "beef."
In 1215 English barons forced King John to accept limits on his power.

In 1215 a group of English barons forced King John to put his seal to a charter limiting his power. It promised, among other things, that no free man could be punished except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land. Most clauses later became obsolete. But the idea that even a king is under the law influenced many later constitutions, including the American one.
He founded the Mongol Empire in 1206, the largest connected land empire in history.

Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and in 1206 took the title Genghis Khan, "universal ruler." He and his successors built the largest connected land empire in history. Under his grandsons, it stretched from Korea to Hungary. It also protected trade along the Silk Road and spread ideas and technologies, though it was founded on terrible violence, and may have helped to spread the plague.
The ruler of Mali whose pilgrimage in 1324 made gold cheaper in Cairo.

Mansa Musa ruled the West African empire of Mali in the early 1300s, and was famously wealthy. In 1324 he traveled to Mecca with thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold. He gave away so much in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. Back in Mali, the city of Timbuktu became a renowned center of learning, with libraries and a university.
A plague that killed perhaps a third or more of Europe between 1347 and 1351.

The plague that swept through Europe between 1347 and 1351 killed perhaps a third or more of the population. It came along trade routes from Asia, spread by fleas on rats, and by people. With so many dead, workers were scarce, wages rose and the old feudal order, in which peasants were tied to the land, weakened. It took Europe about two centuries to recover its population.
Johannes Gutenberg's movable type, around 1450, made books cheap.

Around 1450 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed a way to print with movable metal type. Before that, books had to be copied by hand, and a Bible might take a scribe months. His famous Bible appeared around 1455. By 1500, more than 20 million books had been printed in Europe. Books became cheap, and ideas, from science to religion, could spread quickly.
The Ottoman Turks took the capital of the Byzantine Empire on May 29, 1453.

On May 29, 1453, the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, after a siege of 53 days. His army used huge cannons to batter the ancient walls. The city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul. Greek scholars who fled west carried manuscripts with them, which helped to feed the Italian Renaissance.
In 1492 Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Caribbean.

In 1492 the Italian navigator Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, crossed the Atlantic and landed in the Caribbean. He believed he'd reached the edge of Asia. Millions of people already lived in the Americas, and his arrival began lasting contact between the hemispheres, which brought exchanges of crops and ideas, but also disease, conquest and enslavement for many Indigenous peoples.
The first trip around the world, 1519 to 1522.

In 1519 five ships under Ferdinand Magellan left Spain to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. Magellan was killed in a battle in the Philippines in 1521. Only one ship, the Victoria, under Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the journey around the world in 1522, with 18 men of the original crew of about 270. It proved that the world could be circumnavigated.
After 1492, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic and changed both sides.

After 1492, plants, animals and diseases crossed the Atlantic in both directions, and changed both sides of the ocean. Potatoes, tomatoes, maize and chocolate went to the Old World, and horses, wheat and smallpox went to the New. The historian Alfred Crosby named the process in 1972. Many of the foods that we think of as typical of European countries, like Italian tomatoes, came from the Americas.
Hernán Cortés and his allies captured Tenochtitlan in 1521.

In 1521 Hernán Cortés and his forces captured Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, now Mexico City. The Spaniards didn't do it alone. Thousands of Indigenous allies, who resented Aztec rule, fought with them, and smallpox, which the Europeans had brought, killed a huge part of the city's people. The conquest had many causes, not just Spanish weapons and horses.
In 1517 Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences.

In 1517 Martin Luther, a German monk and professor, wrote a list of 95 arguments against the sale of indulgences, which were pardons that people bought to reduce punishment for sin. According to tradition, he posted them on the church door at Wittenberg. The printing press carried his ideas across Germany within weeks. The Reformation that followed split Western Christianity, and Luther later translated the Bible into German.
An English translation completed in 1611 that shaped the language.

The King James Version of the Bible was completed in 1611 by about 47 scholars, working from Hebrew and Greek texts. It built heavily on the earlier English translation by William Tyndale, who was executed in 1536. Its rhythmic language shaped English literature and speech, giving us phrases like "the powers that be" and "the skin of my teeth."
The Inca citadel in Peru was built around 1450 and abandoned about a century later.

The Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, high in the Andes of Peru, was probably built around 1450 as an estate for the emperor Pachacuti. It was abandoned about a century later, around the time of the Spanish conquest, and the Spaniards apparently never found it. In 1911 the American explorer Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention, although local farmers had known about it all along.
The treaties of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War and set up the idea of sovereign states.

The treaties signed in 1648 in the German region of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War, one of the most destructive wars in European history, which killed perhaps a quarter of the people in the German lands. The agreements said that each ruler would control his own territory, without outside interference, an idea that's often seen as the beginning of the modern system of sovereign states.
The 1666 fire destroyed about 13,000 homes, but only six deaths were officially recorded.

In September 1666 a fire that began in a baker's shop in Pudding Lane burned for four days and destroyed about 13,000 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral. Only six deaths were officially recorded, though the true number may have been higher, since the poor weren't always counted. The disaster led to new building rules, and to the first fire insurance companies.
Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau asked why we obey governments.

Why should we obey a government? Three philosophers gave different answers. In 1651 Thomas Hobbes argued that people give up some of their freedom in return for safety. In 1689 John Locke said that government exists to protect people's rights, and can be replaced if it fails to. In 1762 Jean-Jacques Rousseau said that legitimate government must express the general will of the people.
He argued in 1748 that power should be divided among separate branches.

In 1748 the French thinker Montesquieu published The Spirit of the Laws, in which he argued that liberty is safest when government power is divided among separate branches, so that each can check the others. His idea strongly influenced the framers of the US Constitution, who divided the government into executive, legislative and judicial branches.
Immanuel Kant wrote in 1784: "Dare to know."

In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question in a short essay. He said that enlightenment is people's emergence from their self-imposed immaturity, which he defined as the inability to use one's own understanding without someone else's guidance. His motto was "Sapere aude," or "Dare to know," a phrase that he took from the Roman poet Horace.
Adopted on July 4, 1776, it said "all men are created equal."

On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, which stated that "all men are created equal." Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the text, and Congress edited it. At the time, the words didn't extend to enslaved people or to women. Later movements, from abolitionists to suffragists to civil rights leaders, used them to demand that the promise be kept.
Written in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787.

In the summer of 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia, in secret, to write a new framework of government for the United States. They debated for about four months, and the final document is only about 4,500 words long. It has been amended 27 times, with the first ten amendments, known as the Bill of Rights, added in 1791. It's the oldest written national constitution still in use.
In 1789 the Bastille fell and the Declaration of the Rights of Man was adopted.

On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a royal prison and a symbol of tyranny, and the French Revolution began. Later that summer, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen set out ideas of equality and liberty. The revolution overthrew the monarchy and later descended into the Terror, and then the rule of Napoleon. It spread ideas of equal citizenship and national sovereignty across Europe.
Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue overthrew French rule and founded Haiti in 1804.

In 1791 enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up, in what became the only successful slave revolt in history. Led first by Toussaint Louverture, and after his capture in 1802 by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, they defeated French, Spanish and British forces. Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, becoming the first Black-led republic and the second independent nation in the Americas.
Napoleon was defeated on June 18, 1815 in present-day Belgium.

On June 18, 1815, near the village of Waterloo in what is now Belgium, Napoleon's army was defeated by British and allied forces under the Duke of Wellington and by Prussian forces under Marshal Blücher. It ended 23 years of nearly constant war in Europe. Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of St. Helena, in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
James Watt's 1769 improvements made steam practical for factories.

Steam engines existed before James Watt, but they wasted most of their heat. In 1769 Watt, a Scottish instrument maker, patented a design with a separate condenser, which made the engine far more efficient. With the help of his business partner Matthew Boulton, steam power spread to mills, mines and later to railways and ships, and powered the Industrial Revolution.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825.

The Stockton and Darlington Railway in northern England opened in 1825, using George Stephenson's steam locomotive to haul coal and passengers. Within a few decades, railways spread across the world. By 1850 Britain had about 6,000 miles of track. Trains made it necessary to standardize time, since each town had previously kept its own local time.
Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its empire in 1833.

In 1807 Britain banned its involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, and in 1833 it abolished slavery throughout its empire. The United States abolished it with the 13th Amendment in 1865. Campaigners like William Wilberforce, Olaudah Equiano and Thomas Clarkson used pamphlets, petitions and a boycott of slave-grown sugar to turn public opinion, and the enslaved people themselves resisted constantly.
John Stuart Mill argued in 1859 that society may limit your freedom only to stop you harming others.

In his 1859 book On Liberty, the English philosopher John Stuart Mill argued that society may justly limit a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others. A person's own good, he said, isn't enough reason to force them. He defended free speech even for opinions that are wrong, because a false idea may contain some truth, and because truth that's never challenged becomes a dead dogma.
Mary Wollstonecraft argued in 1792 that women should have the same education as men.

In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, in which she argued that women appear to be less rational than men only because they're denied an education. She called for girls and boys to be taught the same things. It was widely criticized at the time, and later became one of the founding texts of feminism.
The first message, "What hath God wrought," was sent in 1844.

On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message from the Capitol in Washington to Baltimore, 40 miles away: "What hath God wrought." Until then, news could travel only as fast as a horse, a train or a ship. The telegraph made communication almost instantaneous. By 1866, a cable laid under the Atlantic connected America and Europe.
The telephone and the light bulb
Bell's patent was granted in 1876, and Edison's practical bulb in 1879.

Alexander Graham Bell was granted a patent for the telephone in 1876, on the same day that another inventor, Elisha Gray, filed a notice for a similar device. In 1879 Thomas Edison perfected a practical electric light bulb with a long-lasting filament, and the British inventor Joseph Swan had made a working bulb at about the same time. Inventions often arrive in more than one place at once.
A Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, inspired it after seeing a battlefield in 1859.

In 1859 a Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, happened to be near the battlefield of Solferino in Italy, and was horrified by the thousands of wounded left without help. He wrote a book about it, and in 1863 helped to found the Red Cross. The first Geneva Convention in 1864 agreed that the wounded and those who care for them should be protected in war.
New Zealand was the first country to give women the vote, in 1893.

In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections. Others followed slowly. In the United States, the 19th Amendment gave women the vote in 1920, and in France, women could not vote until 1944. Suffragists campaigned with petitions, marches and, sometimes, hunger strikes in prison.
On December 17, 1903, the first powered flight lasted 12 seconds.

On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright made the first powered, controlled flight in a heavier-than-air machine. It lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Later that day, Wilbur flew 852 feet in 59 seconds. Just 66 years afterward, humans walked on the Moon. The brothers were bicycle makers from Ohio.
The "unsinkable" liner struck an iceberg on April 14, 1912.

The luxury liner Titanic, widely described as unsinkable, hit an iceberg on the night of April 14, 1912, on its first voyage, and sank in under three hours. About 1,500 of the 2,200 people aboard died, partly because there were lifeboats for only about half of them. After the disaster, new rules required ships to carry enough lifeboats for everyone and to keep radios staffed around the clock.
The war of 1914 to 1918 killed about 20 million people.

The Great War lasted from 1914 to 1918 and killed about 20 million people, soldiers and civilians. It began after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, and drew in the great powers through a web of alliances. It saw the first large-scale use of tanks, poison gas and aircraft in war, and trench warfare that bogged down fronts for years.
In 1917 two revolutions ended the tsar's rule and brought the Bolsheviks to power.

In 1917 two revolutions overthrew Russia's government. In February, strikes and protests forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate. In October, the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin seized power from a weak provisional government. A bitter civil war followed, and in 1922 the Soviet Union was formally founded. It would last nearly 70 years and shape the 20th century.
The flu of 1918 to 1920 killed at least 50 million people worldwide.

The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1920 killed at least 50 million people worldwide, more than the First World War, and about a third of the world's population caught it. It's called the Spanish flu only because Spain, neutral in the war, reported freely on it, while other countries censored the news. Unusually, it killed many healthy young adults.
The US stock market crashed in October 1929 and a decade of hardship followed.

In October 1929 the US stock market crashed, and the world sank into the worst economic downturn of the 20th century. By 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed, and thousands of banks failed. President Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal brought programs such as Social Security, bank deposit insurance and new labor laws, many of which remain in place.
The deadliest war in history, 1939 to 1945, killed about 70 to 85 million people.

The war that ran from 1939 to 1945 was the deadliest in history, killing about 70 to 85 million people. It began when Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, and eventually involved most of the world's nations. More than half of those who died were civilians, many of them in the Soviet Union and China. It ended with the surrender of Germany in May 1945 and Japan in August.
The Nazi regime murdered about six million Jews, and millions of others.

Between 1941 and 1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with millions of others, including Roma, disabled people, Poles and Soviet prisoners of war. They used shooting squads, ghettos and extermination camps such as Auschwitz. The Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 held leading Nazis to account, and helped to establish the idea of crimes against humanity.
On June 6, 1944, the Allies landed on the beaches of Normandy.

On June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed on five beaches in Normandy, France, in the largest seaborne invasion in history. About 156,000 troops came ashore on the first day, supported by thousands of ships and aircraft. It opened the Western Front against Nazi Germany, and the Allies pushed on to liberate Paris in August.
The only use of nuclear weapons in war, in August 1945.

In August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima, on August 6, and Nagasaki, on August 9. They remain the only use of nuclear weapons in war. Japan announced its surrender on August 15. Estimates of the number killed in both cities by the end of 1945 range from about 150,000 to 250,000.
Founded in October 1945 by 51 countries to prevent another world war.

The United Nations was founded in October 1945, after the Second World War, by 51 countries, to prevent another such war. It now has 193 member states. In 1948 its General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It set out, for the first time, rights that all people should enjoy.
In 1930 Mohandas Gandhi led a 240-mile walk to the sea to make salt in defiance of British law.

In March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi led a 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi to make salt, in defiance of the British law that gave the government a monopoly on it. The walk lasted 24 days, and thousands joined along the way. The salt tax hurt the poorest most. The march drew world attention to India's independence movement. India became independent in 1947.
In 1954 the US Supreme Court ruled that segregated public schools were unconstitutional.

In 1954 the US Supreme Court ruled unanimously that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional, overturning the doctrine of "separate but equal." The case combined several lawsuits, led by the NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall, who later became the first Black Supreme Court justice. Real integration took many years, and in many places it's still incomplete.
On December 1, 1955, she refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama.

On December 1, 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger, and was arrested. Her act led to a boycott of the city's buses by Black residents that lasted 381 days. It brought a young minister, Martin Luther King Jr., to national leadership, and in 1956 the Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation was unconstitutional.
About 250,000 people gathered on August 28, 1963, where King gave the "I Have a Dream" speech.

On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his "I Have a Dream" speech there. The march helped build support for the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which banned discrimination, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
In October 1962 the US and Soviet Union came close to nuclear war.

In October 1962 an American spy plane found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida. For 13 days, the world held its breath as American ships blockaded the island and leaders threatened war. It ended when the Soviets agreed to remove the missiles in return for an American pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove US missiles from Turkey.
Built in August 1961, it came down on November 9, 1989.

In August 1961 East Germany began building a wall to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West through Berlin. At least 140 people died trying to cross it. On November 9, 1989, after huge protests, East Germany announced that its borders were open, and crowds began to tear the wall down. Germany was reunified in October 1990.
The end of the Soviet Union

On December 25, 1991, Mikhail Gorbachev resigned as president of the Soviet Union, and the next day the Soviet parliament voted the country out of existence. Fifteen new countries emerged, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan. It ended 69 years of Soviet rule and the Cold War that had dominated world politics since the late 1940s.
The first message on the internet
On October 29, 1969, computers at UCLA and Stanford exchanged their first message.

On October 29, 1969, a student programmer at UCLA, Charley Kline, tried to send the word "LOGIN" to a computer at Stanford, over the new ARPANET. The system crashed after the first two letters, so the first message was "LO." An hour later the whole word got through. The network started with four computers, and has grown into billions of devices.
The Altair 8800 of 1975, then the Apple II in 1977 and the IBM PC in 1981.

In 1975 the Altair 8800 kit let hobbyists build their own computers. In 1977 the Apple II, a ready-made machine with color graphics, became a hit, and in 1981 IBM introduced its PC. Together, they moved computers from air-conditioned rooms to ordinary desks and homes. By the 1990s, the World Wide Web gave those computers a reason to be connected.
Steve Jobs introduced it on January 9, 2007, and it went on sale on June 29.

Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone on January 9, 2007, describing it as three products in one: a phone, a music player and an internet device. It went on sale on June 29. Its multi-touch screen replaced the keypad. The App Store opened in 2008, and changed how software is made and sold. Within a few years, smartphones had become part of daily life for billions of people.
Smallpox is the only human disease completely wiped out.

Smallpox is the only human disease that has been completely eradicated. It killed about 300 million people in the 20th century alone. A global vaccination campaign led by the World Health Organization reduced cases until the last natural case was reported in Somalia in 1977. In 1980 the WHO declared the world free of smallpox. It's regarded as one of the greatest achievements in public health.
The share of people in extreme poverty fell from over a third in 1990 to under a tenth by 2019.

In 1990 about 36 percent of the world's population lived in extreme poverty, according to World Bank estimates. By 2019 that had fallen to about 9 percent. The World Bank defines it as living on less than about $2 a day in today's prices. Progress has been uneven, much of it in China and India, and the COVID-19 pandemic reversed some of the gains.
Global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900.

In 1900 the average person in the world could expect to live to around 32. By 2019 it was about 73. Much of the improvement came from fewer children dying young, thanks to clean water, vaccines and antibiotics, along with better nutrition. It's one of the biggest changes in human history, though we tend to forget it because it happened gradually.
The share of adults who can read rose from about 12% in 1820 to about 87% in 2016.

In 1820 only about 12 percent of the world's adults could read and write. By 2016 about 87 percent could. Most of that rise happened in the last century, as schooling spread across the world. Still, around 770 million adults can't read, according to UNESCO, and about two-thirds of them are women.
The first mRNA vaccines were authorized in December 2020, less than a year after the virus was identified.

The first vaccines against COVID-19 to use messenger RNA were authorized in December 2020, less than a year after the virus was identified, faster than any vaccine before. That speed was made possible by decades of earlier research, by scientists such as Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who found how to make mRNA work without triggering harmful inflammation. They received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
The smallest unit of information: a 0 or a 1.

A bit is the smallest piece of information there is: a single choice between two possibilities, a zero or a one. In 1948 the engineer Claude Shannon published a paper that used the bit as the basic unit for measuring information, and his colleague John Tukey is credited with coining the word, from "binary digit." Eight bits make a byte, which can hold 256 different values, enough for one letter of text.
A standard that gives every character in every language a number.

Computers store text as numbers, and for years, different systems used different codes, which made text turn to garbage when moved between them. ASCII, from 1963, had only 128 characters, enough for plain English. Unicode, begun in 1991, set out to give every character in every writing system its own number. It now covers more than 150,000 characters, from Chinese and Arabic to ancient scripts and emoji.
The first set of 176 emoji was drawn in Japan in 1999.

The first set of emoji, 176 of them, was created in 1999 by Shigetaka Kurita, a designer working on a mobile internet service in Japan. Each was drawn on a tiny grid of 12 by 12 pixels. They were meant to convey things like weather and traffic quickly on small screens. The original set is now in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
A precise, step-by-step recipe for solving a problem.

An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step method for solving a problem, one that's clear enough that it can be followed without any guesswork. The word comes from the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. A cooking recipe, a method of sorting names alphabetically and the way your phone finds a route all count. What matters is that each step is unambiguous and that the procedure ends.
A way to describe how a program's running time grows as the input grows.

Programmers use "Big O" notation to describe how a program's running time grows as the amount of data grows. Imagine sorting a million items. A simple method that compares every item with every other takes time proportional to n squared, about a trillion steps. A cleverer method, taking time proportional to n times the logarithm of n, needs only about 20 million. At scale, the choice of method matters far more than the speed of the computer.
A compiler translates a whole program into machine code in advance; an interpreter runs it line by line.

Computers can only run machine code, which is long strings of numbers, so a human-friendly program has to be translated. A compiler translates the whole program in advance and produces a file that the computer can run directly. An interpreter reads and carries out the program line by line as it goes. Grace Hopper wrote an early compiler in 1952. C is typically compiled, Python is usually interpreted, and many systems use a mixture.
The program that manages a computer's hardware and runs the other programs.

The operating system is the program that sits between your applications and the hardware. It decides which program gets the processor, manages memory, files and devices, and gives each application a safe place to run. Unix appeared at Bell Labs in 1969. In 1991 a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, began writing Linux, whose kernel now runs most of the world's servers and Android phones.
A processor carries out instructions, billions of times a second.

The central processor is the part of a computer that carries out instructions, and its speed is measured in how many cycles it completes each second. A 3 gigahertz chip ticks three billion times a second. In one tick, light travels only about 10 centimeters. That's one reason that processors have to be tiny: a signal can't cross a large machine in less time than that.
Graphics chips do many simple calculations at once, which is why they power AI.

A graphics processing unit, or GPU, was designed to draw video game images, which involves doing the same simple calculation for millions of pixels at once. A CPU has a few powerful cores that do one thing after another. A GPU has thousands of small cores that work at the same time.
