Training an artificial neural network involves huge numbers of identical multiplications, and it's an ideal job for a GPU.
RAM is fast and forgets when the power is off; storage is slower and keeps its data.

Computers have several layers of memory. The fastest is the processor's own cache, which takes about a nanosecond to read. Then there's RAM, about a hundred times slower, which loses its contents when the power goes off. Then storage, such as a solid-state drive, which keeps data permanently and is about a thousand times slower again. It's a trade-off between speed, size and cost.
A tiny switch with no moving parts, the building block of every chip.

A transistor is a tiny electronic switch with no moving parts. John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first one at Bell Labs in December 1947, and William Shockley improved the design, and the three shared a Nobel Prize in 1956. It replaced the bulky, hot and unreliable vacuum tube. A modern chip contains tens of billions of them, and the largest hold over 100 billion.
The number of transistors on a chip doubled about every two years.

In 1965 Gordon Moore, who later cofounded Intel, noticed that the number of transistors that could be put on a chip was doubling regularly, and predicted that it would continue. In 1975 he revised the pace to about every two years. It held for decades, and made computers ever faster and cheaper. It has been slowing in recent years, as the parts get close to the size of only a few atoms.
They are not the same thing.

People often use the two words as if they meant the same, but they don't. The internet is the global network of connected computers, which began as a standard way for networks to talk when the TCP/IP protocol was adopted on January 1, 1983. The World Wide Web is a system of linked pages and sites that runs on top of the internet. Email and online games use the internet but not the web.
Data is cut into small packets that travel separately and are reassembled.

The internet doesn't send a message as one continuous stream. It breaks it into small packets, each of which finds its own way across the network and is reassembled at the other end. The idea was developed in the 1960s by Paul Baran in the US and Donald Davies in Britain. It makes the network robust, because if one route fails, the packets just take another.
Every device has a number, and DNS turns names into numbers.

Every device on the internet has a numerical address, like 142.250.80.46, but nobody wants to remember those. The Domain Name System, or DNS, works like a phone book: when you type a website's name, a DNS server looks up the matching number and your computer connects to it. Paul Mockapetris invented it in 1983. If DNS went down, you'd be able to reach websites only by typing their numbers.
It means your connection is private, not that the site is honest.

The padlock in the address bar means that the connection between your browser and the website is encrypted, so that nobody in between can read or alter what you send. It doesn't mean the site is trustworthy. Scammers can get the padlock for fake sites, too. It's wise to check the address itself, and to be careful about links in messages, whether or not you see a padlock.
About 99% of international internet traffic travels along cables on the ocean floor.

It feels like the internet is in the air, but about 99 percent of international data travels through cables lying on the ocean floor. There are hundreds of them, adding up to well over a million kilometers, and they link all the continents except Antarctica. Each carries many fibers and is only about as thick as a garden hose. Ships' anchors and fishing nets are the main hazards.
A way to send secrets to someone you have never met.

How can you send a secret to someone you've never met, without first sharing a secret key? Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published an answer in 1976, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created the RSA method. Each person has two keys, a public one to lock messages and a private one to unlock them. British codebreakers at GCHQ had found the idea earlier, but it was kept secret until 1997.
A one-way fingerprint of data: easy to compute, practically impossible to reverse.

A hash function turns any piece of data into a short, fixed-length fingerprint. It's easy to compute, and practically impossible to reverse. Change even one letter of the input, and the hash changes completely. Websites should store hashes of your password, not the password itself, so that even if the database is stolen, the passwords aren't directly revealed. Hashes are also used to check that a file hasn't been altered.
A second proof of identity, besides your password.

A password is something you know. A second factor is something you have, like your phone, or something you are, like a fingerprint. A 2019 study by Google found that even a simple text-message code blocked 100 percent of automated bot attacks, 96 percent of bulk phishing attacks and 76 percent of targeted attacks. App prompts and security keys did even better. It's one of the best things you can do to protect an account.
A long passphrase is stronger than a short string full of symbols.

For years we were told to use short passwords with symbols and numbers, and to change them often. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology revised its advice in 2017. It recommended against forced regular changes and strange character requirements, since they push people into predictable patterns. Instead, long passphrases are better, and passwords should be checked against lists of known leaked ones.
Fake messages that trick people into giving up logins or money.

Phishing is when an attacker sends a message that looks like it's from a bank, a delivery company or a coworker, to trick you into giving up a password or sending money. In Verizon's 2023 report on data breaches, about 74 percent involved a human element, such as a mistake, stolen credentials or social engineering. The best defense is to slow down, and to go to the real website yourself, instead of clicking the link.
The first mass unsolicited email went out in 1978.

On May 3, 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketer at Digital Equipment Corporation, sent an advertisement for a new computer to about 400 people on ARPANET, the forerunner of the internet. Many recipients were annoyed. The word "spam" for unwanted messages came later, from a Monty Python sketch in which the word is repeated over and over until it drowns out everything else.
Someone else's computers, rented by the hour.

"The cloud" is a friendly name for other people's computers. Instead of buying and running their own servers, companies and individuals rent computing power and storage over the internet from big data centers, paying for what they use. Amazon launched its cloud services in 2006. When you store photos online or stream a movie, they're sitting in a data center somewhere, probably far from you.
A set of rules that lets one program ask another for something.

An API, or application programming interface, is a set of rules that allows one program to ask another for something. It's like a waiter in a restaurant: you order from a menu, the waiter takes your request to the kitchen, and brings back the food. You never have to go into the kitchen yourself. When a weather app shows a forecast, it probably asks a weather service's API for the data.
Data is stored in tables that can be linked.

In 1970 Edgar Codd, a researcher at IBM, proposed storing data in simple tables of rows and columns that can be linked to each other by shared values. It was a big change from earlier, more tangled systems. A query language called SQL grew from his idea, and it still underlies most business software today, from bank records to online shopping.
Software that records every change and who made it.

Version control software keeps a record of every change made to a set of files, who made it, and when, so that you can go back to any earlier version. Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005, in about two weeks, after a dispute over the tool that the Linux project had been using. Git lets thousands of people work on the same project at once, and merge their changes.
Software whose code anyone can read, use and improve.

Open-source software is software whose code is publicly available for anyone to read, use, modify and share. The term was chosen in 1998. Much of the internet runs on it: Linux powers most web servers, and the Android phone system is built on it. Wikipedia, begun in 2001, applied a similar spirit of open, collaborative work to encyclopedias.
A rocket blew up 37 seconds after launch in 1996, from a number that did not fit.

On June 4, 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket, built by the European Space Agency, veered off course and blew up 37 seconds after launch. The cause was a software bug. A program reused from the older Ariane 4 tried to squeeze a large number into a space that was too small for it. That caused a shutdown of the guidance system. The rocket and its cargo were worth about $370 million.
Computers stored years as two digits, and later, seconds in a 32-bit number.

Many old computer programs stored years as two digits, so that 2000 would look like 1900. It set off a worldwide effort to repair them, which cost hundreds of billions of dollars, and when the new year arrived in 2000, most systems worked. A similar problem looms for systems that count seconds from 1970 in a 32-bit number. It will run out on January 19, 2038, and older systems will need to be fixed.
A radiation machine overdosed patients in the 1980s because of a software flaw.

The Therac-25 was a radiation therapy machine used in hospitals in the 1980s. Between 1985 and 1987 it delivered massive overdoses to at least six patients, and at least three of them died. The software had a flaw called a race condition, which occurred when an operator typed quickly, and the older hardware safety locks, which would have stopped it, had been removed. It's a classic case study in software safety.
A firm lost $440 million in 45 minutes in 2012 because of a software mistake.

On August 1, 2012, the trading firm Knight Capital installed new software on its servers but, by mistake, put it on only seven of its eight machines. The eighth still had old code, which started buying and selling stocks wildly. In 45 minutes the firm lost about $440 million, nearly all of its capital, and it nearly went out of business. The SEC later fined it.
Programs that learn patterns from examples instead of following written rules.

Traditionally, programmers write rules telling a computer what to do. In machine learning, you show the program many examples and let it find the patterns itself. To make a spam filter, for instance, you show it thousands of spam and non-spam emails. Arthur Samuel used the term in 1959 for a checkers program that got better by playing against itself.
Layers of simple units whose connections are adjusted by training.

An artificial neural network is made up of layers of simple units, loosely inspired by brain cells, whose connections are adjusted during training. Frank Rosenblatt built an early one, the perceptron, in 1958. A 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams showed how to train deeper networks. In 2012 a network called AlexNet cut the error rate in an image-recognition contest from 26 percent to 15 percent, and launched the modern deep-learning boom.
A model that memorizes its training examples fails on new ones.

An overfitted model has memorized its training examples, including their quirks and errors, and so it does badly on new data. It's like a student who memorizes the answers to past exams without understanding the subject, and then fails when the questions change. The remedy is to test the model on data it has never seen, and to keep the model from being more complicated than it needs to be.
Training is the long process of learning; inference is using what was learned.

There are two phases in an AI model's life. Training is the long, expensive process in which it learns from data, which for a large model can take weeks on thousands of specialized chips. Inference is using the finished model, such as when you ask it a question. That takes a fraction of a second. Most of the cost of running a popular system comes from many people using it, rather than from the one-time training.
A system trained on unrepresentative data can work much worse for some groups.

An AI system learns from its training data, and if that data doesn't represent everyone, it can work much worse for some groups. In 2018 the researchers Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested commercial face-analysis programs in the Gender Shades study. The error rate was as high as 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women, compared with 0.8 percent for lighter-skinned men. The study led several companies to improve their systems.
Programs that predict the next word, trained on huge amounts of text.

A large language model is a program trained on enormous amounts of text to predict the next word, again and again, which lets it produce fluent writing, answer questions and carry on a conversation. Most are built on the transformer design introduced in the 2017 paper "Attention Is All You Need." They can be astonishingly capable, but fluent writing isn't the same as accurate writing.
When an AI states something false with total confidence.

When an AI language model states something false with complete confidence, such as a made-up quotation or a nonexistent book, it's called a hallucination. The reason is that these models produce text that's likely, given their training, rather than text that's been checked against facts. It's wise to verify any names, numbers, quotes and citations that an AI gives you, particularly when it matters.
A language model reads chunks of words, and can only consider so many at a time.

A language model doesn't read letters or whole words. It reads chunks called tokens, and a token is roughly three-quarters of an English word. The model can only consider a certain amount of text at once, known as its context window. It's like the model's working memory: if something falls outside the window, the model can't see it, however important it was earlier in the conversation.
Can a machine's conversation be told apart from a human's?

In 1950 Alan Turing proposed an "imitation game": if a person chatting by text can't tell whether they're talking to a machine or a human, the machine could be said to think. In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum wrote ELIZA, a very simple program that rephrased what people typed, like a therapist. Some users became convinced that it understood them, an effect now known as the ELIZA effect.
Computers beat the best human chess player in 1997 and the best Go player in 2016.

In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match, the first time a computer beat a reigning champion under tournament conditions. The ancient game of Go was thought to be much harder for computers, because there are so many possible moves. But in 2016 Google DeepMind's AlphaGo beat the top player Lee Sedol four games to one.
An AI that predicts the shape of proteins from their chemical sequence.

A protein's function depends on its three-dimensional shape, which comes from how a chain of amino acids folds, and working it out by experiment can take months or years. Biologists had tried to predict it from the sequence for 50 years. In 2020 DeepMind's AlphaFold matched experimental accuracy for many proteins. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, with David Baker, for this work.
A shared record that many computers keep and no one can quietly edit.

A blockchain is a shared record, kept by many computers, in which new entries are linked to the earlier ones so that no one can quietly change history. It was invented for Bitcoin, which was described in 2008 by a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. Beyond digital currencies, few uses have proved better than an ordinary database, so its broader value is still debated.
Computers that use quantum effects to solve certain problems much faster.

A quantum computer uses the strange effects of quantum physics, such as superposition, to tackle certain problems far faster than ordinary computers. In 1994 Peter Shor showed that a large enough quantum computer could break the public-key encryption that protects much of the internet. Today's machines are small and error-prone, and such a computer doesn't exist yet. Researchers are already developing encryption that would resist it.
Satellites broadcast the time, and your phone works out where you are.

The Global Positioning System works by satellites that broadcast signals with the exact time. Your phone listens to several of them and, from the tiny differences in arrival times, works out how far it is from each. To fix its position in three dimensions and to correct its own clock error, it needs signals from at least four satellites. The system is run by the US Space Force and is free for anyone to use.
A square barcode invented for tracking car parts.

The QR code was invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at the Japanese company Denso Wave, to track car parts in factories. It can hold much more than a traditional barcode, and it can be read from any angle. Built-in error correction means that a code can still be read even if up to about 30 percent of it is damaged or covered, which is why a code with a logo in the middle still works.
The wireless standard is named for a Danish king.

The wireless technology is named for Harald Bluetooth Gormsson, a Danish king who ruled around 960 and is said to have united Denmark and Norway. Engineers who were working on a standard to connect different devices chose the name, first as a code name, because the technology was meant to unite devices. The Bluetooth logo is a combination of the runic letters for H and B, his initials.
The name is not an abbreviation.

You might assume that Wi-Fi stands for "wireless fidelity," but it doesn't. In 1999 the industry group that certifies the technology hired a branding agency, Interbrand, to come up with a catchy name for what was technically called IEEE 802.11. Wi-Fi was chosen because it sounded like "hi-fi." The invented tagline "wireless fidelity" was used for a while, but it was never what the name meant.
A pack of chewing gum was the first item scanned, on June 26, 1974.

At 8:01 a.m. on June 26, 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a cashier scanned the first product with a barcode: a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum. The pack is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Barcodes were slow to catch on, but they went on to change how stores and warehouses track goods.
Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email in 1971 and chose "@" to separate the user from the computer.

In 1971 Ray Tomlinson, an engineer working on ARPANET, sent the first email between two computers, and chose the @ sign to separate the user's name from the computer's name. He picked it because it was on the keyboard and wasn't used in anyone's name. He later said the test message was probably something like "QWERTYUIOP," and that he couldn't remember exactly.
The more choices you give, the longer it takes to decide.

The more options you offer, the longer it takes a person to decide. In 1952 William Hick showed that decision time rises with the logarithm of the number of choices. It's a reason to keep menus short, and to group options into categories. A screen with twenty buttons will slow down most users compared with one that shows a few and tucks the rest behind a clear label.
The time to reach a target depends on how far it is and how big it is.

The time it takes to reach a target depends on how far away it is and how big it is. Paul Fitts described the rule in 1954, while studying pilots' movements. It explains why buttons should be large, and why items at the edge or corner of a screen are easy to hit: the cursor can't go past the edge, so you can just fling it there.
Interface tricks that push you into things you didn't mean to do.

A dark pattern is a design trick that pushes people into doing something they didn't intend. The designer Harry Brignull coined the term in 2010. Examples include an unsubscribe link hidden in tiny gray type, boxes that are already ticked to add extras to your order, and countdown timers that reset when they reach zero. Some regulators have begun to treat them as illegal.
Systems end up mirroring the organization that built them.

In 1968 the computer scientist Melvin Conway observed that organizations tend to produce systems that mirror their own communication structure. His example: if four groups work on a compiler, you'll get a compiler with four passes. If departments in a company don't talk to each other, the software they build won't work smoothly together either. To fix the software, you may have to fix the organization.
Quick fixes now that cost extra effort later.

In 1992 the programmer Ward Cunningham used a financial metaphor to describe the cost of shortcuts in software. Writing a quick fix now is like taking out a loan: you get speed today, but you pay interest later, in the form of code that's harder to change. That can be a smart trade-off if you pay it back soon. If you never do, the interest builds up until it's hard to make any progress.
Making code fast before knowing it matters wastes time.

Donald Knuth wrote in 1974 that "premature optimization is the root of all evil," and it's become a famous warning to programmers. Making code fast before you know where the bottleneck is wastes time and often makes the code harder to read. But the full quote is more balanced: he said that we should forget about small efficiencies 97 percent of the time, yet not pass up our opportunities in the critical 3 percent.
Explaining your code line by line to a rubber duck helps you find the bug.

Programmers have a trick for finding bugs: explain your code, line by line, to a rubber duck on your desk. Saying the problem out loud forces you to state your assumptions, and often you notice the mistake in the middle of the explanation. The practice was described in the 1999 book The Pragmatic Programmer, and a duck isn't required. A patient colleague or a pet also works.
Accidents happen when holes in several layers of defense line up.

In 1990 the psychologist James Reason proposed picturing the defenses against accidents as slices of Swiss cheese, each with holes. A single hole doesn't lead to disaster, because the next slice blocks it. But sometimes the holes in several layers line up, and a hazard passes straight through. The lesson is to add more layers of defense, and to keep fixing the holes. It's used in aviation, medicine and many other fields.
In very complex, tightly linked systems, some accidents are inevitable.

After the Three Mile Island nuclear accident in 1979, the sociologist Charles Perrow argued in his 1984 book that in systems that are both very complex and tightly coupled, with no slack, some accidents are inevitable. Parts interact in ways that no one expected, and failures spread faster than anyone can respond. Not everyone agrees that this means accidents can't be reduced, but the idea has been very influential.
After a failure, ask what allowed it, not who to blame.

When something goes wrong, the natural reaction is to ask who was at fault. Engineering teams at companies such as Google and Etsy found that punishing people for mistakes made them hide problems, which made failures worse. Many now hold blameless postmortems, asking "how did our system allow this to happen?" instead of "whose fault was it?" People report problems earlier, and the system gets safer.
In 1981 two hanging walkways collapsed in Kansas City, killing 114 people.

On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways in the lobby of the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City collapsed during a dance, killing 114 people. The cause was a change to the design that was made during construction, in how the walkway rods were attached, which doubled the load on a critical connection. No one rechecked the calculations. It's a standard example in engineering ethics classes.
Rechargeable batteries that power phones, laptops and electric cars.

The rechargeable batteries in phones, laptops and electric cars were developed over several decades. Stanley Whittingham made the first working lithium battery in the 1970s, John Goodenough doubled its voltage in 1980, and Akira Yoshino made a safe, practical version in 1985. Sony began selling them in 1991. The three shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The average cost of electricity from new large solar farms fell about 85% between 2010 and 2020.

According to the International Renewable Energy Agency, the average cost of electricity from new utility-scale solar power fell by about 85 percent between 2010 and 2020. A mix of larger production, learning by doing and better manufacturing brought the cost down. In many places, solar is now among the cheapest sources of new electricity, cheaper than building new coal or gas plants.
The guidance computer for the Moon landings had about 4 kilobytes of working memory.

The guidance computer that helped land astronauts on the Moon in 1969 had 2,048 words of erasable memory and 36,864 words of fixed memory, about 4 kilobytes of working memory in modern terms. It weighed about 32 kilograms. A modern phone has millions of times more memory. It was reliable, and it famously handled a series of alarms during the Apollo 11 landing without crashing.
Light travels about 30 centimeters in one billionth of a second.

Light travels about 30 centimeters, roughly a foot, in one billionth of a second. The computer scientist Grace Hopper used to hand out pieces of wire cut to that length when she gave lectures, to show people why speed is limited. A signal can't cross a large machine in less time than that. It's why smaller, closer components make faster computers.
The first known computer worm built to cause physical damage.

Stuxnet was a computer worm discovered in 2010 and designed to attack industrial equipment. It targeted centrifuges used to enrich uranium at an Iranian nuclear plant, making them spin out of control while showing normal readings to the operators. It's widely believed to have been created by the United States and Israel, though neither has officially confirmed it. It was the first known digital weapon to cause physical damage.
One of the first electronic general-purpose computers, unveiled in 1946.

The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946, was one of the first general-purpose electronic computers. It filled a large room, weighed about 30 tons and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes. Its first programmers were six women, including Jean Bartik and Betty Holberton, who had to figure out how to program it by wiring and switching, with little documentation.
Adults are advised 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle work on two days.

The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines say that adults should aim for 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening work on two days. But the guidelines also stress that any activity is better than none. If you can't hit the target, doing even a little less still brings most of the benefit, so don't treat it as all or nothing.
The round number came from a 1960s Japanese pedometer ad, not from research.

The round number didn't come from research. It seems to have started with a Japanese pedometer sold in the mid-1960s, called Manpo-kei, which means "10,000 steps meter." It's often said that the number was chosen partly because the character for 10,000 looks like a person walking. When researchers looked at actual health data in 2022, they found that the risk of early death fell until about 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day for adults over 60, and 8,000 to 10,000 for younger adults. More is fine, but the gains level off.
Meeting the exercise guidelines goes with living about three years longer.

In 2012 researchers pooled data from six large studies covering about 650,000 people. They found that people who got about 150 minutes a week of brisk walking, the recommended minimum, had a life expectancy 3.4 years longer than those who got none. That's an association, not proof of cause, since healthier people may exercise more. But the pattern is strong and consistent across many studies.
We lose muscle gradually from about age 30, unless we use it.

After about age 30, we gradually lose muscle mass, at a rate of roughly 3 to 8 percent per decade, unless we do something about it. The loss is called sarcopenia, and it speeds up in later life, which affects balance, strength and independence. Strength training, such as lifting weights or using resistance bands twice a week, can slow or even reverse it, at any age, and it's linked with a lower risk of early death.
Soreness peaks one to three days after a workout, and lactic acid is not the cause.

The ache that peaks a day or two after an unfamiliar workout is called delayed-onset muscle soreness. It used to be blamed on lactic acid building up, but lactate clears from muscles within an hour or so of exercise. The soreness is thought to come from tiny tears in muscle fibers and the inflammation that follows. It fades as your body adapts, which is why the same workout hurts less the next time.
Long unbroken sitting is linked with health risks, and short walks break it up.

Long stretches of unbroken sitting have been linked to health risks. In one 2012 experiment, people who got up for just a couple of minutes of light walking every 20 minutes had lower blood sugar and insulin levels after meals than those who sat the whole time. How much of sitting's harm is separate from simply not exercising is still debated. Either way, getting up often does no harm.
The best-supported first treatment for chronic insomnia is not a pill but a talking therapy.

For chronic insomnia, the best-supported first treatment isn't a sleeping pill. It's a form of talking therapy called CBT for insomnia, which the American College of Physicians recommended as first-line treatment in 2016. It includes keeping a fixed wake-up time, limiting the time you spend awake in bed, and changing anxious thoughts about sleep. It helps most people, and its benefits last longer than those of sleeping pills.
The most useful sleep habit may be waking at the same time every day.

If you could change just one thing about your sleep habits, a good choice might be to wake at the same time every day, including weekends. It anchors your body clock, which makes it easier to feel sleepy at the right time in the evening. Sleeping in for hours on days off creates a kind of "social jetlag," as if you'd flown across time zones, and it's one reason Monday mornings feel so hard.
A drink can help you fall asleep and still ruin the night.

A drink or two may make it easier to fall asleep, which is why many people use it. But as your body breaks down the alcohol during the night, it disrupts sleep. It reduces REM sleep, the stage when most dreaming occurs, and it fragments the second half of the night. You may not remember waking, but the sleep is lighter and less restful, and you often feel tired the next day.
Sleep is easier at a lower room temperature, around 60 to 67 degrees Fahrenheit.

Most sleep experts recommend a bedroom temperature of about 60 to 67 degrees Fahrenheit, or roughly 15 to 19 degrees Celsius. Your core body temperature naturally falls as you go to sleep, and a cool room helps that happen. The range comes from sleep medicine guidance rather than a single study, and comfort varies from person to person. Heavy blankets and a cool room often work better than a warm room and light covers.
Is the glow of screens ruining sleep?

It's a common worry that the glow from phones and tablets is ruining our sleep. Bright light late in the evening does delay the body clock, and blue-rich light does so a bit more. A 2014 study found that reading on a light-emitting e-reader before bed delayed the release of melatonin. But the effect of typical screens in real life seems small, and what you're doing on the screen, whether it's exciting or stressful, may matter as much.
A hormone that signals night to the body, not a sedative.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain releases at night to signal that it's dark, and the pills are often taken as sleep aids. But it isn't really a sedative. It works best for shifting the body clock, as with jet lag or for people who go to sleep very late. Small doses, around 0.5 to 3 milligrams, work as well as large ones, and tests have found that the amounts in supplements vary widely from what's on the label.
There is no scientific basis for "drink eight glasses of water a day".

You've probably heard that you should drink eight glasses of water a day. There's no scientific basis for it. It may trace to a 1945 recommendation of about 2.5 liters a day, which also noted that most of that is already in prepared foods. Needs vary with your size, the weather and how active you are. For most healthy people, thirst is a good guide, and tea, coffee and fruit all count.
Sugar does not make children hyperactive.

Many parents are sure that sugar makes children hyper. But when scientists tested it in controlled trials, giving some children sugar and others a sugar-free placebo without anyone knowing which, there was no effect on behavior. A 1995 review of 23 such studies found nothing, even in children who were said to be sensitive. In another experiment, parents who were told that their child had had sugar rated the child as more hyperactive, though they hadn't.
Adults need at least 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day.

The official recommended minimum for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day, which works out to about 56 grams for a person of 70 kilograms, or 154 pounds. Some experts argue for more, especially for older adults, who absorb protein less efficiently, and for people who lift weights. It's easy to meet from foods like beans, eggs, fish, dairy and meat.
Most Americans eat only about half the fiber recommended.

Fiber is the part of plants that your body can't digest, and it's good for your gut and your heart. Experts recommend about 25 grams a day for women and 38 for men, but the average American eats only about 16. Beans, oats, vegetables, fruit and whole grains are good sources. Diets high in fiber are linked with a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers.
In a tightly controlled trial, people ate more on an ultra-processed diet.

In a 2019 study at the US National Institutes of Health, 20 volunteers lived in a research center for a month. For two weeks they ate meals made mostly of ultra-processed foods, and for two weeks, mostly unprocessed foods, with the menus matched for calories, sugar, fat and fiber on offer. On the ultra-processed diet, they ate about 500 more calories a day, and gained about a kilogram in two weeks.
A pattern rich in vegetables, olive oil, fish, nuts and legumes lowers heart risk.

A pattern of eating rich in vegetables, olive oil, fish, nuts and legumes, with little red meat, has among the best evidence for protecting the heart. The 2013 PREDIMED trial in Spain found that it cut major heart events by about 30 percent. The paper was retracted in 2018 because of problems with how some participants had been randomized, then reanalyzed and republished with similar results.
The claim that breakfast is the most important meal is not well supported.

"Breakfast is the most important meal of the day" was popularized, in part, by cereal marketing. When researchers reviewed the trials in 2019, they found that eating breakfast didn't help people lose weight, and that those who ate it tended to consume slightly more calories overall. Whether you eat breakfast matters less than what you eat during the day. If you're hungry in the morning, eat; if not, there's no need to force it.
Eating only in certain hours leads to weight loss, but not better than ordinary dieting.

Eating only during a limited window, say eight hours a day, has become very popular. In a 2022 trial of 139 people with obesity, one group ate within an eight-hour window and another simply counted calories. After a year, there was no difference in weight loss. Time-restricted eating works for people who find it easier, but the best plan is the one that you can stick with.
Taking vitamin D does not prevent cancer or heart disease in people who are not deficient.

Vitamin D is essential, and many people take supplements hoping to prevent disease. But in the large VITAL trial, 25,871 healthy adults took 2,000 units a day or a placebo for about five years. There was no reduction in cancer or heart disease. People who are actually deficient do need vitamin D, which a blood test can show, but for everyone else, extra pills don't seem to add protection.
Vitamin C does not prevent colds for most people.

Vitamin C has a long reputation as a cold preventer, popularized by the chemist Linus Pauling. A Cochrane review of dozens of trials found that taking it regularly doesn't prevent colds in most people. It does shorten them slightly, by about 8 percent in adults. The one exception is people under heavy physical stress, such as marathon runners and skiers, among whom it halved the risk.
For healthy adults, a daily multivitamin has not been shown to prevent disease.

A multivitamin is a popular daily habit. In 2022 the US Preventive Services Task Force reviewed the evidence and concluded that there isn't enough to say whether most vitamin and mineral supplements prevent cancer or heart disease in healthy adults. They haven't been shown to do harm at normal doses, but a balanced diet comes first. Some people, such as pregnant women, do need particular supplements.
Supplements of omega-3 fats have not shown heart benefits in large trials.

Eating fish twice a week is linked with better health, so fish oil capsules seem like a natural idea. But in large trials of healthy people, including VITAL and ASCEND, omega-3 supplements didn't reduce heart attacks or strokes. It may be that the benefit comes from eating fish in place of other foods, or from other nutrients in it. For people with very high triglycerides, a prescription form can help.
Twenty seconds with soap removes most germs.

The CDC recommends washing your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, which is about as long as humming "Happy Birthday" twice. Scrub the backs of your hands, between your fingers and under your nails. Soap and friction lift germs from the skin, so they're rinsed away. If you can't wash, an alcohol-based sanitizer with at least 60 percent alcohol is a good second choice.
Do cold weather and wet hair cause colds?
Colds come from viruses, not from chill.

Your grandmother may have told you to dry your hair or you'd catch a cold. Colds are caused by viruses, not by chill. But there may be a grain of truth. Cooling of the nose can weaken its defenses against viruses such as rhinovirus, and in winter, people gather indoors, where germs spread. Going out with wet hair doesn't cause an infection by itself, but it may make you more vulnerable if a virus is present.
About 95% of people need to be immune to stop measles spreading.

When enough people in a community are immune, a disease can't spread easily, and even those who can't be vaccinated are protected. For measles, which is extremely contagious, about 95 percent of people need to be immune. One infected person can pass it on to 12 to 18 unprotected people. That's why even a small fall in vaccination rates can lead to outbreaks.
SPF 30 blocks about 97% of the sun's burning UVB rays.

A sunscreen of SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of the burning UVB rays, and SPF 50 blocks about 98 percent, so the gain beyond 30 is small. In an Australian trial in the 1990s, people told to use sunscreen daily had about half as many invasive melanomas, the most dangerous skin cancer, as the others, after about ten years of follow-up. Reapply every two hours and after swimming, as no sunscreen blocks everything.
Stopping before age 40 gains back nearly all the years lost.

In a large study published in 2013, researchers followed more than 200,000 American adults. Smokers who quit between the ages of 25 and 34 gained about ten years of life compared with those who kept smoking, essentially reaching the life expectancy of those who'd never smoked. Quitting between 35 and 44 gained about nine years, and between 45 and 54, about six. Even those who quit at 65 gained some years.
The World Health Organization says no level of alcohol is entirely safe.

In 2023 the World Health Organization stated that no level of alcohol consumption is entirely safe for health. For years, studies suggested that moderate drinking might protect the heart. But a 2016 analysis found that the apparent benefit mostly disappeared when it was taken into account that the "non-drinkers" in many studies included former drinkers who'd quit because of illness, which made abstainers look unhealthy.
The average is a bit below 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

The "normal" body temperature of 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit came from a huge study of about 25,000 people by the German doctor Carl Wunderlich in the 1850s. Modern measurements find the average is lower, about 97.5 to 97.9, and a 2020 study found that the average in the US has been drifting downward, by about 0.03 degrees Celsius for each decade of birth. It also varies by time of day and between people.
Normal blood pressure is below 120 over 80.

Blood pressure is written as two numbers, such as 120 over 80. The top number is the pressure in your arteries as the heart beats, and the bottom is the pressure between beats. Normal is below 120 over 80. High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so the only way to know is to have it measured. It's a major risk factor for heart disease and stroke, and it's treatable.

The idea that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis is a persistent myth. The popping sound comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid. A doctor named Donald Unger cracked the knuckles of his left hand, but not his right, at least twice a day for more than 60 years, to test it. He found no arthritis in either hand, and he received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2009.
Gum does not stay in the stomach for seven years.

You may have heard that swallowed gum stays in your stomach for seven years. That's false. Gum base isn't digested like other food, but the gut moves it along like other indigestible things, such as seeds or fiber, and it passes out within a few days. Swallowing gum occasionally isn't dangerous, though an excessive amount in a small child can cause a blockage.

It's a classic scary story that hair and nails keep growing after death. They don't. Growth requires the energy supply of living cells. What happens is that skin dries out and pulls back, which exposes more of the nails and the stubble on a face, and makes them look longer. This is the origin of the myth.
Press hard and fast on the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute.

In cardiopulmonary resuscitation, you push hard and fast on the center of the chest, about 100 to 120 times a minute, to keep blood flowing to the brain. The Bee Gees song "Stayin' Alive" has about 103 beats per minute, and in one study, people who practiced to it kept good pace. If you see someone collapse, call emergency services first, and use an automated external defibrillator if there's one nearby.
Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services.

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts. The acronym FAST helps you recognize it: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. Treatment works best within a few hours. On average, the brain loses about 1.9 million neurons for each minute that a stroke goes untreated, which is why doctors say "time is brain."
Women more often have symptoms other than chest pain.

The classic picture of a heart attack, crushing chest pain and pain down the left arm, is more typical of men. Women, while they often do have chest discomfort too, are more likely to have other symptoms: unusual tiredness, nausea, shortness of breath, or pain in the jaw, neck or back. Because the signs can be less obvious, women sometimes delay getting help. Any of these symptoms deserves a call for help.
Drowning rarely looks like thrashing and shouting.

In films, drowning looks like a person thrashing and shouting. In reality, it's usually silent. A person in trouble can't call out because they need all their breath just to breathe. Their arms tend to press down on the water, they stay upright, and it can take as little as 20 to 60 seconds. It's why parents are advised to watch children near water constantly, and not to rely on hearing a splash or a cry.
Pain is not the same as damage
How much it hurts depends on more than how much is injured.

How much something hurts depends on much more than how badly the body is hurt. The brain decides how to interpret signals from the body, and mood, attention, past experience and the situation all change the result. Soldiers with serious wounds sometimes report little pain, and people with no visible damage can have severe pain. Both are real. Understanding this can be a helpful part of managing chronic pain.
Spending about two hours a week in nature is linked with better health and well-being.

In a 2019 survey of nearly 20,000 people in England, those who spent at least 120 minutes a week in green spaces, such as parks and woods, were significantly more likely to report good health and high well-being than people who spent none. There was no benefit with less than that. It didn't matter if the time was in one long visit or several short ones. It's a measure of association, but it fits other research.
Sitting in front of a very bright light in the morning helps seasonal depression.

Some people become depressed each winter, when the days are short. In 1984 the psychiatrist Norman Rosenthal and colleagues described the condition, which they called seasonal affective disorder. A common treatment is to sit in front of a special lamp that gives off 10,000 lux of bright light for about 30 minutes in the morning. It has helped many people, and is considered a first-line treatment for the condition.
Live bacteria in food or pills help some conditions, but claims run ahead of evidence.

Probiotics are live bacteria in foods like yogurt or in supplements, and they're marketed for all kinds of health benefits. The evidence is good for a few things, such as preventing diarrhea that's caused by antibiotics. For general gut health in healthy people, though, results are mixed and depend on the specific strain. Claims on labels often run ahead of what research can support.
Slouching has not been shown to cause back pain.

We're often told to sit up straight to avoid back pain. But reviews of the research haven't found a strong link between slouching and pain. A more useful rule may be that the best posture is the next one: changing position regularly, instead of staying in any one posture for a long time. And for back pain that you already have, staying active generally helps more than resting in bed.
Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

To reduce eye strain from long stretches at a screen, eye doctors suggest this rule: every 20 minutes, look at something at least 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Remembering to blink fully also helps, since we blink much less when staring at screens. The research for the exact numbers is limited, but taking regular breaks from close-up work is sensible and does reduce discomfort.
Holding a stretch for a long time right before lifting or sprinting may briefly reduce power.

Holding a stretch for a long time before lifting weights or sprinting has been found in some studies to briefly reduce muscle power and performance. A better way to prepare is a dynamic warm-up: light movements that resemble the activity, like leg swings, lunges or easy jogging, which raise your temperature and heart rate. Stretching is still useful for building flexibility over weeks, just not as a warm-up.
